#3560. Superman Director James Gunn Explains Departure As DC Studios Co-Head

When the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merger was completed a little over a month ago, questions about the direction of the newly-established mega company Skydance, the formation of which required massive investments from Elon Musk, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi, were myriad. For moviegoers, one of the biggest concerns was the future of the DC Universe. Co-executives James Gunn and Peter Safran had been at the helm for four years, and the results were mixed. Gunn's "Superman" was a blockbuster, while "Peacemaker," "Creature Commandos," "Lanterns," and "Clayface" were popular with fans. They stumbled badly with Craig Gillespie's critical and commercial flop "Supergirl," but a course correction seemed to be on the horizon with the Man of Steel sequel "Man of Tomorrow."

Evidently, something or someone changed Ellison's mind over the last month because Gunn and Safran are out. It's a stunning reversal of fortune for the duo, but at least Gunn and Safran had time to write this statement:

"Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with 'Peacemaker,' 'Creature Commandos,' 'Lanterns,' and 'Clayface.' We're immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews, and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We've shared a creative history with [new DC Studios head] Jeremy [Latcham] going back to Marvel, and we're eager to see the perspective he brings to DC's next chapter. We're excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex's journey in 'Man of Tomorrow.'"

James Gunn also took to Instagram to issue his own statement. He thanked fans for their support, adding:

"When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri, I used to write and draw my own comics with a mix of DC Comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn't know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn't pass up the unique opportunity. I'm glad I took the job."

Yet, despite the "highs" of "Superman," "Clayface," and the upcoming "The People vs. Gorilla Grodd" and "Man of Tomorrow" (which he called "the best experience of my life"), Gunn admitted that he disliked "the at-times corporate nature of the job." He then apologized to his wife Jennifer Holland for being preoccupied with the massively demanding gig of being a filmmaker and a studio executive, explaining:

"And the thing my ADHD hyperfocus has had the most difficulty with has been dividing my time between projects I'm incredibly passionate about and the ones I'm not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head."

Maybe that's why he didn't mention "Supergirl" in either statement? Anyway, Gunn closed out his statement by saying he's excited to get back to "pure filmmaking," which suggests to me that he's eager to make a non-superhero movie for the first time since 2006's gleefully gross alien horror comedy "Slither." (Admittedly, Gunn's 2010 film "Super" wasn't a traditional superhero movie, but it was a riff on the genre.) I wish him the best, and congratulate him for not having to work for David Ellison much longer.

Since Sir Patrick Stewart’s passing, I have spent a great deal of time reading stories from his co-stars about his work and impact. It’s lovely to see tributes continue to pour in, but the sentiments that have truly hit me in my feels have come from Ian McKellen, Stewart's longtime best friend (and sometimes on-screen nemesis). While Sir McKellen broke his silence weeks ago, he just shared additional thoughts on his late comrade, and I may or may not need a tissue.

While Stewart and McKellen battled on the big screen as X-Men's Professor X and Magneto, respectively, the two seem inseparable in real life. They were actually so close that McKellen even officiated Stewart’s wedding to Sunny Ozell in 2013. So, when the actor stopped by Entertainment Tonight to promote his movie, Ebenezer, he got a chance to reflect on his friendship with Stewart, and his comments are just too sweet:

Well, what I thought about Sir Patrick of late is because he did his own version of Christmas Carol. He was a one-man show. He played all the characters. He did it on Broadway and did it on London’s West End a number of times. I think he toured with it. It’s a big part of his life. I just remember his friendship and his - A good man. Serious-minded. And always looking to make the world a better place, and he achieved that.

I think everyone would be better off having a friend who speaks about them as lovingly as McKellen discusses Stewart. To put it simply, the two were the definition of friendship goals, and the seasoned actors elevated everyone around them. I can't imagine it's easy for McKellen not having his good friend around, but I love that he's choosing to remember him in such a positive way.

Of course, given McKellen’s role in Ebezener as Jacob Marley, it makes sense that his friend would be on his mind. Stewart's take on A Christmas Carol still serves as a high point in his career and a benchmark for stage acting in general. It seems I'm not the only one who is feeling a a way about this tribute either based on the comments of the Instagram video. I think toriyikes sums it best: “Making me cry in the afternoon!” Fans may agree after watch ingthe video below:

A post shared by Entertainment Tonight (@entertainmenttonight)

Shortly after Patrick Stewart's death was reported, Ian McKellen took to X to share a sentimental message. In it, the star reflected on his and Stewart's time serving at the Royal Shakespeare Company and discussed their subsequent work and endearing friendship.

While Stewart was greatly known for his work as an actor, McKellen’s words were a a sweet reminder that he was so much more. Yes, he was “serious-minded,” but he was also always up for a laugh and even gave his own eulogy back in 2015 at a Just for Laughs gala. There's a reason his roles as Professor X and Jean-Luc Picard are still iconic, and it's because the compassion that he put into the world. Just as McKellen said, he made it a little better, and that's something we should all remember.

Of course, it should be noted that we will the two X-Men alums together one more time when Avengers: Doomsday hits the 2026 schedule on December 18. The movie will now mark Stewart's final on-screen performance following his death at 86 due to Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. Trailers have already teased that Stewart's Professor X and McKellen's Magneto will share the screen again, and I'm not sure I'm prepared for that reunion.

I'm confident that Patrick Stewart's final turn as the X-Men's leader will be satisfying and that his body of work as a whole will stand the test of time. More than that, though, if the comments from Ian McKellen and so many others are anything to go by, Stewart's kind spirit won't be forgotten either.

#3557. How Original Narnia Star Ben Barnes Really Feels About Netflix's Reboot

We are a couple of months away from Greta Gerwig unleashing her take on the fantasy classic "The Magician's Nephew" for Netflix and a new generation of kids experiencing the world of Narnia for the first time. The film is already making some interesting choices when it comes to adapting the magical world created by author C. S. Lewis, including assembling a killer cast that features Meryl Streep as the lion Aslan and Daniel Craig as the titular magician.

So, since we're waiting for its arrival, it's never a bad time to revisit the previous big-budget movie adaptations of Lewis' fantasy novels. After all, for a certain generation, "Shrek" director Andrew Adamson's film versions of the "Narnia" books were their introduction to fantasy (and to the isekai genre that's come to dominate anime). Indeed, if you were too young to watch Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" movie trilogy in theaters in the 2000s, chances are Adamson's films were the first big-screen fantasy epics you saw (you know, assuming you were alive back then). It makes sense, too, as Wētā Workshop worked on those movies, designing incredible fantastical creatures and props.

Adamson's "Narnia" films also featured a number of actors who have gone on to become bigger names, including James McAvoy and Ben Barnes as Prince Caspian (a role he later reprised in the Michael Apted-helmed "The Voyage of the Dawn Treader"). Now, Barnes shared his feelings about the Netflix "Narnia" reboot, telling ScreenRant that "the trailer looks great" and that he's "always been a fan of directors who are real visionaries."

Ben Barnes went on to praise the decision to start with "The Magician's Nephew" for Netflix's reboot of the "Narnia" movie franchise, saying it's a "brilliant idea."

"I think [Greta Gerwig} has got a great eye for casting. I loved Emma Mackey in 'Sex Education,' I thought she was brilliant. Obviously, Daniel Craig's brilliant in everything. So, yeah, I'm really excited to see it," Barnes added. "Those stories are beautiful, but also, every generation needs to reinterpret things, and pull out of stories what seems visceral and important, and present it in a way that is visually exciting, and I think we can rely on [Gerwig] to do that."

From what we know about the movie, it seems Gerwig is embracing a '70s glam rock and British prog musical sensibility for her take on "Narnia," including giving Aslan a David Bowie-inspired look. That alone makes this a rather interesting adaptation. But most importantly, it is a huge risk for Netflix, between the film's daunting budget and Gerwig's desire for a wide theatrical release leading to some behind-the-scenes drama.

Admittedly, it's a bummer that audiences never got to see Barnes appear in more "Narnia" movies. At the same time, he did go on to join another popular fantasy franchise in the form of Netflix's "Shadow and Bone" TV series (even though it wound up being canceled before its story was completed). As for "The Magician's Nephew," we'll see how Gerwig's take on Narnia fares with the masses when it opens in theaters (including IMAX screens) on February 12, 2027, before debuting on Netflix a couple of months later on April 2.

Discovery — tapped Jeremy Latcham to lead DC. He used to work at Marvel Studios, and coincidentally was a producer on Gunn's Guardians of the Galaxy.

#3555. Avedon Director Ron Howard On Richard Avedon’s “Creative Courage,” and His Favorite Images From 'In the American West'

In his new documentary Avedon, director Ron Howard traces the vivid legacy of the influential photographer Richard Avedon, which premieres November 11 on Netflix. “The subjects he worked with on the commercial side of his career were dazzling and beautiful, and he was so entertaining and expressive in the way that he would shoot them. But I really had no idea how he applied his status, his influence, his access to tell this other kind of story about human beings that was honest, insightful, and more journalistic,” Howard tells Vanity Fair.

The glamorous heights of Avedon’s career were what first caught Howard’s attention. “I became aware of him really in the ’80s. Then it was even his TV commercials, like Brooke Shields [in Calvin Klein ads],” Howard said. Later, he realized a few of his favorite portraits were taken by Avedon. One of these was a portrait of a young Kareem Abdul-Jabbar at a playground in New York holding a basketball “and kind of casually standing there looking straight into the camera. It’s not against a white background…” notes Howard. “I know Kareem a little bit. It so captured the foundational strength of character and intelligence that Kareem carried with him along with his basketball talent.”

Initially, Howard, who spent three years making the film, thought it was going to be more focused on the fashion and celebrity worlds that Avedon inhabited. However, his fascination with photographs like “sad Marilyn” (Avedon’s 1957 portrait of Marilyn Monroe) grew into a respect for the full breadth of Avedon’s career, and his “creative courage as an artist.”

In the film, footage of Avedon and new interviews with Lauren Hutton, Tina Brown, Adam Gopnik, Hilton Als, Joel Meyerowitz, Larry Gagosian, and Avedon’s son John, among others, paint a picture of a driven, curious, and sometimes mercurial artist. In the 1950s, Avedon’s career took off when he began shooting for Harper’s Bazaar, Vogue, and Vanity Fair. He injected a sense of play and prewar European glamour into his images by drawing inspiration from the films of Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers. Eventually, he ventured into documentary assignments and more political subjects, including Nothing Personal (1964), a photobook with text by James Baldwin that captured the tensions of the Civil Rights era alongside a broader look at American life, a three panel portrait of anti-war protesters the Chicago Seven, and members of America’s political and financial elite at the time of the country’s bicentennial (“The Family”) for Rolling Stone. At the height of his career, he seemingly shifted quite easily from photographing celebrities to documenting anti-war protests and the counterculture of the 1960s, even when his work was met with mixed reactions.

Dovima with elephants, evening dress by Dior, Cirque d’Hiver, Paris, August 1955.

James Baldwin, New York, January 9, 1963.

Avedon (left) with Gloria Vanderbilt and Sidney Lumet at a party for the movie premiere of East of Eden (dir. Elia Kazan), 1955.

“We tried to reflect the risks he took and the transitions he made with his art and his career,” Howard shares. Had Howard made the documentary in Avedon’s lifetime, he would have liked to have asked him directly about the turning points in his career. “In all the interviews, he just kind of made it seem like it was a natural step. But to me, it's not a natural step to stop getting thousands and thousands of dollars an hour to shoot commercials and shoot for the world's most read magazines, and go to Vietnam where no one was really. He wasn’t on assignment initially… he just committed.”

In 1979, the Amon Carter Museum of American Art in Fort Worth, Texas, commissioned Avedon to capture a portrait of the West. He worked on this ambitious portfolio periodically through 1984, traveling across 17 states like California, Colorado, Iowa, North Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming, with assistants and a researcher, Laura Wilson, who helped Avedon arrange 752 portrait sittings. (Wilson also documented the making of the project in her own remarkable photographs and writing.) In total, Avedon printed 124 photographs (some as large as four feet tall) and exhibited them at the museum in 1985. The result was In the American West—a turning point in Avedon’s career. Prior to the project’s completion, in 1983, Vanity Fair ran five photographs from the eventual series, showing coal miners covered in dust and one lone oil worker alongside a feature on Wagner’s operas and an excerpt of Gabriel García Márquez’s Chronicle of a Death Foretold.

“One of the reasons I was drawn to [In the American West] is because my family roots are in the Midwest,” Howard says. “I see a lot of truth in these images.”

Avedon conducting a portrait session for In the American West beside his 8x10 camera.

In a similar fashion to August Sander’s massive undertaking People of the 20th Century, Avedon went looking for “men and women who work at hard, uncelebrated jobs, the people who are often ignored or overlooked,” Wilson wrote. In doing so he joined a whole legion of photographers whose images have come to define broad swaths of middle and western America. But unlike common readings of Sander’s project at the time, Avedon was clear that his version of the West was totally subjective, more of a cinematic panorama than an objective record. He was emphatic that all photographs are filtered through the photographer’s eye, and become their interpretation. Through Wilson, he declared, “This is a fictional West. I don’t think the West of these portraits is any more conclusive than the West of John Wayne.”

Below, Howard reflects on five of his favorite photographs from Avedon’s In the American West.

“I asked if that was makeup, and I was assured that none of it was. [Avedon] set up, and just as workers were coming off their shift, he was getting them in front of the camera. I mean, wow, this is what these workers look like. This is what was in their lungs and their pores. I have cousins and uncles who worked in the oil fields. I never had any idea that they had their days looking like they’d been through what this guy has been through on his shift.”

“The boy with the rattlesnake was the first photo that [Avedon] took where he knew he was going to get at something deeper... He felt like this was almost religious iconography in a way, or mythic. [The subject] was a teenager. As Avedon says, he's a boy turning into a man, and here he's doing this kind of work, so it speaks to a transformation. It also speaks of that region as a very pragmatic region. My own dad, to try to get some spending money [in the ’30s], was hunting and trapping raccoons to sell skins to the junk dealer or possums they could eat. Absolutely just a pragmatic way of life there. So that image always resonated with me. It is also featured in the documentary because it was the proof in [Avedon’s] mind that he was going to be able to identify moments and individuals that would be arresting and mean a lot on an artistic level.”

“The beekeeper is, of course, a stunning image–one that doesn't have that much to do with the American West. I think [Avedon] could have found somebody like that in almost any corner of the planet, but it certainly is fascinating and a tribute to the research team that was working with him to help find him.”

“The maintenance worker who’s dressed up in a really flashy suit, suit jacket, tie and hat, that just looks very familiar to me. I mean, the jacket and all the embroidery on it, the flowers, I never saw anything like that with my family. They didn’t have that kind of flourish. This guy looks like he could be a country western singer or could be trying to be a country western star. But the hat, the tie, the gaze, the posture looks very, very familiar to me. That looks like a hardworking guy getting dressed up on the weekend.”

“This young girl is beautiful, and yet you feel she’s a little haunted. She’s at a point in her life where I think the real world is really coming into focus. You can feel that in a very specific way in the region that [Avedon] was covering. I think that also speaks about her generation: young Americans beginning to see the country that they live in; the world that they’re meant to function in and try to thrive in.”

The Soundcore P31i earbuds are down to $32.99 (originally $59.99), which is as low as they’ve been, according to price trackers. At this price, most earbuds stick to the basics, so it’s unusual to see features like active noise cancellation and LDAC included here. These earbuds are light, they fit well, and they don’t get uncomfortable after an hour or two, which isn’t always the case with cheaper earbuds. We can all agree that the Olaf animatronic walking itself around Disneyland Paris is adorable, all on its own. Now it's even cuter, with his own magical sleigh to help transport him around the Kingdom of Arendelle as he makes his way to a stage where the Arendelle Carolers perform for the holidays.

One of the biggest drawbacks that came with introducing a “living” animatronic Olaf to guests in Disney’s European theme park is the fact that it can’t walk very far very quickly. I mean, he is a snowman after all. So now, and just in time for the holiday celebration, the adorable snowman who just wants to live his best summer is taking on winter in style with his own magical sleigh. Check out the short clip of a cast member steering Olaf around as he waves to the adoring masses gathered around:

A post shared by EveryCharacter.com (@everycharacter)

The holidays are in full swing in the Disney theme parks around the world, and no one embodies the winter season better than Olaf the snowman from Frozen, one of Walt Disney Animation Studios’ most popular franchises of all time. As a result, I’m happy to see that the beloved character has his own mode of transportation, especially after a few incidents of Olaf failing, freezing, and falling over. It’s a frightening sight when it happens, though Josh Gad has kept a sense of humor about it all, as the actor who is responsible for the snowman's lovable personality.

Getting to meet beloved Disney characters is a longtime tradition, where animated characters become live-action characters in the parks. While we knew that Disney Parks had been working on robots for a few years, it wasn’t until we actually got to see Olaf in action that I realized just how remarkable the achievement was. I’m also thankful that they’re continuing to build on that by creating this sleigh, which seems to have a purpose bigger than just transporting the character around the World of Frozen in Disneyland Paris.

In the video clip, you can see that Olaf’s sleigh, while too freaking cute just on its own, has the dual purpose of also working as a bridge to get him onto the stage at the foot of North Mountain so that he can join the Arendelle carolers for a 15-minute musical performance where he leads the choir. The sleigh transforms into a short platform that Olaf can shuffle across to the back of the stage where he can do his part in the show, avoiding the need for someone to have to physically lift him up and get him on the stage some other way.

While more Frozen films are in the works, we won’t see Frozen 3 until November 24, 2027. Until then, I’m hoping we’ll get more Olaf fun in and around the Disney theme parks, as he’s a character that would be a welcome addition to the U.S. locations as well.

#3552. Denzel Washington's Gritty Sci-Fi Western Movie Is Worth Revisiting

The Hughes Brothers' 2010 sci-fi Western film "The Book of Eli" stars Denzel Washington as the titular Eli, a machete-wielding rogue who wanders a post-apocalyptic Earth years after a nuclear holocaust has laid waste to vast swaths of the planet's surface. It's not so far in the future that Eli doesn't still have a working mp3 player, though, and he barters things in exchange for battery charges at the occasional mercantile outpost.

Eventually, Eli runs afoul of Carnegie (Gary Oldman), an aspiring post-apocalyptic warlord who is looking for a legendary book, believing it will allow him to take control of the populace. Three guesses as to which book he's looking for.

"The Book of Eli" is pretty badass, with a chalky, dusty aesthetic that's unique in the annals of post-apocalyptic thrillers. Washington, one of the best actors of his generation, gives Eli a soulful humanity while also making him a capable action hero, able to take down teams of attackers with his sword. (He even fights off a guy with a chainsaw in one scene.) And while critics weren't super-high on the film, it was something of a hit, enough so for a "Book of Eli" prequel series to enter development in 2024.

The movie's supporting cast is impressive as well. Mila Kunis, for example, plays Carnegie's daughter Solara, who is unsavorily ordered to seduce Eli when he comes into her father's field of vision. What's more, Tom Waits has a small part as a shop owner, Jennifer Beals plays Carnegie's mistress, Michael Gambon and Frances de la Tour show up as a pair of itinerant cannibals, and Malcolm McDowell has an uncredited role as a much more friendly book collector.

If you don't know the various twists in "The Book of Eli," I would recommend you watch the movie before looking up any plot synopses. There are several notable, fun reveals, especially at the film's end, that should not be spoiled. The one thing I will mention is that Carnegie is, in fact, on the hunt for a Bible. Religion appears to have fallen by the wayside in the movie's dusty wastelands, and Carnegie, while not a believer, seems to know that Christianity can be wielded as a cudgel to control the masses. Indeed, all known Bibles had been destroyed following the global nuclear strike.

It's a pretty damning, almost anti-religious theme, when you think about it. The only legacy that Christianity will bring into the future is the way it was wielded by political leaders as a means to sway votes. Eli, meanwhile, has a much more righteous grasp of the Bible, understanding its philosophies and cultural impact more profoundly. "The Book of Eli" explores themes of God and godlessness in desperate times, its central conflict being a wholly Christian idea of faith vs. ambition. Despite its violence and badassery, one could imagine "The Book of Eli" being shown as the warm-up movie in a Bible study course.

The Hughes Brothers burst onto the scene in 1993 with their crime drama "Menace II Society" before helming other impressive films like "Dead Presidents," the documentary "American Pimp," and the Jack the Ripper film "From Hell," based on a comic by Alan Moore. After "The Book of Eli," the siblings went their separate ways creatively, with Allen Hughes helming the 2013 thriller "Broken City" and the documentary miniseries "The Defiant Ones" and "Dear Mama." Albert Hughes, meanwhile, made the 2018 prehistoric actioner "Alpha." Together, they're responsible for some of the best action movies from Black directors of all time.

As mentioned, critics weren't terribly kind to "The Book of Eli," although several prominent reviewers were on its wavelength. Notably, Roger Ebert gave the film three stars (out of four), feeling that it starts out grim but falls into Western cliches in a way that makes the whole thing more watchable and even enjoyably silly. As he put it:

"[Denzel] Washington and the Hughes brothers do a good job of establishing this man and his world, and at first, 'The Book of Eli' seems destined to be solemn. But then Eli arrives at a Western town ruled by Carnegie, who, like all the local overloads in Westerns and gangster movies, sits behind a big desk flanked by a tall bald guy and, of course, a short scruffy one. How are these guys recruited? Wanted: Tall bald guy to stand behind town boss and be willing to sacrifice life. All the water you can drink."

Ebert added that the movie's ending is "flawed" yet "it's so magnificently, shamelessly, implausibly flawed" that it makes "The Book of Eli" stick in the memory for how gloriously implausible it is. That's not a negative thing.

#3551. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

An era in superhero-related media is officially coming to an end, as James Gunn and Peter Safran are officially stepping down from their posts as the co-CEOs of DC Studios. This surprising news arrives only a few weeks after the finalization of the Paramount/Warner Bros. merger. At this point, the news is still very fresh and, based on social media, the responses to this major development vary tremendously. Interestingly enough, amid all that, one fan brought up a wild fact regarding Gunn’s tenure, and I’m feeling so many emotions.

Gunn and Safran joined DC Studios in 2022 and, from there, they began to construct their DCU continuity, which was to span movies, TV and video games. The pair eventually developed a ten-year plan and, up to this point, that strategy has yielded films like Superman and Supergirl as well as shows like Creature Commandos and Lanterns. The wild comment that was recently shared by an X user had nothing to do with any projects like that, though. Instead, they marked the end of this chapter by naming a long-gestating flick:

Very funny/sad that the entire Gunn era took place between THE BATMAN and THE BATMAN PART 2.

I’m honestly at a loss for words here, as this fact is absolutely correct. Matt Reeves’ The Batman was released in March 2022 months before Safran and Gunn were hired. The sequel was announced in April of that year and, since then, the movie has seen a variety of delays and is currently set to hit theaters in early 2028. On the one hand, it’s understandable that someone would chuckle over the fact that this sequel’s development will have outlasted the Gunn/Safran era. But, on the other hand, I’m actually a bit sad.

James Gunn Doesn’t Hold Back About Rumors Swirling Around Man Of Tomorrow And More DC Projects

As someone who has been interested in the DCU thus far, I’m a bit disappointed over the possibility of another reboot. However, what really makes me sad about the fact pointed out in the social media is that it’s a reminder of just how long The Batman: Part II’s development has taken. Of course, I do understand the reasons, though, as the Hollywood strikes played a key role in that. Also, more recently, Reeves had to take a step back from the film to handle a personal matter, and Steven Soderbergh is stepping in to complete principal photography. Reeves isn’t leaving the movie entirely, though, as he'll remain in touch with Soderbergh during the shoot and completely retake the reins during post-production.

It was just weeks ago that Reeves’ situation was announced and it was mentioned that he had support from Safran and Gunn. That’s just one detail that makes the news of their departure all the more surreal to me. Gunn posted about his exit on his Instagram and reflected on the highs of working for DC. Additionally, the filmmaker praised the various collaborators he had the chance to work with. Overall, Gunn – a longtime fan of DC Comics – seems to have a lot of gratitude for his time serving as co-CEO of the studio.

While James Gunn and Peter Safran will vacate their positions ahead of Jeremy Latcham’s arrival by December 1, their work within the DCU isn’t done just yet as, at the very least, he’s still in post-production on his Superman follow-up, Man of Tomorrow, which is set to be released amid the 2027 movie schedule. Also, Gunn and Safran are still credited as producers on The Batman’s sequel. I’m not sure what lies ahead for DC but, for now, I’m going to be glued to my screen to see if any other fans drop any other wild facts.

Man of Tomorrow soars into theaters on July 9, 2027, while The Batman: Part II opens on February 18, 2028.

Of all the shows in this November's streaming rotation, the most exciting arrival on Netflix is Power, Starz's flagship crime series that spawned four spin-offs (Power Book II: Ghost, Book III: Raising Kanan, and Book IV: Force). The series follows Omari Hardwick's ambitious James "Ghost" St. Patrick, who lives a double life as a wealthy nightclub owner and a drug kingpin in high-flying New York.

Sadly, due to high production costs and viewing figures that, although impressive, didn't reach the required heights, The Boroughs was cancelled after just one season.

#3548. The JBL Vibe Beam Earbuds Are on Sale for $30 Right Now

If you want reliable earbuds that cost less than tonight's dinner, JBL is a reliable brand to fall back on, with plenty of budget-friendly models that lack the bells and whistles of pricier options while still delivering on sound and battery life. One of the most popular picks is the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds, which are down 40% at $29.99 (originally $49.95).

These earbuds aren’t reinventing the wheel, but they do check important boxes. They last up to eight hours without the charging case, and up to 32 hours with the case. #3547. 5 Reasons Why Godzilla Minus Zero Ruled The Box Office

The King of the Monsters is back on top of the box office. Director Takashhi Yamazaki's "Godzilla Minus Zero" stomped into theaters over the weekend and it made quite the impact. Given that "Godzilla Minus One" was officially the first movie in the franchise to win an Oscar, the pressure was on for the sequel. It's safe to say that Yamazaki delivered.

Released by Toho and GKIDS, "Godzilla Minus Zero" opened to $30.5 million domestically to go with $31.4 million internationally for a $61.9 million global debut. That's the biggest opening weekend ever for a live-action foreign-language movie in North America, topping Jet Li's "Hero" ($17.8 million). It's also the biggest global opening for a Japanese "Godzilla" movie. Since we're talking about a 72-year-old franchise, that's pretty darn good.

For context, "Minus One" opened to $11.4 million en route to $114 million worldwide. The fact that the sequel opened nearly three times higher is staggering. Yes, this movie carries a bigger budget, but bigger is relative. It's still believed to be in the $20 million range, which is hard to believe but makes this instantly profitable for all involved.

So, what went right here? How did Toho manage to turn this into a massive breakout sequel? How did Yamazaki manage to live up to such high expectations? We're going to look at the biggest reasons why "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office on its opening weekend. Let's get into it.

Having critics on a movie's side certainly never hurts. Having critics and audiences on a movie's side? That's when good things can really start to happen. And much like "Minus One" before it, "Godzilla Minus Zero" has proved to be a real crowd-pleaser through and through.

The sequel currently holds a stellar 90% critical approval rating to go with an outstanding 96% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. It also earned an A CinemaScore, which bodes very well for word of mouth in the coming weeks. A big opening weekend is one thing, but "Godzilla Minus One" became fall 2023's unexpected box office hero thanks to excellent legs driven by real-world buzz from moviegoers. It looks like something similar is in store this time around, only much bigger.

Takashi Yamazaki's follow-up takes place two years after the events of "Minus One," bringing back much of the same human cast. A new threat in the form of King Ghidorah emerges, plunging Japan into chaos once more, leading to an epic monster bash with Godzilla himself.

/Film's Jeremy Mathai said "Godzilla Minus Zero" is "bigger" and "badder" but "not quite better" in his review. Whether or not one necessarily thinks the sequel is better than its predecessor is a conversation for another time, but it at the very least appears to be satisfying the intended audience. Almost nobody seems to be leaving theaters disappointed. That matters more for the moment than how we, as a society, may ultimately rank these movies in the future.

"Godzilla" has been around as a franchise for more than 70 years. The big lizard is a truly enduring cinematic icon unlike any other. The past few years, in particular though, have been shockingly fruitful. We're truly living in the golden age of "Godzilla." This recent surge in the character's popularity has also brought a lot of new fans on board. In particular, the Japanese movies in the series have been opened up to a much wider audience thanks almost exclusively to "Godzilla Minus One."

This franchise contains multitudes. A lot of people grew up engaging with the Toho movies passively, perhaps seeing something like "Godzilla vs. Mothra" on TV. But "Godzilla Minus One" became the highest-grossing Japanese "Godzilla" movie ever because it was, quite frankly, one of the greatest movies in the history of this cherished series. It was too good to be ignored and people who only passively engaged with the previous movies discovered something to love.

"Minus One" opened Western audiences up to Japanese "Godzilla" movies more than ever before. Yes, the MonsterVerse movies like "Godzilla vs. Kong" have been very successful in North America, but engagement with these Japanese-language entries is now happening on another, much larger level. The fact that "Godzilla Minus Zero" made nearly three times what its predecessor did on opening weekend speaks to that.

Come what may in the weeks andmonths ahead, there's no question that this movie's breakout success is a direct result of "Minus One" opening up this corner of the franchise to a much wider audience globally.

IMAX has proved that it's more important to the box office than ever before time and time again in recent years. Hollywood studios literally plan their biggest releases around the availability of those premium format screens because those higher ticket prices add a lot to the bottom line. Movies like Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and "Top Gun: Maverick," among many others, made a great deal of extra cash thanks to IMAX. The same can now be said for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

According to a press release, the sequel opened to $21.3 million worldwide on IMAX screens, representing the biggest IMAX global opening ever for a Japanese film. Even more impressive? IMAX screens delivered around 34% of the movie's global opening on less than 1% of total screens. Toho benefited greatly from those screens this time around.

But that's only part of the equation. "Minus Zero" earned the "must-see in theaters" label, becoming a true cinematic event. IMAX isn't the only game in town as far as premium formats go; 4DX, Cinemark XD, and Dolby Cinema screens were also packed out across North America and the rest of the world. Comparing Dolby Cinema to IMAX and how these formats differ isn't important to this conversation. All of these formats warrant higher ticket prices, which audiences were clearly happy to pay in this particular case. That played a big role in driving the record-breaking opening.

"Godzilla Minus One" benefited greatly from an early November release date, and "Godzilla Minus Zero" has arrived three years later in a similar spot on the calendar. GKIDS and Toho went with the "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" line of thinking with the scheduling, and it's tough to argue with the results. This was the absolute perfect spot on the calendar for this movie.

There is often a bit of a lull at the box office in early November. There's the post-Halloween horror hangover and studios are generally holding back their biggest, best stuff for the Thanksgiving corridor. "Minus Zero" opened against "The Cat in the Hat," which flopped with $20.5 million, and Angel's "Drummer Boy," which was non-threatening at $9.3 million. Looking ahead, "Ebenezer" may top the box office this upcoming weekend, but it's also going for a very different audience.

A big threat doesn't emerge until "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" on November 20, when "Godzilla" will already be three weekends in. Sure, once Thanksgiving arrives with "Focker In-Law" and Disney's "Hexed" both opening, competition will be more fierce but it's easy to see an R-rated monster movie still serving as solid counterprogramming throughout the entire month.

"Godzilla" has been broadly popular as a franchise ever since its inception. Like any long running franchise though, it's had some peaks and valleys. Right now? It's at an unquestioned peak. So much so that it's easy to make the argument that Godzilla is one of our most important modern movie stars. That may sound silly, but it's no less true.

In the 2020s, few real-life movie stars can compete with the King of the Monsters. Even in 2021 when theaters were on life support, "Godzilla vs. Kong" battled the pandemic and won, proving that blockbuster cinema could still exist. It's arguably one of the most important hits in recent history. That's just the tip of the iceberg though.

We've already mentioned that "Godzilla Minus One" became the biggest Japanese "Godzilla" movie ever, serving as a real shock at the time. Then, just a handful of months later, "Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire" became the highest-grossing "Godzilla" movie ever, pulling in more than $570 million worldwide.

"Godzilla x Kong" pushed the MonsterVerse past the $2 billion mark globally as well. We certainly have to give King Kong his flowers, but Godzilla has been remarkably consistent in the 2020s. Even the re-release of "Shin Godzilla" last year outperformed the movie's original 2016 release in North America. The character is more popular on a global scale than he's ever been seven decades after his inception. That can't be denied and it's beyond impressive.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

#3546. The Best New Video Games of 2026 (So Far)

One last look at the year's best before GOTY deliberations begin

It's hard to believe, but 2026 is winding down. Well, maybe that's easy to believe if you remember that Code Vein 2 and Highguard kicked off the year in January, and both now feel like ancient history. We're getting closer to putting together our year-end game of the year come December, but there's still a long road until then. We're still catching up on a busy year of games, from big-budget hits to indie hidden gems. Oh, and there's still this little game called Grand Theft Auto 6 to consider.

While you'll have to wait for our final list to see where recent releases like The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Phantom Blade Zero will land on our final list, as we're still digesting them, these are just some of the games that are on our mind heading into the home stretch. Mind that this list is not ranked. It is ordered reverse-chronologically.

How we pick the best games of 2026. For consideration, a game has to be out for at least three weeks, so we know it's not just a flash in the pan. We also select games that are beloved not just by their reviewer but also widely across the team. We'll update this article periodically throughout 2026.

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

It's 2026 and pod racing is cool again thanks to Star Wars: Galactic Racer. Fuse Games' impressive debut is the second coming of Burnout, sending you racing across the galaxy in junky vehicles that are ready to explode at a moment's notice. That makes for fast, thrilling races filled with glorious slo-mo explosions. Oli Welsh, Polygon's resident racing game aficionado, called it the "most original and exciting racing game in a generation" in his review, which is very high praise. All of that gives us enough reason to love it even before factoring in the game's breakout star, Biddy Blas.

For a certain kind of RPG sicko, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave might be the most impressive game Nintendo has ever made. The sprawling tactics game, which takes well over 100 hours to complete, ties four wild storylines together into one wartime epic. Though it requires a lot of patience from players, those who click with it have discovered an excellent RPG filled with the series' most weird and wonderful characters to date. "Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is dazzling as much for the scope of its ambition as for how adroitly developer Intelligent Systems executes that vision," Josh Broadwell wrote in his glowing review. "It's a gigantic turn-based tactics game that, despite a few missteps, carries itself with grace and purpose."

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

There's a world where The Blood of Dawnwalker was little more than a pale imitation of The Witcher. Thankfully, we don't live in that timeline. Instead, Rebel Wolves' debut RPG is a bold riff on CD Projekt Red's formula, drenching it in blood and innovation. The star of the show is its controversial timer, which forces you to spend time wisely as you prepare to save Coen's family from vampires. While it's stressing some players out, Polygon's Marloes Valentina Stella praised the system for pushing players to use their time meaningfully. "Usually, when I play an open-world RPG, I follow the main story for an hour at most, and then I forget all about it while I'm off doing a bazillion other things," she wrote in her review. "But in Dawnwalker, I've met Coen's family, I've felt his despair, and I've only got 30 days to save them. Knowing every time segment brings me closer to their moment of doom, every action I take must bring me closer to victory."

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

Star Wars: Zero Company was a bit of a shocker when it launched in August as one of the best reviewed Star Wars games of all time. In retrospect, that response should have been obvious from the outset. Created by veterans of the XCOM series, Zero Company took everything that made Firaxis' genre-defining tactics game great and combined that with the rich lore of the Star Wars universe. It was a match made in heaven, something that Polygon's Elijah Gonzalez praised in his review. "On top of delivering the XCOM-lite thrills of playing as a field commander, it nails the specifics of this particular time in the Star Wars mythos," he wrote. "Unlike the halcyon image of a 'more civilized age' promised by Ben Kenobi, we see the Republic as the messy, flawed institution it was to the average person not living in a Jedi temple on Coruscant."

Big Walk is unforgettable. Untitled Goose Game developer House House evokes the puzzle-solving exploration of Myst in a brilliant co-op adventure that's all about hanging out with your best pals. It looks silly, what with its goofball characters, but Big Walk's trick is that it's a surprisingly emotional journey built to sharpen your communication skills with the people you love. It all pays off in an astounding ending sequence that you have to experience to truly understand. If you can't find a crew to play with but want to know more, you can read Polygon's journal-like review that chronicles our playthrough from three perspectives.

Where to play: PS5, Switch 2, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

There was never any doubt that Denshattack! would be a special game. Right from its debut trailer, the indie about a kickflipping train felt like a jolt of Dreamcast energy. What's so impressive about the final game, though, is that it's not just a one-trick gimmick. Developer Undercoders went all out to build a varied platformer that combines the best elements of Sonic the Hedgehog, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, and Jet Set Radio. As I wrote in my review: "Denshattack! remembers that reinvention is what made games of the time so radical, and it isn’t afraid to totally jump the shark in creating an over-the-top variation of an old extreme sports formula that’s just ridiculous enough to work."

Where to play: PS5, Switch, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

Mina the Hollower, Yacht Club Games’ ode to the top-down Zelda era, pulls off something remarkable. Rather than settling for easy Game Boy nostalgia, it reinvents a retro adventure format in so many notable ways. Its perfectly-implemented Bloodborne inspiration, for instance, could have felt forced and frustrating in less capable hands, but Yacht Club pulls it off with finesse by understanding where 40 years of video game history naturally intersects. “FromSoftware’s games draw on foundational game design principles that powered ‘80s adventure games,” I wrote in my review. “Mina the Hollower is just the link between worlds.”

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

It’s been a long time since we’ve gotten a great James Bond video game, but IO Interactive has ended a long drought in spectacular fashion. 007 First Light nails the assignment, combining the cinematic highs of Uncharted with Hitman’s immersive sim brilliance. That’s all anchored by Patrick Gibson’s strong take on a young Bond that sells First Light’s origin story premise. “He's exactly as you'd expect a younger, bright-eyed, bushy-tailed Bond to be,” Ford James wrote in his review. “Far more talkative than his jaded, older self, but with the perfect amount of defiance for authority, back-chat, and quick-wittedness, alongside enviable levels of suavity.”

Where to play: PS5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

Zero Parades: For Dead Spies is the kind of game you need a little distance from to appreciate. Haunted by the drama surrounding its developer, Disco Elysium studio ZA/UM, it was initially too easy to write off the spy RPG as a hollow copy. In actuality, Zero Parades tells a remarkable story about a career screw-up embarking on an apology tour. "You have to go through the work of earnestly apologizing to an old crewmate, knowing the entire time that Cascade’s end goal is roping them into another suicide mission that she can’t get a handle on," I wrote in my review this spring. "Forgiveness is always just out of reach, because you’re ultimately in a line of work that forces you to backstab your colleagues to survive."

The Forza Horizon series is about as reliable as it gets in gaming. Playground Games' open-world racing games never cease to impress, even if they're not trying to do anything particularly new. That's true for Forza Horizon 6, which doesn't mess with an excellent formula. "Forza Horizon 6 is excellent, because of course it is," Oli Welsh wrote in his review. "It's polished, welcoming, huge, sensible, gorgeous, flexible, intense, relaxing, lavish, detailed, tasteful, dorky, glamorous, and upbeat, because of course it is." Even if it's more of the same, the gorgeous Japanese scenery and some much-needed progression tweaks make Forza Horizon 6 another victory for a series that's all gas, no brakes.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

I can barely remember a time when Carson Daly wasn’t hosting something on my TV screen.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Carson Daly has been a host and a constant presence in my life since the ‘90s. I first became aware of him with his spot as a nighttime host on L.A.’s influential and highly rated alternative rock station KROQ-FM. So, by the time he became a presence on MTV with Total Request Live when the show debuted in 1998, he was already a trusted voice in music and pop culture for me.

Before YouTube and social media, MTV was the place to go if you wanted to be exposed to music you might not have already been aware of yet, and TRL brought heightened awareness to the pop princesses and boy bands of the era. You could catch the hottest music videos of the time while also seeing celebrities drop by to chat with Carson Daly about projects they were promoting.

He always had an ease and comfort with the talent but could also engage with the very passionate viewers as they agreed and disagreed with him. And there’s something comforting about seeing him officially step into the gig as co-host of Saturday Today, all these years later. The Voice host expressed his gratitude to People when reflecting on his latest gig:

I started many years ago at MTV and I feel like I’ve been really lucky. I’ve sort of grown up with an audience. So, if you were 18 and came to TRL, you might be 38 now and have a couple of kids and come to the Plaza. And so, I’ve just been lucky generationally to continue to work in TV, have new opportunities and people have been there with me.

While I never went to TRL in person, and likely won’t make it to the Plaza where they shoot Today, I did tune in often, especially when the likes of Britney Spears or any other popular pop stars were performing, so that I could teach myself the dance steps, to varying degrees of success. I am part of that audience that has grown up with Carson Daly, and I continue to watch him across a variety of projects to this day. And although I do miss the glimpse Total Request Live gave viewers into the lives of the biggest music stars of that era, the most recent attempt at a revival and the decline of MTV in general have made that impossible to recapture.

As someone who has had the successful host on my own TV screen over the decades, I found it particularly touching that when he officially added the Saturday Today co-anchor job in New York City to his already busy schedule that includes shooting The Voice in Los Angeles, he immediately thought of his mother watching the Today Show in their kitchen while he was getting ready for school. He clearly knows how proud his mother would have been to see her son become a part of something that was so important to her own life. Daly explained:

Well, I thought about my mom. My mom, God rest her soul, was the biggest ‘Today Show’ fan of all time. When I was growing up – elementary, junior high and high school – every morning I went in the kitchen, the ‘Today Show’ was on a tiny little TV. And when I got this job, just being here, she was here.

Admitting he teared up over how his mother would feel about his latest hosting gig made me tear up in the process, knowing firsthand how hard it is not to share such a big accomplishment with the one person you know it would mean the most to. He also joked that the other bonus of being gone on Saturday mornings is that it gets him out of making breakfast for his kids, but that they better not DoorDash as a replacement since that’s just too expensive.

There are still rumors that Carson Daly will be leaving The Voice after Season 30 wraps on the 2026 TV schedule, which likely won’t die down anytime soon, especially with Keke Palmer stepping in as host for Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity. But until we know for sure, the former TRL host can be seen doing his thing on Saturday Today as well as guiding the The Voice singers through the return of the Live Shows as they get closer to announcing a winner in December.

#3544. James Gunn And Peter Safran's DC Exit Exposes A Bigger Hollywood Problem

James Gunn and Peter Safran are officially out as DC Studios co-heads in what is a major shock to both the industry and fans expecting much more from their still burgeoning DC Universe. The pair were announced as the shepherds of DC's cinematic enterprise back in November 2022. But four years later, their journey has come to a premature end. What comes next is anyone's guess. All we know for sure is that former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham is taking over and that Gunn will still release his "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow."

In fairness, Gunn and Safran's approach seemed ill-advised from the outset. The now shuttered DC Extended Universe, or "Snyderverse" as it was known, went out in 2023 with a string of flops that proved audiences were tired of what Warner Bros. and DC were providing. Instead of starting from scratch, though, Gunn and Safran rebooted the franchise with a few caveats, retaining elements of the previous cinematic universe while jettisoning most of the major characters and storylines. At a time when superhero movies were already starting to lose their box office appeal, it seemed like an odd approach, at the very least.

On the plus side, Gunn was allowed to take big swings by green-lighting projects based on little-known DC characters. That, at a time when popular IP is being mined for all its worth, was refreshing, if risky. Now that he and his DC Studios co-head are gone, however, we'll almost certainly see much less of that and a lot more focus on well-known characters with proven box office appeal. It's a complex and nuanced situation that ultimately leaves DC in a precarious position ... and audiences even more confused and frustrated than they already were.

The Warner Bros. Discovery/Paramount merger became official in October 2026, after which it looked as though James Gunn and Peter Safran were relatively safe in their roles as DC Studios co-heads. David Ellison, CEO of the newly-christened Skydance,  previously seemed to support the pair's vision for the DCU going forward. He even flew to the "Man of Tomorrow" set prior to the merger becoming official, in what appeared to be tacit approval of Gunn's DC roadmap. Alas, it seems Ellison had other plans all along.

At this point, we don't know the details of Gunn and Safran's departure. As we await further information about what Jeremy Latcham has in-store, it seems almost certain he won't be green-lighting shows such as "Creature Commandos," the animated series that Gunn used to kick off his DC Universe, or movies such as the box office flop "Supergirl." Instead, we're likely to see DC double down on its marquee characters: Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman.

On the one hand, that is a real shame, as it reinforces Hollywood's fixation on established IP and suggests filmmakers with more interesting creative visions will be sidelined. On the other, you have to wonder what Gunn and Safran were thinking with these projects based on characters of whom mass audiences had little to no awareness. By all means, make an animated "Creature Commandos" show and talk up your movie based on the "Authority" comics. But maybe save them for after we've gotten over the whole superhero fatigue issue and restored DC's cinematic fortunes?

Ironically enough, former Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav, who appointed James Gunn and Peter Safran as DC Studios co-heads, couldn't get enough of IP. In his first investor conference, he told shareholders that Warner Bros. was "the greatest treasure of global IP," prior to approving a Harry Potter reboot series that surely stands as the most conspicuous symbol of Hollywood's obsession with IP and nostalgia. When Gunn laid out his vision for the DC Universe, he wisely touted "Superman" as the centerpiece of his plans. But he also spoke enthusiastically about projects based on characters nobody outside of comic book fandom had heard of.

Since then, he's overseen some hits: the aforementioned "Superman," the HBO series "Lanterns," and the most recent DC Studios movie, "Clayface." But at the same time, he's overseen "Supergirl" flopping in spectacular fashion, and his animated series "Creature Commandos" didn't make the kind of splash that the DCU needed (despite being well-received by those who watched it). What's more, we've been getting podcasts in which he discusses whether his 2021 film "The Suicide Squad" is canon to the DCU or not. I think this is the sort of stuff that, viewed in hindsight, will seem so obviously misguided.

Meanwhile, the threat of a DC cinematic universe populated by bland, big-budget movies designed to capitalize on audiences' awareness of IP looms. Viewed from any perspective, this is a pretty dire situation that will do nothing to help bring superhero movies back to prominence, and it may even actively hasten their decline. And to think, all we needed was a full DC reset in 2022.

#3543. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3542. The Story Behind Why Smallville’s Ending Didn’t Reveal Clark In The Superman Suit

It's a bird... It's a plane... It's not Tom Welling in tights...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Before the Arrowverse existed, fans had a Superman show without Superman called Smallville, and that series defined my childhood. Now, it’s celebrating it’s 25th anniversary (and making me feel old). The series focuses squarely on Clark Kent, and it makes some interesting choices regarding the DC mythos. Interestingly, the show never saw Tom Welling's Clark fully suited up as the Man of Steel, and the actor himself shared some BTS details about why that was the case.

Just to refresh fans' memories, Clark never wore the classic red-and-blue suit, and barely hit the skies. However, the final moment gave a little wink at who this fan-favorite Clark Kent had become by showing him running across the rooftop of the Daily Planet and ripping open his shirt to reveal the classic S on the chest. This was the closest fans came to seeing the actor in the hero tights.

When Welling and his co-star, Michael Rosenbaum, (who played Lex Luther) spoke with Variety, he revealed the reason behind the lack of a super suit:

We got to set that day, and they had given me just a T-shirt with no sleeves to wear underneath the shirt. Because they didn’t have the money to put the suit on, and they weren’t going to see it anyway.

The absence of a full suit wasn’t a major surprise, given creators Alfred Gough and Miles Millar initiated a “no flights, no tights” rule when they started the show. Only one of those was ever broken. While Welling admits that they “toed the line a few times” when it came to the suit, they never did get the actor in a pair of tights. The reason for that was pretty simple. They weren’t able to do so unless Welling gave the “all right,” and to this day, this iteration of Clark has not suited up.

Funny enough, the closest we came to seeing Clark in a hero costume was when he wore the Green Arrow suit for an episode. Years later, along with Erica Durance (who played Lois Lane), Welling did reprise his role as Clark for a scene in the Arrowverse's "Crisis on Infinite Earths” crossover event, though even by that point, the character had given up his powers and retired as a hero. Despite Kent not taking to the skies in the final shot, Welling enjoyed the series, and he had this to say about his character's status:

We can’t go with him. But he’s out there.

This is technically true, and there have also been plenty of Supermen before and after Smallville. Yet fans have remained dedicated to the series. That's partially thanks to Welling, Rosenbaum, and several cast members reuniting conventions around the country. Plus, Rosenbaum and Welling host the re-watch podcast “Talkville,” which is currently recapping Season 9. With that, fans continue to hear BTS stories and re-live their favorite moments.

While there have been other Supes shows, the former WB/CW series still stands as the only series to solely focus on Clark and not his alter ego. But this could change if Welling and Rosenbaum succeed in reviving the series. The duo have been reportedly attempting to bring back Smallville via an animated sequel, and this could potentially mean (finally) seeing Clark in the suit.

I'd still actually like to see Tom Welling don the costume in a live-action production, though, even if the chances of that happening seem slim to none. At the very least, fans can enjoy Clark's entire journey by streaming all 10 seasons of Smallville with a Hulu subscription.
