#3541. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3539. David Carradine Faced Off Against An Action Legend In A Forgotten 1983 Neo-Western

David Carradine came to prominence playing a martial arts master so it was only right that he eventually found himself in a duel with the great Chuck Norris. As Shaolin monk Kwai Chang Caine in "Kung Fu," Carradine traveled the Old West facing down all manner of challenger. But he never reckoned with the might of a solitary Texas Ranger with a deadly aim — that is, until 1983's "Lone Wolf McQuade," which saw Carradine and Norris do battle in what was one of the better projects of the 1980s for both actors.

By 1983, Carradine had come a long way from his TV debut in the short-lived Western series "Shane." Having become a household name thanks to "Kung Fu," the actor tried to subvert audience expectations by appearing in a number of exploitation flicks and B-movies. More well-known 1970s examples include "Cannonball," "Death Race 2000," and "Deathsport." In the 1980s, however, Carradine was basically churning out direct-to-video fare, and in "Lone Wolf McQuade" he came face to face with the king of schlocky DTV actioners, Chuck Norris.

The neo-western was directed by Steve Carver, who'd worked at Roger Corman's New World Pictures at the same time Carradine had fronted several of the studio's features in the 1970s. With "Lone Wolf McQuade," Carver paid homage to the Spaghetti Westerns that had helped move the Western genre into its revisionist era. As such, there was a self-aware aspect to the movie, which knew exactly what it was and wasn't about to apologize for it. The final showdown between its two stars was emblematic of its excess and was, it turns out, a lot more real than you might imagine. In fact, Carradine and Norris seemingly gave everything they had to their climactic battle and ended up injuring themselves.

"Lone Wolf McQuade" isn't the type of '80s actioner that gets mentioned alongside such legendary features as "First Blood" or "Die Hard." But it's also not the kind of movie that should be lumped in with the worst examples of the decades' bombastic nonsense. In fact, it's easily one of the best Chuck Norris movies, and in its unapologetic embrace of the uber macho ethos of the era and its reverence for the great Spaghetti Westerns, manages to turn it into a sort of paean to both the golden age of action cinema the influential films that preceded it.

That's not to say the film is some sort of artistic masterwork. This is, at the end of the day, a film in which Norris and David Carradine beat each other senseless for our entertainment. "Lone Wolf McQuade" stars the former as Texas Ranger Jim "J.J." McQuade, an ex-Marine who is the epitome of the '80s action stereotype: a lone wolf lawman who routinely flouts the rules and lives a solitary existence in the wake of his divorce. Oh, and he also literally has a pet wolf.

The film follows McQuade as he tangles with David Carradine's Rawley Wilkes, an arms dealer who also happens to be a martial arts expert. It seems Carradine's Kung Fu specialist is selling weapons to terrorists, and J.J. isn't about to let that go unpunished. When Wilkes captures his daughter, Sally McQuade (Dana Kimmell), he all but guarantees a confrontation with J.J., which is exactly what we get in the film's climactic moments. That particular battle is a protracted slog in which Norris and Carradine go all out.

In a 1990 issue of Psychotronic Video (via archive.org), David Carradine recalled his showdown with Chuck Norris in "Lone Wolf McQuade." Neither actor opted to use a stunt double, making for what sounds like a brutal on-set experience. "We worked on that fight for four days," he said. "We shot it for four days. And we were little old men by the end of it. All our old injuries came back, we got new injuries, and we were stumbling around like little old men."

According to the actor, he and his co-star needed canes and crutches by the end of shooting their fight, which in Carradine's recollection was the result of Norris wanting to outdo his famous showdown with Bruce Lee in 1972's "The Way of the Dragon." "We were actually trying to go beyond that," continued Carradine. "I think we did. I think photographically we didn't. But as far as the fight was concerned, the combination of the two styles, you know, because I was very flowing and loose, and he was very solid and hard, I think we accomplished what we set out to do."

I'm fairly confident in saying that Jim "J.J." McQuade vs. Rawley Wilkes was not, in fact, quite as memorable as Tang Lung vs. Colt. But it was an impressive ending to one of Norris' best films and reminder of the physical talent that had made Carradine a star a decade prior.

#3537. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3536. 5 Possible Reasons Behind James Gunn And Peter Safran's DC Studios Exit

The hierarchy of power in the DC Universe is about to change. The Paramount/Warner Bros. Discovery merger was recently made official, with a new mega-corporation, Skydance, emerging on the other side. As a result, major changes are being made at all of the companies under the corporation's umbrella, and those changes have come for DC Studios.

In a surprise move, James Gunn and Peter Safran are exiting as co-heads of DC Studios, with former Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham taking over. What this means for the future of the DC Universe that Gunn and Safran have been building together since 2022 remains to be seen, but this is one of the bigger shake-ups in the realm of superheroes and comic book happenings in a long time.

For now, we have more questions than answers, and the biggest question on everyone's minds right now is what, exactly, prompted the divorce between Gunn, Safran, and DC Studios. While we don't have a definitive answer yet, there are some strong possible reasons for the man behind Marvel's "Guardians of the Galaxy" trilogy and his trusted producing pal to exit the company.

We're going to look at some of those reasons as we try to make sense of what just happened and what might come next. Let's get into it.

In early 2023, when James Gunn announced the first chapter of the new DC Universe and called it "Gods and Monsters," it was clear the idea was for DC Studios to focus on characters other than Batman, Superman, and Wonder Woman. Yes, Gunn was going to direct "Superman," but projects like "Swamp Thing" and "The Authority" were also in the mix. Many of the projects have yet to come to fruition, but others, such as "Clayface," have. They've delivered mixed results.

Gunn and Safran weren't focusing all that much on A-list DC characters at the time. A new Batman is due to debut in "The Brave and the Bold," but that movie doesn't even have a release date, and Gunn has confirmed that Robert Pattinson's Batman won't join the new DCU. It admittedly complicates matters with "The Batman Part II" now in production. All the same, the new DCU absolutely needs a Batman. It needs a Wonder Woman. It needs A-listers.

Skydance is now a mega-corporation that is tens of billions of dollars in debt. On paper, it might be good to have a movie like "Clayface" make well over $100 million on a $44 million budget. But that's relatively small potatoes compared to what a "Batman" movie can make. Skydance wants to focus more on those A-list characters. Right or wrong, the company is likely eager to get a new Wonder Woman on screen and a new Batman cast to exist alongside David Corenswet's Superman.

There may well be room for movies like "Swamp Thing" or "The Authority," but not before the A-listers get sorted out. Again, this is speculative, but since IP is still king in Hollywood, there's good reason to believe the brass is looking at DC with more urgency in this regard.

We can have creative discussions all day, and undoubtedly, people will be sharing a lot of opinions on what James Gunn and Peter Safran have produced during their time as the heads of DC Studios. However, at the end of the day, Hollywood is a business, and from a business perspective, the box office returns just haven't been good enough. In particular, "Supergirl" is a glaring issue that needed to be addressed.

Gunn's "Superman" was the biggest comic book movie of 2025 at the box office with $618 million, but that was still less than Zack Snyder's "Man of Steel" ($670 million) did 13 years earlier, unadjusted for inflation. It was a promising enough start, but not a resoundingly great one. Superhero movies are no longer automatically successful in theaters like they were in the 2010s, which certainly doesn't make things any easier. All the same, results are not just expected, but needed to justify the sky-high budgets for these blockbusters.

"Supergirl" flopped at the box office earlier this year, taking in just $126 million worldwide on a $170 million budget against mixed reviews. While Supergirl isn't quite an A-list character, she's a heck of a lot bigger than Clayface or Peacemaker. The fact that the movie bombed in such high-profile fashion was not a good look for DC Studios. Ultimately, it reflects back on Gunn and Safran, even though Craig Gillespie was in the director's chair.

In truth, DC is in the midst of one of the biggest box office bad streaks ever. The misses far outweigh the hits. Not all of that can be placed on Gunn and Safran, but something needs to change. Relatively modest hits like "Clayface" aren't going to cut it forever.

James Gunn worked as a smaller filmmaker for years before he ascended to Hollywood's A-list. When "Guardians of the Galaxy" became Marvel's most unlikely box office smash hit, everything changed. That eventually led to him becoming a studio head, but occupying an executive suite was never his ambition. He wanted to be a director. Put simply, it sounds very much like Gunn didn't want to be a Hollywood executive anymore.

After the news about his exit broke, Gunn explained his departure as DC Studios' co-head and his statement made it seem like the job was very taxing on his personal life, as well as his creative life. "DC Studios has been trying, to say the least," he said. "I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job."

Gunn also noted that he had a tough time "dividing my time between projects I'm incredibly passionate about and the ones I'm not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head."

Not to say that there weren't other factors involved, but if we take Gunn at his word, the last four years have been pretty difficult for him. He wasn't just making giant movies like "Superman" and next year's "Man of Tomorrow," but he's been creatively managing all of the output at DC Studios. It's not terribly hard to see why he might want to go back to just being a writer and director.

There's no telling what has been going on behind closed doors at Skydance ever since the merger went through. CEO David Ellison has his own ideas of how he wants the company, and its various divisions, to run. Ellison isn't the guy who launched DC Studios when James Gunn and Peter Safran's new division started at Warner Bros. It's entirely possible there was a bit of a culture clash.

It's certainly interesting to note that Both Gunn and Safran were announced as part of the executive structure at Skydance after the Warner Bros./Paramount merger was made official. That was just a few weeks ago. Would Ellison have announced them as part of the new company if the plan was to move on and have Jeremy Latcham take over? It's hard to imagine. That implies that something may have happened in recent weeks that prompted the exit.

What could that be? There are a lot of moving parts. Ellison, as well as his new film chiefs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, undoubtedly had their own ideas about how to handle things at DC Studios. If Gunn and/or Safran bumped up against them in ways they didn't with the previous regime, it's not hard to imagine the camel's back breaking under the weight of one too many straws.

Without aimlessly speculating as to what they all could have disagreed about, it seems probable that if all sides got along and shared a vision for the future, they could have figured something out.

DC Studios was under the Warner Bros. umbrella, but it seemed like James Gunn and Peter Safran were granted a great deal of creative freedom to shape this new DC Universe as they saw fit. There's virtually no question that Skydance, David Ellison, and the rest of the new brass at the studio have their own ideas about what to do with the treasure trove of IP that is the DC Comics library. It's not hard to surmise that Skydance's ideas didn't align with Gunn and Safran's intended plans.

James Gunn's DC Universe plans shifted after Warner Bros.' initial announcement, but that never meant that Gunn and Safran lost control of the ship. They were steering. They were making sure things were lining up for eventual, future plans. Those plans haven't fully revealed themselves (and we may never know the full scope of what they wanted to do), but it's clear there was an ultimate plan in place.

If Skydance has different ideas (and it feels safe to assume they do), that would complicate matters. If Gunn and Safran spent years building out this slate only to have to bend to what the new leadership wants, that would be frustrating. Without putting words in anyone's mouth, it could even be taken as an insult.

Again, I'm not here to recklessly speculate, but these two guys had a vision that Warner Bros. bought into. If Skydance doesn't share that vision, or something close to it, Gunn and Safran making their way to the exit door makes a lot of sense.

#3534. As a Lord of the Rings Fan, Here's How I'd Rank Every Book

The Lord of the Rings is still considered the greatest fantasy epic put to paper, and for good reason. J.R.R. Tolkien was a master at work when he spent decades crafting the mythology and lore behind Middle-earth. After The Hobbit first revealed this high-fantasy world, he expanded upon it in The Lord of the Rings, which was split by publishers into three volumes: The Fellowship of the Ring, The Two Towers, and The Return of the King. But did you know that each of these books was split in half?

Avid Tolkien fans are already well aware of this fact, that Tolkien's three-part epic is, in some sense, actually a six-part epic. Some editions, such as the 1999 "Millennium Edition" by Houghton Mifflin, actively split the story into these six installments with their own unique titles. To shake things up, we've chosen to follow this same methodology when ranking the books in The Lord of the Rings, and while there is no "worst" volume, there are certainly some parts of the story we love more than others.

The fourth book in the six-part set is the second half of The Two Towers. This portion of Tolkien's masterpiece follows Frodo, Sam, and Gollum as the latter leads them toward Mount Doom. Along their way, they pass the Dead Marshes, decide to take the One Ring to the southernmost end of Mordor, and are eventually captured by Faramir. Despite everything that Frodo does here to save Gollum's life, the creature would still come to reject the ring-bearer (and all goodness) when Sam inadvertently "defeats his repentance," as Tolkien once put it.

The Two Towers is considered by some to be the pinnacle of The Lord of the Rings, but perhaps the story's most memorable moments occur in the previous book. "The Ring Goes East" is a Frodo-centric collection of chapters that, while pivotal to the larger story, is sometimes a challenge to work through. This book ends after the trio have made their way to Shelob's Lair, separating Sam from Frodo for the first after the latter is taken — having been poisoned by the spider — by orcs.

The next portion of The Lord of the Rings comes from the beginning of The Return of the King. The "War of the Ring" finally comes to a head as many of the other segmented plotlines from the last book come together. After Pippin used the palantír and uncovered Sauron's plot for Minas Tirith, the White Wizard Gandalf journeys with the Hobbit to Gondor to prepare for war. As Théoden mobilizes Rohan, Aragorn takes Legolas and Gimli with him to venture through the paths of the dead to find an army to aid them in battle. Meanwhile, Éowyn and Merry disguise themselves among Rohan's army, hoping to do their part in saving Middle-earth.

"The War of the Ring" climaxes with the famed Battle of the Pelennor Fields, as the forces of Mordor clash with the free peoples of Middle-earth. After the battle and some healing has taken place, Aragorn leads the armies of Men against Mordor itself, buying Sam and Frodo (who are not separated by Gollum, by the way) time. In many respects, the bulk of The Return of the King (as viewed by most) takes place here. Aragorn proves himself the only true king of the Reunited Kingdoms of Gondor and Arnor, and the tide truly turns in our hero's favor.

After the Fellowship is fractured, The Two Towers begins with tragedy. This book picks up with Boromir's tragic death. Although he saved the Hobbits, Merry and Pippin, they have been taken by orcs. This leads Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli to chase after their comrades — at least until a resurrected Gandalf, now clothed in white, redirects their path. As Merry and Pippin rally the Ents against the forces of Saruman and Isengard, Aragorn and his companions do the same in Rohan. It's easily one of the best portions of the journey.

Not only does "The Treason of Isengard" cover the Battle of Helm's Deep (without any Elves but Legolas, by the way), but it carries on to the defeat of Isengard as well. Everything with the palantír occurs here, setting the stage perfectly for what is to come in the previous book we listed. Of course, it's in the beginning of The Two Towers that Tolkien offers some of his best worldbuilding, establishing not only the other kingdoms of men but also expanding on the other beings that exist within Middle-earth.

It's hard to believe that only one book in The Lord of the Rings features a united Fellowship of the Ring. Unsurprisingly, that chapter of the saga comes from the larger book of the same name. After Frodo awakes in Rivendell, Elrond's council is formed to determine what to do with the One Ring entrusted to him. Thus, the adventure begins as the nine companions — Frodo, Sam, Merry, Pippin, Aragorn, Legolas, Gimli, Boromir, and Gandalf — make their way through Moria. After Gandalf's apparent demise, they meet Galadriel, and the book concludes with a broken Fellowship.

"The Ring Goes South" is arguably among the most pivotal installments of Tolkien's masterwork. From the decision that the ring must be destroyed, this is the foundation from which the rest of the saga is built. It's here that the nine are forever bonded together, forged in the fire of singular purpose. Although Gandalf's demise is one of the most harrowing moments in fantasy literature, Tolkien uses his death and resurrection to paint a deeper picture, one that would continue upon his rebirth.

If you thought that The Return of the King movie had too many endings, then you will be floored by "The End of the Third Age." The final chapters in Tolkien's saga chronicle the final destruction of the ring, Sauron's defeat, Aragorn's coronation, the disbanding of the Fellowship, and the Hobbits' eventual return home. Of course, unlike the movie, the return home is not exactly what the four halflings had hoped for. "The Scouring of the Shire" reveals that Saruman, upon his previous defeat, has overtaken the Hobbits' home, forcing the four to rally the troops against his efforts. In the end, Frodo leaves for the Undying Lands.

"The End of the Third Age" may not rank this high for all Tolkien lovers, but after adoring the entire story from the beginning, it brings a satisfying conclusion to the journey that one can only appreciate after everything the Fellowship has been through. It may not be the homecoming that Frodo and his companions expected, but it is a fantastic finale that hits home the main themes of Tolkien's epic. Perhaps one day we'll see this portion of the novel adapted in earnest...

Who doesn't love the Shire? The Fellowship of the Rings begins with "The Ring Sets Out," nearly two decades after Bilbo bequeaths Frodo the One Ring. Upon discovering for sure which magic ring this is, Gandalf sends Frodo and Sam out to Bree. Along the way, they meet up with Merry and Pippin, spend some quality time with Tom Bombadil, and eventually encounter Strider, a ranger from the north revealed to be Aragorn in disguise. Pursued by the Ring-Wraiths, Frodo is eventually injured and taken by Glorfindel (the most underrated character in the books) to Rivendell.

Good beginnings are just like good endings in that they inspire the reader to revisit even the most familiar material. One cannot be captivated by Tolkien's world without reading about the simple life of Hobbits and Frodo's earliest adventures. There's a reason that so many were disappointed that Bombadil was removed from the finished product of the live-action films — and why so many prefer The Fellowship of the Ring to begin with. "The Ring Sets Out" is exactly as it seems, the first journey across the Middle-earth map that leads to all the others, and it's a journey worth undertaking again and again.

#3532. George Lucas Expected Star Wars To Be Compared To A Sci-Fi Movie He Says Is Even Better

It's easy to underplay just how monumental "Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope" was at the time of its original theatrical release in 1977. George Lucas' decision to keep the licensing and merchandising rights for the film resulted in a multi-billion-dollar lesson for every studio in Hollywood, while the special effects pioneered by the movie paved the way for the VFX industry we have today. It's also, quite simply, a very good film that combines an eclectic collection of influences to deliver a hugely entertaining space opera with the flair of Westerns and samurai flicks.

Still, while "Star Wars" is typically counted amongst the best sci-fi movies of all time (including by us here at /Film!), Lucas doesn't entirely consider it a sci-fi film. In a 1977 interview with Rolling Stone, he even described the movie as being closer to a Western than, specifically, Stanley Kubrick's classic 1968 sci-fi saga "2001: A Space Odyssey." As Lucas put it:

"I am fairly pleased that they haven't compared it that much to '2001.' Actually, it is being compared more to Westerns than '2001,' which is really what it should be. On a technical level, it can be compared, but personally, I think that '2001' is far superior."

But Lucas wasn't merely being coy about his admiration for Kubrick's movie, he was being practical about the stark differences between the two films. "You know, it had 10 times more money and time, and obviously, it came out better. In special effects, one of the key elements is time and money," he continued. "Most of those special effects in 'Star Wars' were first-time special effects — we shot them, we composited them, and they're in the movie."

It's neither news nor a surprise that George Lucas has always admired Stanley Kubrick's "2001: A Space Odyssey." After all, Lucas originally went to Douglas Trumbull, who had done the visual effects for Kubrick's film, to work on "Star Wars." However, it was only after Trumbull passed on the project that he recommended John Dykstra instead. This resulted in a collaboration that changed the special effects industry forever, as Dykstra pioneered a motion control camera that allowed Lucas to pull off the climactic Death Star trench run in "Star Wars."

But it wasn't just Trumbull that he tried to recruit from the crew behind Kubrick's film. In fact, Lucas' first choice of cinematographer for "Star Wars" was "2001" director of photography Geoffrey Unsworth, who seemed like an ideal pick to capture the documentary feel that Lucas wanted while at the same time being able to handle the movie's visual effects demands. And when Unsworth declined the offer, Lucas ended up going with a different Kubrick cinematographer in the form of Gilbert Taylor (who had worked on "Dr. Strangelove").

Yet again, this creative decision proved essential to making "Star Wars" as unique and effective as it is. Indeed, Taylor managed to ground the movie's operatic spectacle, at times creating a fly-on-the-wall visual sensibility. It makes it seem as though you're not just watching some grand fairy tale set in space but real events that happened a long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away.

#3531. How to get the Biggoron Sword in Ocarina of Time

'From a Pocket Egg Comes...' quest walkthrough

Biggoron's Sword is the strongest sword in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. However, it's also the most time-consuming weapon to get in the entire game.

You'll need to go on a wild goose chase all around Hyrule, trading items like a blue Cucco named Cojiro and the Poacher's Saw to people that you most likely never interacted with. This quest is also fairly difficult if you don't know your way around the map, as you do need to get from point A to point B within a certain amount of time.

Here's how to get Biggoron's Sword in Ocarina of Time remake, along with what to do with every item and who to trade them to.

You can start your hunt for the Biggoron Sword as soon as you become an adult in Ocarina of Time, but to get the sword, you must bottle some blue fire from the Ice Cavern and thaw King Zora.

To get the Biggoron Sword, you need to progress through the "From a Pocket Egg Comes..." event given to you by the Cucco Lady in Kakariko Village.

For more information on how to complete each step, check out the sections below.

First things first, head to Kakariko Village and talk to the Cucco Lady. She'll give you a Pocket Egg that will hatch into a Pocket Cucco at dawn. To speed up the process, you can play the Sun's Song until the egg hatches.

Now, you need to find someone to wake up with the Pocket Cucco.

Luckily, the heavy sleeper is very close to the Cucco Lady. Head into the house northeast of the Shooting Gallery. You'll also find Richard, the white dog from Hyrule Castle Town, running around outside with his owner. On the first floor, you'll find Talon sleeping in a bed. Take out the Pocket Cucco and use it to wake him up. He'll go running back to Lon Lon Ranch, but now you have to go back to the Cucco Lady.

Now, you must find the Cucco Lady's big brother, who happens to be in the Lost Woods. From the Kokiri Forest entrance, turn left and you'll find him sitting next to the tree that the Skull Kid used to be on. Walk up to him and use Cojiro to wake him up.

He'll tell you that he needs to drop something off at Granny's Cauldron, but you must be quick.

The Master Craftsman's Son will give you an Odd Mushroom, and you must take it to Granny's Cauldron in Kakariko Village in four minutes or less, or else it will rot. You cannot use any of the songs to warp during this portion.

The best route that we've found is to go through the Lost Woods to the shortcut that takes you to Goron City, which is straight from the area with the Cucco Lady's big brother, then left and straight. Then, go down Death Mountain Trail into Kakariko Village. Enter the Potion Shop, which is the first building on your left, and go through the door to the left of the shopkeeper. Finally, enter the building on the right, and show Granny the Odd Mushroom.

Remember to hold A to dash, and this should all take you a little over a minute to two minutes. If you forget where to go, you can pause the game at any time, and time will stop.

Granny will give you Odd Poultice, which you need to take back to the Master Craftsman's Son. As this isn't timed, you can take your sweet time and go through Kokiri Forest or back the way you came.

Once you make it back, you'll realize that the Master Craftsman's Son is missing, and Fado has taken his place. Give her the Odd Poultice, and she'll give you the Poacher's Saw.

Take the Poacher's Saw to Gerudo Valley, which is on the west side of Hyrule Field. Cross the bridge with Epona, and you'll find the Master Carpenter by the tent. Show them the Poacher's Saw, and they'll give you a Broken Goron Sword.

Take the Broken Goron Sword to the top of Death Mountain Trail. If you completed the Fire Temple, you can use the Bolero of Fire to get there almost immediately. If not, you can climb up Death Mountain Trail, and you'll find a big Goron named Biggoron at the top.

Unfortunately, a bunch of ash got into their eyes, and now they're very itchy. Biggoron will give you their prescription, so you can get some eye drops from King Zora.

Now we've reached the point in the quest where you must head into the Ice Cavern to collect some blue fire and melt King Zora.

After you've melted him, show him the prescription from Biggoron, and he'll tell you that you need to take an ingredient to the scientist at the Lakeside Laboratory at Lake Hylia. However, you'll need to be quick again.

You need to quickly take the Eyeball Frog to the scientist inside the Lakeside Laboratory at Lake Hylia, and this time you'll only have two and a half minutes. Again, you can't use any songs to warp during this portion.

The quickest way to get there is to swim through the shortcut that takes you to Lake Hylia from Zora Domain, but this is only possible if you've completed the Water Temple.

The alternative route is to leave Zora Domain through Zora River, and ride Epona over to the laboratory. Just remember that Lake Hylia is the southern exit of Hyrule Field, and you'll make it with barely any time to spare.

The Lake Scientist will give you Specialty Eye Drops to take to Biggoron, but they'll only stay fresh for three and a half minutes. And no, you still can't warp using songs during this part.

Call Epona over using Epona's Song (X- Y - A - X - Y - A), and cross Hyrule Field as fast as you can. Then, go up Death Mountain Trail and try your best to avoid the rolling boulders. Once you make it to the top, give Biggoron the Specialty Eye Drops.

After you give Biggoron the Specialty Eye Drops, he'll give you the Biggoron Receipt, but you need to wait three days before you can claim it. You can play the Sun's Song to speed up the process, and he'll give you the Biggoron Sword. The Biggoron Sword is a two-handed sword that deals twice the damage of the Master Sword. The only downside is that, because it's two-handed, you can't use a shield at the same time.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a little bit different than the original game, so if you need guides to help you through, we don’t blame you. We have walkthroughs for all the dungeons, from the Deku Tree to Ganondorf's Castle. We also have guides for the sillier, in-between parts of the game, like when you have to find Richard (the dog) or Cuccos.

For those going for 100% completion, we also have guides on where to find every Piece of Heart, every Gold Skulltula token, and where to plant every Magic Bean.

#3530. This Samsung 32-Inch OLED Gaming Monitor Is $300 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3529. Black Doves' Spy Organization Explained: Every Member & Who They Work For

Warning! This article contains SPOILERS for Black Doves season 2.Netflix’s spy action thriller Black Doves primarily focuses on the titular spy agency, but given the nature of their covert work, it can be hard to determine who's actually part of the Black Doves and what the company does. The cast of Black Doves, as well as the show itself, revolves around the titular organization. Even as the show focuses on Helen, Sam, and Reed's personal lives and history, everything circles back to the work of the Black Doves.

Black Doves season 1 revealed precious little about the organization, but by the end of Black Doves season 2, the company's lore and personnel list had increased exponentially. Now, the Black Doves are an international agency with a decades-long history that operates around the world. They've even gained a new rival in the form of Kestrel, the anarchist spy network founded in East Berlin and revived by Vita and Franz.

As the Black Doves have gotten larger and more important, it's gotten harder to keep track of who is actually part of the organization, who its enemies are, and why it even exists in the first place. Those distinctions are incredibly important, though, as Black Doves season 2 is filled to the brim with betrayals, double agents, and enemies both old and new. Here's everything we know about the Black Doves, including their leaders, agents, and history.

The Black Doves spy organization is an independent capitalist enterprise; as such, its primary goal is to earn money. As Reed explained to Helen when they first met, the organization’s employees retrieve information and sell it for the highest possible amount. The lack of ties to any particular government or country allows its spies to be hired by anyone, anywhere, regardless of the person or group’s ideological interests or country of origin. This likely bolsters its profit margins.

Black Doves, Netflix's action thriller starring Keira Knightley, included a twist that will create a huge problem for the show’s second season.

Though Black Doves season 1 only introduced the audience to four members of the spy agency (along with several freelance assassins and secret agents), season 2 drastically expanded the scope of the company. Previously, the Black Doves were thought to be an all-female organization based solely in Britain. Now, we know that the Black Doves have been in operation since at least the 1980s, that they operate throughout Europe, and that it has dozens of agents, executives, contractors, and analysts of every gender.

Helen Webb, played by Keira Knightley, is the show's protagonist and one of the top agents in the spy organization. While her past is shrouded in mystery (and Helen isn’t her real name), she was recruited into Black Doves, at least in part, due to her shady background. All that’s really known is that when interviewing for a translator job, the interviewer knew all about her mother’s death and stepfather’s murder at the hands of her stepsister. The interviewer refers her to Reed, who is immediately taken by her calculating manner and fierceness.

She is married to prominent politician Wallace Webb and publicly lives a domestic life with her husband and children. However, she’s been stealing government secrets from her husband the whole time and passing them on to the Black Doves organization. She also had an affair with a man named Jason (Andrew Koji), whose murder kicks off the events of the Black Doves series. By the end of season 1, Helen has avenged her lover, reconciled with her husband, and found a best friend in Sam Young (Ben Whishaw).

In season 2, Helen is tasked with discovering what happened to her handler, Mrs. Reed, and uncovering the truth of a past Black Doves operation she knows only as "Wildflower." By the end of the season, Helen is forced to reveal her identity as a spy to Wallace, putting her cover in jeopardy and likely ruining any chance of continuing to extract information out of him. Reed, however, offers Helen a chance to move up in the Black Doves organization and take on more responsibility besides being a "spy wife."

Dani is one of the newer members of the Black Doves, and she was originally embedded as Wallace's new assistant. Reed deployed Dani to seduce Wallace and replace Helen in season 1, as Reed felt Helen was getting uncontrollable. Helen, however, managed to defeat Dani in a brawl, though she spared her life. In season 2, Helen convinces Dani to search through the Black Doves' archives looking for Wildflower. Dani is then approached by Patrick and Kestrel, and she ultimately decides to betray the Black Doves by letting Kestrel into the building. Dani is then killed by Eleanor in the finale.

Marie was a Black Doves agent who was embedded in the Webb household as their nanny since the series began. In season 2, Reed revealed that she placed Marie there to keep an eye on Helen and her whereabouts. However, Marie was also turned by Kestrel and convinced to bring Helen's children to the London Zoo as hostages during the finale. Despite her protestations that she never would have harmed the children, Helen shot and killed Marie.

During a flashback to Mrs. Reed's youth in Black Doves season 2, the show revealed that the Black Doves organization has been in operation since at least the 1980s. There are presumably hundreds of former and deceased agents, but we know of at least three other operatives active in East Berlin in the 1980s and one from the modern day.

Much of Black Doves season 2 revolves around three former Black Doves agents who worked with Reed in her youth in East Berlin. The leader of the group, Peter Maddison, codename Thunder, engaged in a romantic relationship with Reed only to later be killed by her. Melanie Ambrose aka Spitfire and Erik Klein aka Zeus were there as hired muscle to support Reed's undercover work. As season 2 revealed, Sam killed Ambrose and Klein on Kestrel's behalf. In modern day, a Black Dove named Ida Povetkin was inserted as Alexi Chernov's maid, though she was killed off-screen.

In addition to dedicated agents and executives, the Black Doves also employ a wide range of hired guns on a contract basis. The most notable of these contractors is Sam Young, who met Helen through his work for Mrs. Reed. In season 2, Laila also worked for the Black Doves and did off-the-books work for Reed specifically. Additionally, Mr. Conteh mentions that the Black Doves send clean-up crews when their operatives make a mess, such as when Helen killed Marie.

As a private company, the Black Doves' leadership structure closely resembles that of a regular corporation. While there's no company charter to reference, the Black Doves did have an executive committee that was composed of at least five different people, as revealed in season 2. Unfortunately, it's only clear what two of those members actually did for the organization.

Elizabeth Reed spent her entire life as a Black Dove. As season 2 revealed through flashbacks, Reed spent much of the 1980s as an undercover agent embedded in an East Berlin anarchist spy network known as Kestrel. During her five years of undercover work, Reed gave birth to a daughter, Vita. Her mission ultimately ended when she fabricated a story about Kestrel planning to bomb an American checkpoint, causing the rest of her Black Doves team to execute the spy network's members. Reed then had to kill her boss and lover, Peter, after he discovered her lie.

By the time of Black Doves season 1, Elizabeth Reed had risen through the ranks of the organization and became Helen's handler in addition to serving on the company's executive committee. Reed managed several spies and assassins, and her work mainly focused on stealing government secrets and presumably selling them to the highest bidder. At the end of season 2, Reed expresses a desire to actually hunt down criminals and terrorists and make the world a better place.

The only other member of the Black Doves' executive committee who gets any attention is Mr. Conteh, a new addition to season 2. Much of Conteh's personal life is shrouded in mystery, though he seems to have an extended history with Reed. Conteh mentions that Reed never respected him, and he also delights in being able to take her down. It's not clear what Conteh does during normal times, but it's safe to assume he manages a different team of agents, considering how he was chosen to become Helen's new handler in Reed's absence.

As previously mentioned, there were several other members of the Black Doves executive committee who didn't survive Kestrel's attack. In addition to Conteh and Reed, the Black Doves were led by three other executives: Ms. Conduct, Mrs. Burkinshaw, and Mr. Rodgers. These three may have also handled agents personally, or they may have been more involved in executive functions like meeting clients and overall corporate strategy.

Though Netflix hasn't officially renewed Black Doves season 3 yet, the ending of the second season leaves the door wide open for its story to continue. If it does continue, the Black Doves will have quite a bit to do going forward. Helen will presumably move up in the ranks of the organization, either becoming a handler herself on the executive committee as the company rebuilds. Alternatively, she could simply gain more field work aside from her marriage to Wallace.

As Reed explained, the Black Doves are also presumably going to make it a point to hunt down what remains of Kestrel and its operatives. Patrick managed to escape the battle at Black Doves HQ, and Reed mentioned that he was seen boarding a plane to Tokyo. Even though Vita is dead, Kestrel has survived and remains a major threat. Where and how they strike next is impossible to predict, though it's safe to assume the Black Doves will attempt to stop them.

The Black Doves also may be expanding in season 3. Now that Kestrel has made itself known to the world, they've also made global enemies. The United Kingdom and MI6 will likely want retribution for a terrorist attack on its soil and an attempt on the Prime Minister's life. The United States will likely want retribution for the murder of a political delegate. In short, Black Doves season 3 may see the titular organization becoming a major player in global politics and among information agencies.

#3528. How To Watch Brad Pitt's Heart Of The Beast At Home

David Ayer's "Heart of the Beast" wasn't really a sleeper hit, given that it stars Brad Pitt, but the harrowing survival film turned out to be a surprisingly leggy box office performer thanks to solid word of mouth. Now it's about to find a wider audience as it moves to streaming on November 10 (as the opening of Pitt's kinda-sorta anticipated "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" nears).

The film caught on with moviegoers due to its deeply affecting narrative about a retired Army veteran (Pitt) and his combat dog struggling to survive in the Alaskan wilderness after their seaplane crashes. The crash is caused by Pitt's character having a heart attack, but he's not down for the count — not yet. He and his dog are uniquely equipped to hoof it 58 miles back to civilization, but this terrain is every bit as treacherous as a battle zone. Along the way, they encounter wolves (dredging up memories of Joe Carnahan's "The Grey"), a grizzly bear and other obstacles that test their resolve. Each challenge leaves them a little (or a lot) worse for the wear, but they are determined to emerge from this ordeal as they've done so often in their war-torn past.

Again, "Heart of the Beast" will begin streaming via Premium VOD on November 10, and consumers will get a few extras to go along with their purchase.

According to a press release issued by Paramount today, the PVOD "Heart of the Beast" will include a behind-the-scenes featurette titled "One Last Mission," which is said to be a "love letter to the land, the people, and most of all the dogs who made this film shine." (Their names are Uber, Seeka and Ryker.) Because you can never get enough good-dog footage, there's also "Uber & Brad: A Soulful Bond." Not sure why Seeka and Ryker were denied a mention here, but I guess I'll find out when I watch it. Finally, there are deleted scenes that promise to "play tug of war with your heart strings," so get ready to weep some more once you've finished the film (and you will weep).

While it would've been nice if this visually stunning film remained in theaters for a little while longer, it was clear from jump that its destiny was to become a dad movie classic. It'll be streaming for years and years to come, forcing grown men to complain about their dusty living rooms/man caves. #3527. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3526. Chris Hemsworth’s ‘Heat’ Replacement Officially Steals a New Prime Video Milestone

The last few years have been absurdly busy for Chris Hemsworth, who is now over three years removed from his last solo Thor movie. Hemsworth reunited with Thor: Ragnarök director Taika Waititi for Thor: Love and Thunder, but the film came out of the gates with poor reviews as many critics and fans felt it leaned too much into the silliness and less into the seriousness of Hemsworth’s character.

Hemsworth will return as Thor later this year in Avengers: Doomsday, but he is not yet confirmed for a role in the follow-up, Avengers: Secret Wars, which is coming to theaters in 2028. There is growing speculation that Hemsworth’s Thor will be one of the victims of Doctor Doom in the film, which would be a good way to establish the high stakes for the team-up movie.

Between this myriad of Marvel releases, though, Chris Hemsworth is still finding the time to star in new projects. Earlier this year, he reunited with his long-time Marvel co-star Mark Ruffalo for Crime 101, the new Heat replacement film also starring Halle Berry and Nick Nolte. The film left theaters after grossing only $72 million at the global box office, falling well short of its estimated break-even point calculated using its $90 million budget, but it has since gone on to become one of the most-watched movies of the entire year on Prime Video. Crime 101 is still hanging around in the top 10 in a few countries, months after its debut, and the film has now been in the top 10 for over 200 days on the platform. Barry Keoghan also has a small role in Crime 101.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

The most popular show in the world right now is the second season of The Terminal List, starring Chris Pratt. To take the #1 spot, The Terminal List had to dethrone Carrie, the new horror thriller show inspired by the novel of the same name by Stephen King. Both the flagship Reacher show and its first spin-off, Neagley, are also sitting handily in the Prime Video top 10 right now. One of the most-watched movies in the world on Prime Video at the time of writing is Love of Your Life, which stars Lanterns veteran Aaron Pierre and The Night Agent’s Gabriel Basso.

Check out Crime 101 on Prime Video and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Chris Hemsworth’s future projects.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Crime 101 is an old fashion TV movie of the week. By traditional Hollywood standards, it was a box office flop. But apparently it was popular on TV - for free. (I regret buying my ticket now.). The movie meanders, cutting from Hemsworth’s storyline, then to Berry’s, then to Ruffalo’s. You know they’ll eventually all connect, but it takes long a while to get there. Hemsworth’s character is stoic, barely expressing any emotion. The movie’s centerpiece is a long and pointless car chase through the streets of Los Angeles. Here’s something odd: while there are a couple of relatively minor fist fights in the movie, the credits list dozens of stunt performers (per IMDb, there are over 80 of them). Is there another cut of the movie with more action scenes?

#3525. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.
