#3524. Game Awards 2026: All Game of the Year Front-Runners and Predictions

What’s in pole position for gaming’s top prize? Let’s make some predictions

With only a month to go until the 13th Game Awards, set for Dec. 10, every key competitor but one (the big one) has been released. The likelihood of anything emerging to stop Grand Theft Auto 6 from sweeping the night looks increasingly slim in what is turning out to be a much weaker year than it looked on paper.

At this point, we have a clear idea of what games will be favored by The Game Awards' voting body: A high Metacritic rating (preferably over 90) is a must; role-playing games and action-adventures are strongly favored, as are games with strong narrative elements; indie and multiplayer games struggle harder for recognition than AAA single-player adventures. We used these metrics to correctly predict last year's winner, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, and the 2024 winner, Astro Bot. In 2025, we also predicted all six GOTY nominees and correctly called 20 other categories.

Below, you'll find our predictions for the most likely nominees, of which there are six each year, for Game of the Year 2026 — taken only from games that have already been released (or made available for review). We'll update these rankings throughout the year as new games are released. We'll also list some likely upcoming contenders and some of the 2026 GOTY race's dark horses, too.

Update (Nov. 9): The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has emerged as the highest-rated game of the year to date, and critical acclaim has been followed by a huge wave of social love as players share their rediscovery of the classic adventure. Ocarina's status as a dead-cert for a GOTY nomination is only matched by the seeming impossibility of a remake of a 28-year-old game winning Game of the Year. That said, it looks stronger than much of the competition, most of which is struggling to maintain momentum in one way or another; the most recent entry, Phantom Blade Zero, seems to have failed to capture the conversation.

Why it could win: Resident Evil is a reliable contender at The Game Awards, with three GOTY nominations since 2019, and many more in other categories. Requiem combines the fan appeal of the remakes with the freshness of a new entry, and blends their gameplay successfully, too. It's slickly produced, digestible, thrilling, with both global appeal and a serious side: a perfect Game Awards GOTY contender.

Weaknesses: Requiem's critical reception was very good overall, but perhaps a tiny bit soft to be a true GOTY contender — it sits in the high 80s on Metacritic and OpenCritic. How well it fares in the long run will depend on the strength of the competition, but for now, it's in the lead.

Momentum (holding steady): Potential challengers to Requiem's status as pack leader just keep falling by the wayside. Nothing else released this year combines critical acclaim with a perfect Game Awards genre profile so effectively, and nothing else will until GTA 6 comes out. It's a lock for a nomination.

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of Resident Evil Requiem.

Why it could win: A beloved classic, with a reputation as the best game ever made, lavishly remade by a team at the top of their game, and showered in critical plaudits like no other game this year. It may be just a remake, but Nintendo has mustered a huge sense of event around Ocarina, from its dramatic visual reinvention to its bold positioning against GTA 6 in the calendar.

Weaknesses: After all, though, it's still a remake of an old game, and a very faithful one. The jury will want to recognize Nintendo's achievement here (as it has done for the likes of Resident Evil 4 and Final Fantasy 7 Remake in the past), but a Game of the Year win seems inconceivable for such a well known quantity.

Momentum (new entry): Shortly after launch, Ocarina fever is at an all-time high and shows little sign of abating. And while the art direction initially seemed divisive, players and press alike seem united in their praise.

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

Why it could win: House House's co-op puzzle adventure has a fantastic critical reputation — it currently sits at 91 on Metacritic, higher than any other game on this list. The developer has pedigree: Untitled Goose Game was a dark horse GOTY contender in 2019, and even won the overall award at DICE. It's a refined design in a currently voguish genre. Co-op games go down well at The Game Awards (It Takes Two won in 2021). And there's a good chance jury members have had a good time playing it together.

Weaknesses: As an online multiplayer game, best experienced with a group of friends, Big Walk requires time and social organization to experience properly, which may be tricky for many jury members.

Momentum (📈 from No. 4): Big Walk is now fully confirmed as the top indie title of 2026, and while it doesn't look like a traditional GOTY contender, that could be to its advantage amid a field of underachieving AAA games.

Read Giovanni Colantonio, Julia Lee, and Johnny Yu's full review of Big Walk.

Why it could win: Reviews are very strong, at 89 on Metacritic. Critics love that Fortune's Weave has united strong storytelling with refined combat in a Fire Emblem game for the first time in a long time, and it helps that it's done so on an epic canvas. There's growing recognition at the TGAs for deep and authentic Japanese-developed RPGs like Metaphor: ReFantazio, and there's big fan support too: Fire Emblem: Three Houses was an unlikely winner of the Player's Voice award.

Weaknesses: Fortune's Weave is a tactics RPG, but the Game Awards jury always nominates Fire Emblem games in the Sim/Strategy category, which never overlaps with Game of the Year. If it is nominated, it will be the first strategy game ever to break into GOTY consideration. And as a Nintendo release, it may be eclipsed by the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake.

Momentum (📉 from No. 3): Fortune's Weave still looks like the best-positioned RPG (or RPG-adjaccent game) of 2026. But it hasn't quite managed to break containment and reach beyond series and genre fans, while some aspects of the game are proving more divisive than they seemed at first.

Read Josh Broadwell's full review of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave.

Why it could win: Phantom Blade Zero is this year's Black Myth: Wukong, a visually spectacular action game from an exciting new Chinese studio that muscled its way into the GOTY race. Unlike Black Myth, and unlike this year's Korean competitor Crimson Desert, it's got strong reviews (88 on Metacritic, 90 on OpenCritic).

Weaknesses: While it has reviewed well, Phantom Blade hasn't quite pulled away from a crowded action-adventure field that will be competing for the last couple of nominations, including Control Resonant and 007 First Light.

Momentum (📉 from No. 2): Phantom Blade Zero had a colossal launch on Steam (presumably powered by its Chinese fans) but has notably failed to inspire any conversation at all in critical circles, which doesn't bode well for its status with the jury.

Read Paulo Kawanishi's full review of Phantom Blade Zero.

Why it could win: IO Interactive's debut James Bond game has made a confident splash with critics, earning a decent 87 Metascore. This kind of slick, cinematic action-adventure usually goes down well with the jury, while the inclusion of some of Hitman developer IO's trademark "social stealth" gameplay lends it additional gamer cred.

Weaknesses: Licensed games very rarely get nominated for Game of the Year, and First Light's critical reception is a little soft, with some reviewers unimpressed by IO's shift in a more commercial direction.

Momentum (holding steady): Like Crimson Desert before it (only better), 007 refuses to be dislodged from this list. Until GTA comes along, it stands as the best-executed classical AAA adventure of the year, which stands it in good stead for GOTY.

Read Ford James' full review of 007 First Light.

The Blood of Dawnwalker: This vampire RPG from key talent behind The Witcher 3 underwhelmed a little on release, and lives deep in its big brother's shadow, but it's going to be a Best Narrative contender and is a perfect Game Awards game in many ways.

Star Wars Zero Company: It would be unprecedented for one strategy game to breach the GOTY field, never mind two, but jury members who have stuck with Bit Reactor's tactics game have universally fallen in love with it, and will be strong advocates for it.

Pragmata: Capcom's endearingly old-school sci-fi action game has some strong sentiment behind it, and gameplay that's innovative enough to register.

Pokémon Pokopia: On review sentiment alone, Pokopia would be a lock for a nomination, but as a life sim and a Pokémon game, it isn't what we usually think of as GOTY material. Nevertheless, it remains in the conversation.

Crimson Desert: Pearl Abyss' much-hyped everything game never gathered the critical support necessary to compete, and yet it remains on the fringes of the competition through sheer tenacity.

Control Resonant: Never rule out Remedy Entertainment at The Game Awards, although Resonant's reception is perhaps not what the developer was hoping for.

Grand Theft Auto 6: The presumptive Game of the Year looks like a dead cert… as long as it makes its release date, which is only days before The Game Awards' eligibility deadline.

#3523. Christopher Nolan's Batman Begins Borrowed Part Of Its Plot From A Beloved Animated Series Episode

In each of the three "Dark Knight" trilogy films, the villains make an attempt to destroy Gotham City from within. In "Batman Begins," one of those villains is Doctor Jonathan Crane/The Scarecrow (Cillian Murphy). The head of Gotham's Arkham Asylum, Crane is obsessed with fear. With ingredients provided by the League of Shadows, he's manufactured a "fear toxin" that can drive anyone exposed to it to terror. Using Arkham inmates, Crane has been dumping the toxin into Gotham's water supply via the asylum's pipe systems.

"Scarecrow tries to infect Gotham City with fear toxin" has become a stock "Batman" plot, like in the 2015 video game "Batman: Arkham Knight" or the 2021 comic crossover "Fear State." Look back, though, and you'll find it before "Batman Begins" — specifically, in "Batman: The Animated Series" episode "Dreams in Darkness," written by Judith and Garfield Reeves-Stevens. Batman, exposed to the Scarecrow's fear toxin and suffering hallucinations, is judged insane and locked inside Arkham as a patient.

Under his doctors' noses, Scarecrow plots to dump his toxin into an underground river that flows into Gotham's reservoirs, infecting the city and sparking a mass frenzy of fear. Crane isn't doing it for ransom or a statement; a former academic, he's running a mass experiment in studying the psychological effects of fear.

Still, it's hard to write off the similarities between "Dreams in Darkness" and "Batman Begins" as coincidental. The scene of Batman (Christian Bale) defeating Crane is even taken from a different "Batman: The Animated Series" episode: Scarecrow's debut, "Nothing to Fear." Batman poisons Scarecrow with "his own medicine," causing Crane to hallucinate Batman as not merely a man in a bat costume but a demonic, man-sized bat creature.

Whereas in "Dreams in Darkness" Crane is moving in and out of his cell, "Batman Begins" put him in control of Arkham (reimagining Crane's original backstory as a college professor). "Dark Knight" trilogy co-writer David S. Goyer has said he convinced Christopher Nolan that Scarecrow needed to wear his mask, and they devised a practical reason: The mask is a gas mask that keeps Crane from ingesting his fear toxin and scaring his victims who do. That is not the case in "Dreams in Darkness," where Crane is exposed to the toxin while in costume and ends the episode back in his cell as a hysterical mess.

Goyer has said the selection of Scarecrow as the villain of "Batman Begins" came out of the movie's theme of confronting fear. If you're going to steal, steal from the best, because "Dreams in Darkness" is a masterclass at showing Scarecrow getting under Batman's skin. It's the most frightening Scarecrow episode of "Batman: The Animated Series" and the only one that actually comes close to being a horror story, thanks to Batman's repeated and menacing hallucinations.

The first fright is a jump scare; Batman sees the Joker walking towards him reflected on the Batcomputer's screen, only to turn around and find it was Alfred. The terror doesn't let up, and once Batman makes it to Arkham, there's also the dash of psychological horror. Batman is locked in the same asylum as his greatest foes, where no one believes his pleas, and their doubt could cost a city's worth of lives. Granted, the doctors' refusal to believe Batman does border on incompetence. Scarecrow wanting to poison the city is just another night in Gotham, but Arkham's staff treat Batman like he's raving mad.

Many of the best "Batman: The Animated Series" episodes feel like 22-minute film noirs, and "Dreams in Darkness" is no exception. The episode begins in media res at Arkham, with the opening twist that the "new patient" the doctors are talking about is Batman. Batman gets a voiceover narration — a noir staple — as flashbacks explain how he ended up in a straitjacket.

The hallucinations get worse before they get better. Batman's cell door swings wide open, bathing him in a hellish red light. His parents walk into a dark tunnel, disappearing as that tunnel becomes the barrel of a giant handgun. Once Batman escapes and makes it to the caverns where Scarecrow dwells, he imagines a rat taking on the Joker's face. Imagined villains then keep gruesomely metamorphosing into others. As Batman imagines himself falling into an abyss, the darkness becomes a spiral shape with Scarecrow's face in the center.

It's beautifully animated and genuinely creepy stuff; the central image of Batman falling looks right out of Alfred Hitchcock's "Vertigo."

As for the straw-man of the hour, Scarecrow doesn't appear much. He only shows up onscreen halfway through and spends his time waiting on a countdown for his experiment. But "Dreams in Darkness" is Scarecrow voice actor Henry Polic II's best, and most subtle, performance in the role. His baritone is soft, almost mellifluous, which only makes moments like Scarecrow's cruel snicker at how he's left Batman "much, much worse" off than death more unnerving. Polic's time as Scarecrow can be overshadowed by Jeffrey Combs' later, superior performance on "The New Batman Adventures," but "Dreams in Darkness" shows he could be as great a Scarecrow as Combs — or, indeed, Cillian Murphy.

#3522. Alan Ritchson's R-Rated Sci-Fi Thriller Is One Of Netflix's Best

Netflix has many exciting sci-fi movies and TV shows, but this one starring Alan Ritchson is easily one of the best when it comes to the popular genre on the streaming service. Ritchson has become one of the biggest names in the world. He was already popular with superhero fans, given that the actor's list of projects includes Smallville and Titans.

However, it was as Jack Reacher, the live-action take on the action hero from Lee Child's bestselling novels, in Prime Video's Reacher that Ritchson became a global star. Now, the actor has pretty much his choice of projects, with each new season of Reacher breaking records for Prime Video and Ritchson signing on for creative action movies of different tones outside his work on the thriller series.

Now take Netflix's slate of releases, which has quite a few major sci-fi projects, ranking from TV shows that have become forever linked to the streamer, such as Stranger Things and Black Mirror, and movies that dominated streaming for a time, like Sandra Bullock's Bird Box. Ritchson added to that sci-fi slate on Netflix in 2026 with one of its most action-packed releases.

The actor might have become famous for his work on Reacher on Prime Video, but Ritchson proved in 2026 that he could excel in other streamers without the built-in Jack Reacher audience. War Machine is a violent R-rated sci-fi thriller movie starring the actor, and while Netflix has released many exciting original movies over the years, it is safe to say that Ritchson's action flick is among the streamer's best.

Story-wise, War Machine is pretty straightforward, as it starts as a simple war movie, with Ritchson's 81, a US Army Staff Sergeant, in Afghanistan going through a traumatic encounter with the Taliban that leads to significant losses. However, when the movie switches genres, with a training exercise a couple of years later leading to the Reacher star's character and his new unit coming face to face with a deadly alien killing machine, the sci-fi thriller becomes one of the most intense films on Netflix's catalog. Ritchson is a mountain of a man, but even he is no match for a giant robot.

#3521. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3520. This Classic Marvel Villain Could Reshape The MCU — And Introduce Nova

With heavy-hitting villains like Loki, Thanos, the Red Skull, Galactus, and now Doctor Doom already featured — and in most cases, thoroughly defeated — in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, it's easy to wonder who might be next in line to pose a threat to the Avengers. It is, after all, pretty difficult to raise the stakes higher than the death and resurrection of half the universe in "Infinity War" and "Endgame," even when there's an entire multiverse out there just waiting to be put in danger. There is, however, one major Marvel Comics villain who has yet to step into the spotlight in the movies, with a track record as one of the deadliest enemies not just to a single team of heroes, but to the entire cosmos.

Annihilus, the insectoid ruler of the Negative Zone, has over 60 years of comics history and has proven himself to be every bit as deadly as Thanos, but without the veneer of nobility that came with the goal of seeking some kind of cosmic balance. Annihilus has no noble goals or grand designs, just a massive army of mindless drones hellbent on consuming everything in its path, and if he's introduced into the MCU, he has the potential to not only wreak havoc across the entire universe, but also pave the way to finally introduce the fan-favorite hero Nova to the big screen.

Originally introduced in 1968's "Fantastic Four Annual" #6 with the ominously over-the-top nickname of "The Living Death That Walks," Annihilus was at one point considered by director James Gunn to be the villain of "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3," and with good reason. While he's been a perennial foe for the Fantastic Four, Annihilus' most prominent and destructive moments came in the 2006 crossover "Annihilation," which saw him unleash billions of locust-like drones across the galaxy in an "Annihilation Wave" that toppled long-established star-spanning empires and still has lasting effects on the Marvel Universe two real-time decades later.

Perhaps most importantly, "Annihilation" paved the way for the introduction of the modern Guardians of the Galaxy. Rather than the original Guardians concept of a team of sci-fi heroes in the distant future of the 30th century, Annihilation and its sequel, "Annihilation Conquest," rebooted them as space-faring hard-luck heroes led by Star-Lord, which led directly to the version that made it to the MCU. As a result, Annihilus is a natural fit to face off against the Guardians in some form, so it makes sense that he'd be considered for the third film, even if the decision was ultimately made to focus more on Rocket's origin and pit the heroes against the High Evolutionary instead.

Despite not making it into "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3," Annihilus remains one of the biggest comic book supervillains who hasn't been tapped for a role in the movies, providing the MCU with an opportunity — although not necessarily one that fans might expect. After "Annihilation," Annihilus wasn't just tied to the Fantastic Four, but found a new arch-enemy: Nova.

The Nova Corps were introduced to the MCU back in the first "Guardians" movie as an organization of galactic peacekeepers, but Earth's representative, Richard Rider, has been floating around for years as a potential addition to the franchise. We haven't seen him yet, but if the films continue to draw on the events of "Annihilation," the fact that the Corps is already established makes it possible for the films to recreate one of the comic's biggest moments. As the opening shot in his war against the rest of the galaxy, Annihilus, well, annihilates the Nova Corps on the planet Xandar, leaving Rider as the sole survivor. Rich does eventually get his revenge, literally punching down Annihilus' throat and tearing out his guts in one of the most truly badass moments in Marvel Comics history, and one that plenty of fans would love to see recreated in the films.

Of course, insectoid space dictators and comic books being what they are, Annihilus did eventually make his way back from the dead, but that could be very beneficial considering that unlike the comics, the movies have a tendency to kill off their villains. Giving them the ability to return and rise again allows their characters to develop over time alongside the heroes, even if some of them definitely deserve their fate.

#3519. HBO Max and Paramount+ Are Officially Headed for the End of an Era

It's been just over a month since the merger between Skydance and Warner Bros. was finalized, yet the full impact of the over $110 billion megadeal is only just beginning to be felt. David Ellison's combined media giant agreed to produce and release a slate of at least 30 films a year, which should be easy to accomplish with both WB and Paramount remaining creatively independent from one another and 2027 already having 36 projects lined up. To fit the companies together, however, Skydance is seeking to cut $6 billion in costs, which has so far resulted in layoffs across all sectors of the company, most recently at Skydance Games. Changes are also coming to the company's streaming strategy.

On Monday, the company shared in its latest quarterly earnings report that it will begin packaging HBO Max and Paramount+ in a "single bundle" that will provide access to both streamers for better value starting in early 2027. That's no real surprise, considering Warner Bros. was already aggressive in bundling its platform with competitors, but this combination is particularly meaningful. It's described as a "first step toward bringing together Paramount+ and HBO Max" into one "fully unified offering." Since the merger, Ellison has been vocal about wanting to marry the two under a single service, but details are scarce on how that will be done exactly. At the very least, Skydance believes the timeline for aligning the two platforms' backends will be quicker than how long it took to integrate Pluto TV with Paramount+.

Combining the two platforms will be a tall task for Skydance, considering the technological lift such an app will require. There's an understandable fear that, like with HBO Max's merger with Discovery+, there will be a wave of content removals to consolidate the two forces. So far, though, no date is set for this union, and no strategy has been publicly shared as to how it'll be accomplished. However, there's confidence the company's new tools and experience with Pluto TV will also lead to a quicker process for creating one app that will bring shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Pitt, and Lanterns under the same roof as the wider Star Trek and Yellowstone universes once the backend systems are in line. The company wrote in its letter to shareholders:

“The integration of Pluto TV with Paramount+ took about 18 months. Drawing on that experience, our combined technology team, and the latest in AI tools, we expect to bring Paramount+ and HBO Max together much faster, aiming to align our backend systems within a year of closing, enabling us to quickly deliver a unified product.”

More details about the Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle and the future of the two platforms will be shared in the coming months. Stay tuned here at Collider for further updates.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3516. Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Gives Its Best Boy the Happy Ending He Deserved Decades Ago

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a mostly faithful remake, true, but there's a generous handful of tweaks and expansions that fill out this version of Hyrule beautifully. Most of those changes are grim. This game is sad — if speaking to the Kokiri after clearing The Great Deku Tree dungeon didn't clue you in on that, just chat to people with the Mask of Truth on — and it wants you to be sad too. One of these changes flies in the face of misery and is defiantly happy, though, and it involves the game's bestest boy: Richard.

Richard is a dog, a very good dog. You might even say the best dog. Though even if you didn't, his owner, Mamamu Yan, certainly would. She lives in Castle Town at the start of the game, and her favorite things to do are watch Richard play and talk about how much she loves Richard. It's cute! Less cute when she's rude about the town's other dogs, but no pup can choose their owner, I guess. It's not Richard's fault. He's a blameless angel.

And in the 2011 Nintendo 3DS version of Ocarina of Time, he's a literal angel. After young Link spends seven years in the Sacred Realm, Castle Town is in ruins thanks to Ganondorf and an army of ReDead, the Zelda series' version of zombies. Navi doesn't say it when you get her to tattle on the monsters, but given how much of a horror show the rest of the game is, it seems pretty likely these creatures used to be the denizens of Castle Town. Not all of the town's weird and wonderful folks died, though. Some of them escaped to Kakariko Village, including Mamamu Yan. In the 3DS version, she speaks of Richard in the past tense. He was the best dog, a famous one, even. Mamamu Yan doesn't seem particularly distressed about Richard's death, but I certainly was when I played.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

In the Switch 2 Ocarina of Time remake, Richard lives! He's alive and well, frolicking happily around Kakariko Village during the daytime and remaining decidedly un-lost at night. Little guy obviously learned his lesson back in Castle Town. Anyway, I originally thought maybe Mamamu Yan was one of those people who names every pet the same thing. Maybe this was Richard the Third or something. But no, it's the same wonderful little fuzzball from before. Mamamu Yan waxes at length about the virtues and splendor of her Richard, with no mention of ancestors or dead Richards or anything of that kind.

It's a sweet little bright spot and a welcome one after stumbling into the village following the horrors of Future Castle Town. Good boy, Richard. May you live forever.

#3515. Shonen Jump's New Final Villain Transformation Is The Best In 15 Years

WARNING: SPOILERS FOR ONE PIECE MANGA CHAPTER #1198Most of Shōnen Jump's best manga feature incredible character designs, especially for their final-arc villains, and author Eiichiro Oda has delivered arguably the most intimidating antagonist the medium has seen in years. Beloved series like Dragon Ball, Naruto, and Jujutsu Kaisen each gained considerable fan bases worldwide during their years of publication. Those stories introduced progressively intense villains, but as One Piece approaches its final arc, it's delivered in ways that others have not.

One Piece’s manga began its long journey almost 30 years ago with chapters released weekly on Shōnen Jump. Since then, the rate of its releases has changed, and so has the quality of its storytelling. Few series earn the chance to continue their tales in the highly competitive publication, but even fewer manage to grow as One Piece has. After 33 story arcs, the series has managed not only to avoid becoming stale, but it continues to grow an audience at a rate that's beaten Dragon Ball for years. And it's not done yet.

One Piece is one of the most iconic, beloved, and long-running anime and manga ever. In all of its history, what are the best arcs in the story?

The ongoing joke is that One Piece will never end, but author Eiichiro Oda declared that Luffy's story has reached its final saga. Events that have transpired during the Egghead and Elbaph arcs have delivered several extremely satisfying plot twists the epic has teased for years, with one of my personal favorites being the reveal of the secret King of the World, Saint Nerona Imu. A shadowy, otherworldly figure who has taken on a new form that oozes final boss aura.

In One Piece chapter #1198, the Straw Hat Pirates and their Giant allies are completely overshadowed by Imu's latest transformation that towers far above the clouds of the Elbaph, the Giants' homeland. When the mysterious ruler of the World Government first arrived on the island, his overwhelming presence and Haki could be felt across the entire landmass, and even knocked out many with his aura alone. While Imu's first form resembles an imposing devil, his latest transformation makes him look more like a colossal divine being of punishment and a mix of something like Bleach's Arrancar and Neon Genesis Evangelion's Evas.

Anime has exploded in popularity recently, so it's natural to wonder what series in the medium rank among the best to watch all the way through.

Imu's new form far surpasses Loki in size, which is saying something because he's one of the largest Giants in One Piece’s history. The secret ruler is now clad in a long white robe, covering his dark skin while huge black rings covered in eyes rotate around his horned figure. Huge black wings also surround Imu, who is shockingly fast for his colossal size, as displayed by his quick dispatching of Loki's new Hybrid Dragon form. The villain has shifted their size before, but this is easily one of, if not the largest characters in One Piece's world.

According to Usopp, Imu's current overwhelming appearance looks like "It's the end of the damn world!" and it's tough to disagree with him. Although Imu states in chapter #1198 that his current power requires too heavy a toll on him to last much longer, it's difficult to see how any of One Piece's strongest characters could do anything against the figure. But Luffy's brand-new beast Nika transformation is sure to provide some surprises for both readers and Imu. But there is no denying that One Piece has reached a scale worthy of the best final arcs that Shonen can provide.

As a huge fan of the Naruto series, I am no stranger to incredible villain introductions, with Madara's assault against the Allied Shinobi Alliance being a personal favorite. Dragon Ball, Jujutsu Kaisen, and My Hero Academia have all provided top-tier moments that have made their antagonists intimidating and badass at the same time. Still, the levels of shock and dread that Eiichiro Oda has been able to deliver with his villains are something to behold, and worthy of taking notes on for aspiring storytellers.

The way that One Piece has gradually built up its world, mysteries, and characters ranks among the best that fiction can provide. The World Government's shadow leader, Saint Nerona Imu, is a prime example of all three of those important storytelling facets. A balance that very few of the world’s most popular stories accomplish with their antagonists.

For years, it was assumed that the World Government's darkest deeds were organized by the mysterious Five Elders, but everything was flipped on its head in chapter #908 when the Elders were shown bowing to Imu's silhouette as he sat on the World Government's symbolic Empty Throne. It took over 20 years for the secret ruler of One Piece's World Government to enter the story, and chapter #1198 felt like the first real look at the demonic ruler’s full majesty.

It’s unlikely that any other series will be able to build up to such a moment that One Piece has pulled off with Imu’s assault on Elbaph. But what’s even more exciting is that Oda has yet to reach the climax of his story, and readers are likely in for many more surprises in the last couple of years of One Piece’s publication.

#3514. All 5 Finalists For The Next James Bond, Ranked

Now that Amazon has paid an exorbitant price for the James Bond franchise and made us all wait what seems like an eternity to find out who will play the new 007, it's almost time for an official announcement. At this point, plenty of names have been bandied about and auditions have been ongoing for some time. Now, however, it looks as though Amazon is preparing to crown a successor to Daniel Craig.

Producers have reportedly whittled prospective James Bond actors down to five finalists, including "Disclosure Day" and "Wake Up Dead Man" star Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner of "Fantastic Beasts" and "Eternity" fame, and Jack Lowden, who plays River Cartwright on the best spy show on TV, "Slow Horses." The trio are said to have carried out screen tests alongside Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult, though at this point it remains unclear who will actually don the tux and embark on yet another mission for King and country.

But that just means we have time for a bit more speculation ahead of an official announcement. Bearing in mind Craig's "Casino Royale" casting prompted a major backlash in the early 2000s, before he delivered the greatest James Bond movie ever made, all of this should be taken with a pinch of salt. Nobody can say for sure how well suited an actor is to a role, and whoever is cast will no doubt put their all into bringing England's greatest spy to life. But Amazon MGM Studios sure are taking their sweet time announcing the next Bond, so in the meantime we might as well rank the frontrunners.

Thus far, Nicholas Hoult has missed out on playing both Batman and Superman, losing the former to fellow Bond contender Robert Pattinson. As talented an actor as he is, if we're considering him alongside these other candidates, he should probably miss out on Bond, too.

That's not to say he wouldn't do a decent job in the role. Hoult has proven himself a versatile performer, delivering memorable turns as villains in both the critically-acclaimed 2024 crime thriller "The Order" and "Superman," in which he played an intensely odious tech bro Lex Luthor. But there's just something a bit too boyish about Hoult, and it's not just the fact he came to prominence as a child actor.

It all depends on what sort of story director Denis Villeneuve has planned for his Bond movie. Perhaps Hoult has exactly what the "Dune" filmmaker is looking for. But in a general sense, not only does the British star seem to lack a bit of the grit required to play a decent 007, he's also already a well known actor. The best Bonds have all been relative newcomers with a bit of a darkness to them. I'm sure Hoult could manage it, but compared to the other frontrunners, I just don't see it.

Callum Turner isn't the most recognizable face among the five Bond finalists, but I think that's a good thing. What's more, while he's yet to deliver a definitive performance and might be seen as perhaps a tad forgettable based on his performances in the "Fantastic Beasts" films, I get the sense that, with 007, Turner could prove the naysayers wrong.

As Idles frontman Joseph Talbot once sang, "I don't care about the next James Bond / He kills for country, Queen and God / We don't need another murderous toff." But what about a murderous spy with a working class background? The best James Bond, Sean Connery, took the long road to acting, having grown up in the working class area of Edinburgh known as Fountainbridge before dropping out of school at 13 and considering a career as a professional soccer player. When he debuted as 007, he was still a little rough around the edges and that served him well in the role.

Turner similarly grew up on a council estate and, oddly enough, was also committed to a soccer career. As such, there's an authenticity and an edge to the British actor. If Villeneuve can help him capitalize on that, and Turner can find a fresh way to work it into his performance (Connery, Timothy Dalton, and Daniel Craig have all brought a similar roughness to their Bond portrayals) then he could make a great Craig replacement.

At first, Robert Pattinson seems like a bit of a safe choice for Bond. A well-spoken London boy with a middle class upbringing and a string of well-received performances — if Denis Villeneuve and the Amazon MGM producers wanted to play it safe, Pattinson seems like the man. But this is an actor who, over the past decade especially, has consistently proven his ability to completely disappear into a role.

Since giving his most Pattinsonian performance in the Safdie Brothers' "Good Time," the actor has shown a particular affinity for playing creepy little weirdos, such as the lascivious Rev. Preston Teagardin in "The Devil All the Time." But he's also delivered a compelling, understated turn as the Dark Knight in "The Batman" and an uncanny rendition of "To Catch a Predator" host Chris Hanson in "Primetime." At this point, Pattinson is easily one of the most talented and chameleonic actors working today.

With that in mind, it's impossible to imagine him dropping the ball with Bond. Pattinson always makes interesting choices and that hasn't failed him yet. As safe as he might seem on the surface, he could prove to be the biggest wild card of the bunch, and unlike Nicholas Hoult, is much more capable of completely disappearing into a role. That's a major advantage for anyone taking on Bond, which, coupled with everything else Pattinson could bring to the role, surely makes him one of the most exciting candidates.

Josh O'Connor has all of the makings of a great James Bond, even if they're not as apparent on the surface. One might look at the star of "Challengers" and assume that he doesn't have the look to play 007, or that he's not muscular enough. However, virtually every Bond actor that came before had to live in the shadow of whoever preceded him. The worst thing the producers could do is to just try and replicate Daniel Craig.

Shifting to a guy like O'Connor would be an unexpected move, yet an exciting one. For one, he meets all of the James Bond requirements according to the casting director. He can look like a regular guy and, most importantly, he's a brilliant actor. He starred alongside Craig in last year's "Wake Up Dead Man," alongside some truly phenomenal, established actors, and went toe-to-toe with all of them. So much so that he came out of that film with quite possibly the best performance of them all. That's no small thing.

O'Connor is also responsible for some of the sexiest moments in "Challengers," while starring alongside Zendaya and Mike Faist. He can be sexy. He's a great actor. He's done action in movies like "Disclosure Day." He's also not so famous to have built up a fixed perception among audiences. He can make Bond his own and mold himself into the role, while clearly being a very different actor than the man who went before him. O'Connor is, using history as our guide, right for the job.

"Slow Horses" is one of the best spy shows on TV. While much of that is down to an unforgettable performance from Gary Oldman as the delightfully disheveled Jackson Lamb, as River Cartwright Jack Lowden has quietly been making a case for himself as one of Britain's best actors.

The Scottish star plays his misfit sleuth with an intriguing mix of world weariness and ambition, crafting a fully realized performance that is one of the best parts of "Slow Horses." His Season 6 relationship with Olivia Cooke's Sidonie Baker was one of the most surprisingly affecting aspects of the entire series — a testament to both actors' talent for convincingly emotional performances. He's also more than proven he has a razor sharp comedic sense that allows him to nail the sardonic wit of author Mick Herron, which originated in the "Slough House" novels and pervades the Apple TV series adaptation.

Bond is, obviously, a very different character. But Lowden has demonstrated such talent as River, clearly has major potential, and isn't yet a major A-lister. Add to that his ability to deliver darkly funny dialogue and his naturalistic sensibility which has made River feel so human, and Lowden is surely the most exciting Bond prospect. I'd be fascinated to see what he does as 007, more so than anybody else on this list, and that's why he's here at number one.

#3513. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3512. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3511. Clint Eastwood’s True-Crime Thriller Is Officially Netflix’s Next ‘Mindhunter’

There's something about these true-crime stories that gets us particularly riled up and curious, isn't there? After all, truth is stranger than fiction and so on, and so forth. And we love them, don't we? Netflix has made an entire industry out of exploring complicated investigations, miscarriages of justice, and the darker corners of American criminal history, but few of its productions have left quite the same impression as Mindhunter. And while fans are still mourning the loss of David Fincher's extraordinary psychological thriller, one of Clint Eastwood's most overlooked movies has just arrived to help fill the void.

Eastwood's 2019 true-crime drama Richard Jewell has officially landed on Netflix in the United States, joining the platform on November 1. The movie is based on one of the most stunning and dramatic crime sagas in recent American history, exploring how an ordinary American hero ended up at the center of one of the country's biggest ever criminal investigations.

The world is first introduced to Richard Jewell (Paul Walter Hauser) as the security guard who reports finding the device during the 1996 Atlanta bombing – his report making him a hero whose swift actions saved countless lives. But within days, the law enforcement wannabe becomes the FBI’s number one suspect, vilified by press and public alike, his life ripped apart. Reaching out to independent, anti-establishment attorney Watson Bryant (Sam Rockwell), Jewell staunchly professes his innocence. But Bryant finds he is out of his depth as he fights the combined powers of the FBI, GBI and APD to clear his client’s name, while keeping Richard from trusting the very people trying to destroy him.

The cast stars Hauser (Black Bird) and Rockwell (Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri), alongside Kathy Bates (Misery) as Bobi Jewell, Jon Hamm (Mad Men) as Tom Shaw, Olivia Wilde (House) as Kathy Scruggs, Nina Arianda (Goliath) as Nadya, Ian Gomez (Cougar Town) as Agent Dan Bennet, and Dylan Kussman (Dead Poets Society) as Bruce Hughes.

The film earned approximately $22.3 million domestically and holds a 77% critics' score and 96% verified audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Bates also received an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress.

Richard Jewell is streaming now on Netflix in the United States, and is available to purchase on digital. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.

#3510. Catherine O'Hara's 8 Funniest Movie & TV Performances Ranked, Including Home Alone

Catherine O'Hara was one of the funniest people to ever grace entertainment. She has an amazing ability to make even the weirdest characters feel like real people. Whether she was giving a ridiculous line or showing a depth of emotion that you wouldn’t expect behind her wacky characters, she always knew how to create some incredible comedy with subtlety. Often her acting would be very detailed, and audiences could get as much enjoyment out of the smallest of facial expressions or change in tone as from the script itself.

Over the course of more than five decades, O'Hara has been involved in many different forms of comedy, including sketch, indie films, blockbusters and TV. She has worked with some of the most unique comedians and had some incredibly successful long-term partnerships with Eugene Levy and Christopher Guest. Theses led to some incredible mockumentaries where her improvisational skills could truly flourish.

O'Hara's greatest comedic achievement was arguably her fearlessness. She could play characters who were desperately self-important, spectacularly oblivious or completely detached from reality without losing the humanity that made them so enjoyable.

Christopher Guest's Hollywood satire For Your Consideration is a particularly entertaining exploration of the absurdity surrounding movie awards. O’Hara plays Marilyn Hack, an actress starring in the independent period drama Home for Purim, whose prospects suddenly change when rumors circulate that she might receive an Academy Award nomination.

O'Hara expertly conveys Marilyn's increasingly desperate relationship with celebrity. Her performance captures the way an ordinary person can become almost unrecognizable when surrounded by agents, publicity campaigns and the possibility of professional validation.

The funniest moments are often when O'Hara exposes Marilyn's insecurity without making her entirely unsympathetic. Her increasingly affected behavior and awkward attempts to navigate Hollywood's publicity machinery make for excellent satire, particularly alongside Eugene Levy's similarly recognition-hungry character.

It's a wonderfully observed performance, although Marilyn's comic predicament doesn't quite offer the same memorable character work as O'Hara's strongest collaborations with Guest.

Christopher Guest's A Mighty Wind is an affectionate mockumentary about a reunion concert celebrating several influential 1960s folk groups. O’Hara plays Mickey Crabbe, formerly one half of the successful musical duo Mitch & Mickey, alongside Eugene Levy's Mitch Cohen.

Their complicated history provides the film's emotional center. After considerable professional success together, their romantic relationship ended painfully, leaving Mitch with unresolved feelings that become increasingly apparent as they prepare for their reunion performance.

O'Hara is particularly funny when Mickey discusses her musical career with an almost entirely straight-faced seriousness, especially when recalling the duo's unusual experiences and the peculiar circumstances surrounding their separation.

The highlight is undoubtedly the Oscar-nominated song "A Kiss at the End of the Rainbow." O'Hara and Levy make the performance genuinely moving, allowing the characters' complicated feelings to emerge through their music. This emotional sincerity in A Mighty Wind is precisely what makes the comedy work so well.

O'Hara's years on SCTV established the foundations of her distinctive comedic style. It allowed her to experiment with impressions, exaggerated personalities and recurring characters over several years. Having joined Toronto's Second City before becoming part of the television ensemble, she developed an impressive collection of comic creations that demonstrated her extraordinary versatility.

Among her most memorable characters was Lola Heatherton, an aggressively cheerful lounge singer whose confidence dramatically exceeded her actual talent. O'Hara's exaggerated smiles, theatrical gestures and increasingly desperate attempts to maintain her glamorous image made Lola an exceptionally funny parody of entertainment personalities.

O'Hara tackled celebrity impressions including Brooke Shields, Lucille Ball, Meryl Streep and Katharine Hepburn, frequently finding hilarity in their speech patterns and public personas rather than relying on superficial physical resemblance.

Although her later film and television characters became more widely recognized, Second City Television was where O'Hara proved just how inventive her comedy could be.

O'Hara's first major collaboration with Christopher Guest remains one of her funniest. In Waiting for Guffman, O’Hara plays Sheila Albertson, a travel agent in the fictional Missouri town of Blaine who dreams of becoming a successful theatrical performer.

Married to Ron (Fred Willard), Sheila considers herself part of an exceptionally talented entertainment partnership, despite the couple's rather limited abilities. Their audition for the town's anniversary musical, featuring a hilariously awkward rendition of "Midnight at the Oasis," is an absolute masterclass in playing complete artistic incompetence with absolute sincerity.

O'Hara's comic timing is particularly effective during the couple's interactions. She frequently anticipates Ron's dialogue, enthusiastically joining in before he has finished speaking.

The Chinese restaurant scene is another standout. As Sheila becomes increasingly intoxicated, O'Hara gradually shifts her delivery and physical mannerisms. Her ability to play drunkenness without losing Sheila's underlying personality makes the sequence especially memorable.

Playing Kate McCallister in the first two Home Alone movies required O'Hara to balance broad family comedy with the increasingly frantic emotions of a mother who has accidentally left her youngest child behind. Considering how ridiculous the premise becomes, her performance is essential to making the situation believable.

In the original film, Kate's gradual realization that Kevin (Macaulay Culkin) is missing culminates in her unforgettable scream of his name. O'Hara makes the moment hilarious through its sheer desperation.

The sequel gives her another opportunity to explore that same panic. Her determination to get back to her son provides the emotional backbone to the movies, offering the ideal counterbalance to the increasingly elaborate slapstick surrounding him.

O'Hara brings genuine warmth to Kate's reunion with Kevin, particularly in the original film's final moments. Her ability to make the character simultaneously exasperated, loving, and completely overwhelmed is a major reason the Home Alone movies are still so enjoyable.

Tim Burton's Beetlejuice gave O'Hara one of her most distinctive film characters ever in Delia Deetz. Delia is an aspiring artist with pretentious sensibilities who moves into the home of a recently deceased couple, Adam and Barbara Maitland (Alec Baldwin and Geena Davis).

Delia is determined to transform the property into a showcase for her avant-garde artistic vision. She is completely convinced of her own sophistication, even when her creative decisions are utterly bewildering to everyone around her.

Her interactions with Winona Ryder's Lydia are particularly enjoyable, as Delia repeatedly attempts to impose her artistic philosophy on a stepdaughter who has absolutely no interest in participating. Importantly, O'Hara gives Delia an exaggerated sense of self-importance without turning her into a conventional villain.

The unforgettable dinner-party sequence demonstrates her physical comedy at its finest. When the guests become possessed and begin singing Harry Belafonte's "Day-O (The Banana Boat Song)," O'Hara delivers a brilliant performance through her facial expressions and precisely synchronized movements. Delia is wonderfully ridiculous, and O'Hara's commitment makes her one of Beetlejuice's standout elements.

Moira Rose is O'Hara's definitive comedic creation, bringing together virtually every strength she developed throughout her career. In Schitt's Creek, she plays a former soap opera star whose wealthy family loses its fortune and is forced to relocate to a small town they purchased as a joke.

Moira's response to her circumstances is consistently hilarious. Her vocabulary, elaborate wardrobe, and seemingly endless collection of wigs make her look as though she has arrived from an entirely different television program. However, O'Hara's performance goes considerably further than making an extravagant character look ridiculous.

Her vocal delivery is extraordinary, particularly the deliberately unusual pronunciations that turn ordinary words into elaborate theatrical performances. Even something as simple as saying "bébé" becomes a memorable comic moment. Her attempt to advertise Herb Ertlinger's fruit wine produces one of the show's funniest sequences.

Moira's relationship with her children, David (Dan Levy) and Alexis (Annie Murphy), also gives O'Hara plenty of opportunities to demonstrate her emotional range. Beneath the vanity and theatrical self-absorption is a mother who genuinely loves her family, even if expressing that affection rarely comes naturally.

More importantly, Moira brings together Catherine O’Hara’s extraordinary vocal comedy, physical expressiveness, and ability to find humanity in even the most ridiculous personalities. It's a fitting showcase for one of comedy's most distinctive performers.

#3509. This New Chrome AI Feature Reads Your Gmail to Make Filling Out Web Forms Easier

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3507. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.
