#3506. Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Thunders with $31.6 Million, Scoring the Biggest Debut Ever for a Live-Action, Foreign Language Film

The year of unlikely box office smashes continues as “Godzilla Minus Zero” opened to a thunderous $31.6 million, shattering records to become the biggest North American debut for a live-action foreign language film in history. It easily toppled the previous benchmark established in 2002 by the wuxia epic “Hero,” which kicked off with $17.8 million. Globally, “Godzilla Minus Zero’s” haul stands at $63 million.

And it comes on the heels of a string of films that have defied conventional wisdom to resonate with moviegoers. Yes, the box office is still dominated by sequels and comic book movies like “Toy Story 5” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” but there’s been a lot more variety. Audiences have turned out in force for an original sci-fi adventure (“Project Hail Mary,” $684.6 million worldwide); a pair of low-budget horror films from 20-something auteurs with YouTube pedigree (“Obsession,” $524.3 million worldwide; “Backrooms,” $400.6 million worldwide); an adaptation of a Greek epic we were all forced to read in school (“The Odyssey,” $1.8 billion worldwide), and a three-hour documentary about a Silicon Valley cheat (“You Can See Everything,” $73.7 million and counting). Clearly, people are looking for something different. Related Stories ‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

In the case of “Godzilla Minus Zero,” it helped that the first film, 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One,” was an unexpected sleeper hit, grossing an impressive $57.1 million. But the first “Godzilla” opened to a mere $11.4 million, showing that the audience for the first monster movie grew on home entertainment. “Godzilla Minus Zero” is poised to bypass its predecessor to become the highest-grossing live-action Japanese movie in history. Once again, the film was directed by Takashi Yamazaki, who also worked on the special effects, produced by Japan’s Tojo, and distributed in the U.S. by GKids.

The success of “Godzilla Minus Zero” also demonstrates that subtitles are no barrier to box office success, something that Netflix and other streamers discovered with the popularity of local-language programming like “Squid Game,” “Money Heist,” and “Lupin.” The story at multiplexes is no different. U.S. audiences have filled auditoriums to watch “Parasite” ($53.8 million domestic), “Ne Zha 2” ($23.2 million domestic), and “Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba – The Movie: Infinity Castle” ($136.9 million domestic). The outsized grosses for “Godzilla Minus Zero” probably mean we haven’t heard the last of the fire-breathing Kaiju.

The monster movie made quick work of its main competition, Warner Bros. Animation’s “The Cat in the Hat,” which stumbled with $20 million domestically and $30 million globally. The family film cost $92 million to produce and extends a string of misses for Warner Bros., which was recently purchased by Skydance. Insiders say that the studio has lost hundreds of millions of dollars on bombs like “Digger,” “Supergirl,” and “The Bride!” and “The Cat in the Hat” won’t do much to mop up all that red ink.

#3504. 3 Best Movies on Prime Video This Week (Nov 9-13)

The number one movie on Prime Video this week is James Nunn’s 2026 creature feature Hungry. Starring Madison Davenport, the film follows a group of vacationers on a boat trip in Louisiana, where they encounter a deadly hippopotamus. While it’s had somewhat mixed reception from critics, it is a fun movie, but Hungry is hardly the only movie worth checking out on the streaming platform. Here’s a look at three great movies that we think you should watch on Prime Video this week.

For more recommendations, check out our list of the best shows and movies on Prime Video.

A film adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s novel directed by Mary Harron and starring Christian Bale, American Psycho is truly a 21st-century classic. The plot follows Bale’s Patrick Bateman, a wealthy New York City investment banker obsessed with his status, who leads a double life as a serial killer, hiding his psychopathic ego from his friends and acquaintances. The film also stars Willem Dafoe, Jared Leto, Justin Theroux, Chloë Sevigny, and Reese Witherspoon in notable roles.

Though initially considered an unfilmable novel, American Psycho has since become an icon of its genre, marked by Bale's disturbingly brilliant performance as the unhinged yuppie. The film can be called a darker mirror to 1987’s Wall Street, which blends psychological horror and black comedy to satirize the 1980s consumerist culture. When it first premiered in 2000, American Psycho received polarized reactions from critics and fans, receiving praise for the writing and acting, but also criticism for its gore and violence, though the latter has become significantly more appealing to audiences in subsequent years.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

Based on the romance novel of the same name by Melissa Hill, Something from Tiffany’s is a holiday romance comedy directed by Daryl Wein. Starring Zoey Deutch as Rachel, the film sees her life suddenly upended when she mistakenly believes that her boyfriend, Gary, was going to propose to her, unaware that his real gift got switched, setting off a chain of serendipitous events. Kendrick Sampson, Ray Nicholson, and Shay Mitchell star as other key characters.

Something from Tiffany’s is a comforting, charming romcom that warms its way into your heart without needing any big moral or life lesson. The film has generally received a positive reception from critics and fans alike and has been praised for its lighthearted comedy and seasonal story. Something from Tiffany’s might not rank among the best Christmas romance movies of all time, but it surely does make the holiday movie experience cozier with its festive setting and adorable love story.

Actor-comedian Aziz Ansari’s feature directorial debut starring himself, Good Fortune follows Arj, a down-on-his-luck gig worker working for an uber-wealthy man named Jeff, whose life gets swapped with Jeff’s after an angel named Gabriel fails to show Arj the right path. This results in Gabriel losing his wings and living with mortals, while Arj and Jeff’s respective lives begin to unravel, leading to hilarious outcomes for all three of them. Keanu Reeves and Seth Rogen round out the main trio, with Keke Palmer and Sandra Oh as other notable characters.

Good Fortune is a strong directorial debut for Ansari, who brings his brand of humor alongside the phenomenal comedic deliveries of Reeves and Rogen, a combination that makes this film a delightful experience. While sometimes heavy-handed, the timely social satire and the comedic timing of the film are unmissable. The movie premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and has received generally favorable reviews from critics, earning praise for its quality humor and the comedic timing of its leading cast. The film easily ranks among the best comedies of 2025.

#3502. Harlan Coben Will Officially Replace The Lincoln Lawyer In 2027

Netflix’s adaptation of The Lincoln Lawyer has thrilled audiences for almost five years, but now it’s drawing to a close. The next season of maverick lawyer Mickey Haller’s story will be his last new case on the streaming platform. The literary half-brother of fellow Prime Video’s Harry Bosch is being retired from streaming, it seems.

Season 5 of The Lincoln Lawyer will be released in March, after which Mickey’s detective sister Emi Finch is getting her own Netflix spinoff series, but he’ll be nothing more than a bit-part player in her story. Meanwhile, the streaming giant’s next multi-season adaptation of a hugely popular literary character – who also happens to have trained as a lawyer – is just getting started.

However, his 14th Netflix series will be a very different story. David E. Kelley and Kyle Long’s as-yet untitled Myron Bolitar project brings the character who launched Coben’s literary career to the screen for the very first time. What’s more, he’s going to front the first multiseason serial drama Coben has ever agreed to.

Netflix’s Myron Bolitar series was only confirmed back in May 2026, yet it’s already wrapped filming, and is slated for release at some point in 2027. We can expect it to follow hot on the heels of The Lincoln Lawyer’s final season, giving those in need of a good procedural mystery something similarly gripping to get hooked on.

The protagonist of 12 novels by Harlan Coben, including his 1995 breakout success Deal Breaker, Myron Bolitar is a would-be basketballer whose childhood dream of turning professional is suddenly ended by a freak injury. He turns his attention instead to becoming a sports agent, after qualifying as a lawyer from Harvard.

Harlan Coban is one of contemporary crime fiction's most prolific authors; these are the thrillers and mysteries he's been reading the last few years.

Bolitar isn’t just a taller, literary version of Jerry Maguire, though. His quick wits, keen eye for detail, rough-and-ready approach to work, and insistence on a stringent moral code, invariably take him down a rabbit hole of crime investigation, too. In fact, it’s a wonder he didn’t set out to be a private eye in the first place.

The upcoming TV adaptation of Coben’s Myron Bolitar novels will star The Continental’s Colin Woodell as its central character, alongside familiar faces such as Chloe Fineman (Saturday Night Live) and Jabari Banks (Bel-Air). Funnily enough, it also features two actors who’ve made appearances in The Lincoln Lawyer.

Besides Netflix’s Myron Bolitar adaptation borrowing Jamie McShane and Diane Guerrero from The Lincoln Lawyer, where they play Detective Lee Lankford and a season 5 character called Natalia, respectively, it looks set to steal the thunder from Mickey Haller’s last case in 2027. As Harlan Coben’s first show with multiple seasons, it’s bound to wrack up serious viewing numbers on streaming for several years to come.

Coben has had two different global number 1 hits on Netflix in 2026 alone, in the miniseries adaptations Run Away and I Find You. His most celebrated literary creation’s screen debut will be on a whole other level, though. It’s no accident that producers appear to have fast-tracked the rollout of this series to coincide with the end of The Lincoln Lawyer’s run.

Myron Bolitar’s arrival on Netflix appears to be specifically designed to replace the massive success of its flagship legal thriller, with David E. Kelley on board, no less. The similarities between Bolitar and Mickey Haller are uncanny. Both are uncompromising mavericks whose legal qualifications often conflict with their unorthodox approaches to ensuring justice is served, founded on morals they fiercely defend.

Myron and Mickey are both at their happiest enjoying their sports as well, whether it’s basketball or surfing. The Lincoln Lawyer might be ending next year, but fans can rest assured there’s already someone out there preparing to fill the void Mickey Haller will leave behind. It’s time for Michael Connelly to step aside. Harlan Coben’s best-loved protagonist is taking center stage.

#3501. Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

“You Can See Everything,” an intimate look at Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has earned nearly $80 million at the domestic box office, becoming A24‘s third-highest-grossing release in North America. It bypasses “Everything Everywhere All at Once” and its $77 million haul to take its spot on the indie studio’s chart, and that film won the Oscar for Best Picture.

With $79.8 million stateside, “You Can See Everything” sits behind the summer blockbuster “Backrooms” ($197 million) and 2025’s “Marty Supreme” ($96 million) on the list of A24 releases. Other A24 films made more globally, with “Backrooms” earning more than $400 million, “Marty Supreme” grossing $192.4 million, and “Everything Everywhere All at Once” netting $147.9 million. However, “You Can See Everything” has yet to be released in most international markets. It’s unclear if Holmes’ fraud will resonate with moviegoers so far from Silicon Valley. It doesn’t matter if it doesn’t connect, because with a budget of $7 million, “You Can See Everything” is already wildly profitable. Its success means that Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the directing duo behind the doc, are now in high demand.

“You Can See Everything” also jumped ahead of “March of the Penguins” ($77 million) on the list of highest-grossing documentaries in North America. Variety reports that makes it the second highest-grossing doc behind Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” which earned $119 million domestically. That doesn’t account for music documentaries like “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour” ($267.1 million) and “Michael Jackson’s This is It” ($268 million), which were far more popular.

A24 is on a hot streak. In addition to “Backrooms,” the indie studio has released hits like “The Drama” and “Primetime.” Its latest film, “Club Kid,” grossed an impressive $390,583 this weekend when it opened on six screens in New York and Los Angeles. That’s a per-screen average of $65,097. A24 acquired the drama about a hard-living gay man and his son out of the Cannes Film Festival, where it debuted to raves. The studio hopes to position the film and its writer, director, and star Jordan Firstman in the Oscar race.

#3499. Security Bite: The record $6.3B Binance heist started with a fake Homebrew install on Mac

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Last week, news broke that hackers had stolen $6.3 billion from wallets on Binance, the most popular cryptocurrency exchange in the world. The company was able to freeze about nearly $3 billion of it, but the attack quickly made headlines, and rightfully so, as the largest financial heist in human history.

At the time, I suspected, along with security researcher Christopher Lopez and plenty of others, that this could have very well started on a Mac. As Lopez pointed out, the $1.5 billion Bybit heist last year also began on a developer’s Mac. On top of that, Macs are hugely popular among DevOps engineers and crypto folks, and they’ve been on the receiving end of a steady stream of malware and social engineering campaigns over the past few years.

I can now say any suspicions that this heist originated on Mac were right. I’m still in a state of shock. Dazed not by the amount stolen, but how the said hackers did so using the same ol’ social engineering tricks they’ve been using for years. No sophisticated multi-milllion dollar underground zero-day here.

Yesterday, Binance published a more detailed breakdown of the attack. The company never actually says “Mac,” but the malware it published targeted /opt/homebrew, which is where Homebrew lives on Apple silicon Macs. In other words, this was almost certainly an M-series MacBook.

The attack basically transpired in two steps.

According to Binance, in June this year, a DevOps engineer working on Wallet searched for an AI coding tool and downloaded a malicious clone of the Homebrew installer in Google Search. Binance claims it caught it early and stopped any damage. However, what it didn’t know was that it allowed the attackers to learn which employees worked on its wallets. This was phase 1.

Fast forward a few months to September, a different engineer who, you guessed it, worked on wallets for Binance, was lured into a fake job interview. As these sort of social engineering attacks normally go, they told to run a coding “assignment” on their work computer. This was not caught by Binance security, and on October 29, the world learned that hackers (now widely speculated as North Korean hackers) walked off with billions.

Of course, most of what we know so far comes directly from Binance, so if you’re looking for more details on exactly how this happened, you’ll likely be left empty-handed.

It’s important to note here though, none of these two attack vectors are new. Back in early 2025, I wrote about fake Homebrew ads at the top of Google Search pushing Atomic Stealer to Mac users. Binance only says the engineer found his installer through “a search engine.” Of course, I can’t confirm it was a sponsored ad, but if history tells us anything…

This is a rather uncomfortable situation for Apple to be in. The largest financial heist in history happen on Mac last week, though to be fair, there’s no security feature that can stop a developer from running a script he wants to run.

Sure, the Terminal paste warnings introduced in macOS 26.4 could have helped here. But realistically, if someone’s convinced they’re doing a coding test for a job they really want, a warning pop-up probably isn’t going to stop them.

I’m having Christopher Lopez (@L0Psec) a professional macOS reverse engineer back on the Security Bite Podcast this week to talk about the Binance situation with me. Follow the show so you don’t miss that.

“You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s phenomenally successful documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, swept the Critics Choice Association‘s documentary awards tonight, winning each of its five categories — including Best Documentary Feature. Ava DuVernay’s “14th,” which headed into the night with the most nominations (six), went home empty-handed.

#3496. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3495. Cinematographers’ Favorite Festival Is All About AI This Year — but Artists Still Hate the Tech

During the opening ceremony of the 34th ToruńCAMERIMAGE International Film Festival on Saturday, November 7, audience members saw a human replaced by a machine right in front of their eyes. The festival’s founder and artistic director Marek Żydowicz was invited to the stage, only for a robot to walk out in his place and begin addressing the audience and thanking sponsors.

Żydowicz took the stage a few moments later and joked that none of us are immune to the threat of AI and robots coming for our jobs. (The machine was Edward Warchocki, a humanoid robot “influencer” who has gone viral in Poland for videos in which it chases wild boars around Warsaw.) The stunt set a fitting tone for a festival that has devoted this edition to covering the film industry’s most controversial topic. Warchocki remained on stage for much of the opening ceremony, later joined by an actor in an “Inland Empire” rabbit costume who helped tee up an AI-generated video in which the rabbit symbolically opened the festival gates to the new technology. Anyone hoping for a boring, consensus-driven film festival immediately had their expectations adjusted. Related Stories ‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

A festival devoted to the technological craft of filmmaking is a fitting place for these discussions. ToruńCAMERIMAGE (formerly known as Camerimage before changing its name to include its Polish host city) is an annual homecoming for cinematographers. Directors of photography are treated like rockstars at the festival, and the entire profession makes an effort to descend upon Toruń each November to discuss their craft and party late into the night. The main competition screenings are crucial to the Best Cinematography Oscar race, with so much of the voting branch in one room. Panels and Q&As often focus on the specific technical details that the overwhelmingly below-the-line audience wouldn’t hear at other festivals. The job of a cinematographer is uniquely positioned at the intersection of art and technology, and the festival was right to assume that its audience would have a lot of thoughts about the topic.

ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 is taking a pluralistic approach to the subject by giving AI advocates and opponents equal time, and the programming appears more interested in stirring the pot and sparking discussion than taking a firm position. The festival gave an honorary award to Darren Aronofsky, who has founded an AI studio that works with Google DeepMind, yet also programmed Luca Guadagnino’s biting Sam Altman satire “Artificial” as its opening night film. The opening ceremony was interspersed with video clips featuring the likes of Aronofsky, Steven Spielberg, Gal Gadot, and Ben Affleck sharing views on AI that ranged from optimistic to paranoid. The message was clear: All opinions are welcome, but we can’t put off talking about AI.

Broadly speaking, directors have been more open to the technology than cinematographers — before “Artificial” screened, Guadagnino stressed that his film was driven more by opposition to the consolidation of wealth and power in a few individuals than AI itself. He explained that he simply sees AI as a neutral tool, though he described its current filmmaking applications as a “cheap” trend that he expects to fade with time in the same way that 3D did. And while Aronofsky avoided the topic in his award acceptance speech, a video message from him played during the opening ceremony saw him repeating his mantra that film has always been a technology-driven medium and AI is simply the latest tech innovation that storytellers need to embrace.

But the cinematographers in attendance have not shied away from the bleak reality that the technology is creating. The term “we’re fucked” has been thrown around a lot, and audience questions have been fiery. The program is filled with panels about AI’s influence on cinematography, many of which focus on the rise of “greybox” filmmaking. The technique, notably employed on Doug Liman’s upcoming “Bitcoin” movie and rapidly popping up on other projects, involves filming actors on a neutral background before using AI to add all the production design and lighting during post.

Nobody is denying the practicality of the rapidly improving technology, which eliminates logistical problems relating to weather and locations that have plagued filmmakers for as long as the art form has existed. But it fundamentally alters the role of a cinematographer, whose job has always been to use light and composition techniques to create images in camera. Cinematographers speak about directors asking them for the softest, most generic lighting on set — not because it looks the best, but because it provides the blankest canvas for changing things in post. Even if you’re still booking gigs as a cinematographer, are you even doing the same job if you’re no longer lighting each image?

Cinematography has always been an art form that’s easy to recognize but hard to describe. Countless moviegoers have walked out of theaters praising a film’s cinematography while having no idea what a director of photography actually does on set and how that job overlaps with other positions. A cinematographer’s job is to make images beautiful (or ugly, when the script calls for it) with their knowledge of light and camera equipment. But directors can theoretically frame their own shots, gaffers can light them, and colorists play an increasingly large role in shaping the final look of each image. A recurring topic at the festival has been the fear that new technologies could freeze cinematographers out of the process altogether.

At a debate titled “State of the Image,” Polish cinematographer Bartosz Nalazek was initially presented as the most pro-AI voice on the panel. He explained how he recently wrapped a major TV show that used greybox techniques for 40 percent of its scenes. His message was that cinematographers have to embrace and adapt to the technology in order to keep working. After he finished his opening statement, fellow cinematographer Arthur Reinhart, a two-time recipient of the festival’s Golden Frog award, asked a simple question: “Are you enjoying the work?”

Nalazek did not hesitate to respond. “Totally not,” he said. “It’s horrible, I’m brain-dead.” He went on to explain that while hybrid production is technically easier for cinematographers, moving so much of the artistry to post-production means that “an elevated camera operator could do it.”

The topic represents a seismic change to a constant that cinematographers could always take for granted: their status as the most technologically savvy person on set. Even as filmmaking tools shifted from film stock to digital cameras, DPs stayed employed and respected because they knew how to use those tools better than anyone else. Now, for the first time in history, technology threatens to be the force that pushes them out of the decision-making process.

“I think what made cinematographers become who we are is the leverage over technology and the creative input. When we were shooting on film, that leverage was tremendous because nobody knew how to do it except the cinematographers,” Nalazek said. “What worries me is that we have this feeling that our position is undoubtable and unchangeable. We have this feeling that the director should respect us, the producer should respect us. I think running on that thought is pretty dangerous. We’re kind of in a time where we have to prove our worth. And that’s sad.”

One advantage of having these conversations at such a technically-oriented festival is that the cinematographers are also honest about what AI isn’t doing. Criticisms are often preempted with the caveat that AI is a broad, loaded term — anyone who edits in DaVinci or uses biometric functions on cameras has technically been using AI tools for years. Cinematographers who have worked on greybox sets make it clear that hybrid AI films are not made by one guy typing prompts in a room by himself. It can be true that AI has shrunk crew sizes enough for the community to feel strained while still acknowledging that these projects often employ hundreds of traditional film workers. And speakers have at times pushed back against audience questions that blame all AI adoption on strawman arguments about greedy producers and execs who could afford to pay artists but simply don’t want to. But nuance doesn’t make the problem any less existential.

Nobody knows where things are going next, but there’s a deep sense that every option and idea should be on the table right now. Some cinematographers are making peace with the notion that traditional filmmaking will become a specialized niche product, akin to artisanal pottery or handmade furniture, rather than the norm for everyday entertainment. We’ll be making a luxury product for a smaller audience willing to pay for it, and we’ll have to charge them accordingly, the thinking goes. Others have floated the idea that the on-set cinematography work of setting up shots will become a lower-level, commoditized job. Directors will still need masterful artists like Roger Deakins to advise them on lighting and image composition, but that high-level work could become more of a post-production role.

The only idea that nobody is taking seriously is that there’s anything cinematographers can do to put the AI genie back in the bottle.

“Camerimage is a place where all the cinematographers from around the world are coming,” Reinhart said. “If we had a voice, then it should be coming from here, and I hope it will. But I am not very optimistic it will change anything.”

Keeping a routine is easier when there’s something to look forward to. Mio pairs self-care and habit tracking with a pixel companion that grows as you make progress. Check off habits, earn coins, and unlock new companions and collectibles, with friends and groups adding a social reason to keep going.

Mio took Shipaton’s Grand Prize, with RevenueCat highlighting its revenue and growth in a crowded habit-tracking market.

That dog you met on your morning walk can become part of your collection. Boop identifies cats and dogs and turns their photos into stickers for a digital book, giving pet lovers a playful reason to pay attention to the animals around them.

Creator Taiwo Omisore’s “100 Boops” challenge took the app into the real world, where printed pet portraits and conversations with owners helped shape the product. That hands-on approach earned Boop first place in #BuildInPublic.

If you have fond memories of futuristic arcade racers, Nitelore has a familiar appeal: hovering vehicles, neon tracks, and plenty of speed. Chase your own ghost in time trials, take on combat races, or compete online.

Free tracks offer a starting point, while paid unlocks and daily and weekly challenges give players more to explore. RevenueCat’s Best Game judges singled out the art direction, effects, and haptics.

Explaining how you see color can be surprisingly difficult. See as Me: Colorblind makes that conversation visual, using a split-screen camera to compare different types and degrees of color blindness. A shareable link lets someone else see the comparison without installing the app.

Developer Javier Jiménez drew on his own experience with protanopia. That personal perspective helped the app earn the RevenueCat Peace Prize.

Clucky’s rooster is determined to get you out of bed. Turning off an alarm can require solving a problem, moving around, or finding an object, bringing a little friction to the temptation to snooze.

Its personality runs through the entire interface, including a time picker that uses the rooster’s scrolling eyes and yellow beak. That consistent character, animation, and attention to detail earned Clucky the RevenueCat Design Award.

Adversary starts with a familiar challenge: flip cards and find matching pairs. The catch is a hidden Danger card with no matching partner. Reveal it, and an ad becomes part of the board you’re trying to remember.

That idea earned Niv Ben-porath’s game the Catvertising Award. Players can continue with ads after an initial ad-free period, or choose a permanent unlock that removes ads and adds difficulty options.

Put a few phones on the table, and Bubble Games turns their screens into a shared game board. Objects move between devices as friends compete in minigames, including a virtual hot potato.

Built by four software engineering students at Université Laval, the Next Gen Award winner uses the phones people already have to create a shared activity. Its Shipaton submission includes ten minigames. The winner announcement links to the Android release on Google Play.

1st place • HAMM Award (Help Apps Make Money)

GRIDLOCK takes a game everyone knows and adds up to four players, online rooms, and eleven special moves. The result offers more ways to disrupt an opponent’s plans than the familiar three-by-three board.

Its HAMM Award win recognizes how the business model fits the game: a shared Credits currency connects rewarded ads, optional packs, and a subscription, while core modes remain free. Players can choose the option that fits how often they play.

1st place • Influencer Award – Nutrition & Healthy Eating: Abbey’s Kitchen

Just Add begins with a craving. Type what you feel like eating, describe it aloud, or take a photo, and the app suggests three meals built around it, adding protein, fiber, and healthy fats to round out the plate.

Shopping support, hands-free cooking, and remembered preferences help carry the idea through to dinner. The winner of Abbey’s Kitchen’s nutrition challenge also impressed judges with a dinner-host feature that accounts for other people’s preferences.

1st place • Influencer Award – Productivity: Christopher Lawley

The reply you send every week, the PDF you keep hunting for, and the image you paste repeatedly can all live in SnipStash. It organizes reusable text, images, and files across iPhone, iPad, and Mac, with a keyboard, Mac quick palette, hotkeys, and Shortcuts bringing them within reach.

Private iCloud sync connects the library across devices. Its speed and native interface helped it win Christopher Lawley’s productivity challenge.

1st place • Influencer Award – Career Coaching: Leadership Heather

Knowing what you want to say and saying it aloud are different things. Rehearse – Hard Conversations gives you an AI counterpart to practice with before a difficult workplace discussion.

Choose from 33 prepared scenarios or bring your own situation, then review feedback on clarity, empathy, assertiveness, and structure. A prep card helps you take the useful points into the real conversation. The app won Leadership Heather’s career-coaching challenge for its focused, straightforward approach.

1st place • Influencer Award – Gaming: Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming

You see a game in a short video, mean to look it up later, and forget its name. Game Magnet lets you share the clip to identify the games and save them to your backlog.

Processing happens in the background, with a notification when the result is ready. Shelves, ratings, and ranked lists help organize what comes next. The app won Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming’s challenge by making discovery and keeping track of games easier.

1st place • Influencer Award – Yoga & Fitness: Simone Sharice

FeelGood: Movement Menu starts with a short check-in about your energy, available time, and how you want to feel. It then offers a small menu of movement, with an appetizer, main, and optional sides.

The options span yoga, Pilates, strength, walking, stretching, and breathing. Rest is part of the experience, too. Yusra Salam and Ameena Malik’s app won Simone Sharice’s yoga and fitness challenge, with judges praising its calm, inviting design.

BoatBrawl brings arcade boat battles to a group of up to eight players. Steer, fire, and scramble through interactive arenas, with bots and shared-screen play offering more ways to join in.

Rehaan Cubes and Ashwin K M used Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform to bring the game across phones and computers, including iOS, Android, Mac, Windows, and the web. Its smooth browser play helped it take JetBrains’ Ship Kotlin Everywhere award.

Trazo: Golf Ball Tracer adds a ball-flight line to your own golf videos. Select the ball twice to start, and the processing runs on the phone.

Julian Praest’s app won Most Viral App for the way its team introduced the product through organic content. Golf humor and practical advice set up the tracer reveal, making the finished video part of the pitch. For golfers, the appeal is simple: make the shot easier to follow when you share it.

One Piece Card Game collectors know that similar-looking cards can be very different finds. Grandfolio helps identify artwork variants, manage duplicates, and track collection prices and progress.

The Best App for Galaxy winner impressed judges with layouts that adapt to folded, tabletop, and open-screen use. There’s an App Store release for Apple users, too, making this a relevant discovery even if your collection starts on an iPhone.

Let’s Get Support by 3Dadz is designed for partners, parents, and friends affected by someone else’s addiction. Check-ins, journaling, boundary-setting tools, and local resources give those supporters a place to focus on their own needs.

Joshua Burgess and Aaryn B. built the app from community conversations in British Columbia, using Replit to turn the idea into a live product. It won Replit’s Idea to Income award. The announcement links to its Android release.

PoquitoTalk: Bocas del Toro turns English into local Spanish voice notes for WhatsApp and helps translate the replies. The recipient doesn’t need to install the app, keeping the conversation in a tool people already use.

Creator Dorien Van den Abbeele drew on years of life in Bocas del Toro. Its Growth Loop Award recognizes extensive growth experiments and an honest account of what the measurements could show. The announcement links to Google Play.

Parky! combines wait times, dining availability, and memories from Disney and Universal visits. Built by former Disney Cast Member Chase Van Derrick, it aims to offer useful help throughout a park day.

Dining alerts can become conversations on the Lock Screen, where you can ask about another time or restaurant. Alongside queue Live Activities and recap messages, those interactive notifications helped Parky! win the Keep Them Coming Back Award.

In Your Own Words offers short, real-world speaking scenarios and feedback on pace, hesitation, and filler words. Speech analysis takes place on the phone, giving users a way to practice the words before they need them.

Natasha Wilson’s app won the Funnel Vision Award for connecting a web quiz, a relevant practice deck, and a web purchase that unlocks access in the app. The introduction to the product begins before the download.

Friendpire turns the idea of a board-game night with friends into a shared hex-tile world. Gather resources, build farms and docks, and grow an empire together. RevenueCat employee Erik MacInnis built the game to make it easier to stay connected with friends who rarely find time to play.

Friendpire won the separate Conflict of Interest Award, which was open to RevenueCat and sponsor employees and judged by Shipaton participants. It is included here as an optional sidebar and is not part of the 20 first-place count above.

From a useful tool for the workday to a game for your next night in, Shipaton’s winners show how much can come from taking an idea all the way to a shipped app. Explore the winners above, or browse RevenueCat’s full announcement for more apps from the competition.

#3493. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3492. Gilmore Girls: Every Main Character's Ending, Ranked

There's nothing that Gilmore Girls fans like better than a debate about the fates of the characters on the show. There's no shortage of discourse about the way every main character's arc ends. Some characters got satisfying, beautiful conclusions that made long-time viewers emotional. However, others left us disappointed, as even if their development made sense, it was still hard to watch.

Every episode of A Year in the Life delves into the lives of not only the Gilmores but also their loved ones and the residents of Stars Hollow. It's a nostalgic return to the town and the beloved characters, as well as an opportunity for the series to right some wrongs that happened in the original series. There are some harsh realities of being a Gilmore Girls fan, as the characters don't always make the decisions we want them to, but many character arcs come full circle in the series.

Lane is one of the best and most underrated characters in all of Gilmore Girls, and there's a general consensus that she deserved a lot better than her ending in Gilmore Girls. After Zack nearly destroys the band's chances of making it big, Lane ends up marrying him and then almost immediately getting pregnant. After working so hard to establish an independent life and break out of her mother's constraints, Lane ends up with a life she didn't initially intend for.

Of course, she loves her children and family, and she does seem content in A Year in the Life, but Lane deserved to see the world as a musician and leave Stars Hollow like she always dreamed of. Lane had just as much promise as Rory and was ready to work even harder than her friend to achieve her dreams. Lane should've had a different ending and gotten credit for being such a standout character in the series.

It's simultaneously true that Rory's arc on Gilmore Girls and A Year in the Life was disappointing and also deeply accurate. From the beginning of the series, it's hinted that Rory is doomed to repeat the same cycle of mistakes characteristic of the Gilmore family by not living up to the high expectations of others and the great promise she showed when she was young.

To be a high achiever and then struggle to find her place in the world when she isn't constantly handled and sheltered by Lorelai, Emily, and Richard is exactly what was always going to happen to Rory. It's hard to watch her fail and make mistakes as she realizes her life didn't turn out the way she thought it would. However, it's fitting and narratively sound, even if it doesn't make it easy to side with Rory.

Gilmore Girls had a distinctly early-2000s feel, but these actors could make a modern-day remake of the beloved drama feel just as cozy.

As Rory's final boyfriend in Gilmore Girls, and on-and-off flame in A Year in the Life, Logan is one of the most consistent and best-suited romances of Rory's life. It's unfortunate that season 7 undid some of his character development by having him give Rory an ultimatum to marry him and break things off when she wasn't ready. This went against much of the work that audiences saw him do throughout the show.

In A Year in the Life, Logan and Rory are still seeing each other despite Logan's relationship with another woman and Rory's aimless lifestyle. However, it seems that he's found some balance between what's expected of him and what he wants to do with his life. His final adventure with Rory is a touching sendoff for their relationship, and shows that Logan will always have a rebellious streak, even if he's learned how to grow up.

It comes as no surprise that Paris is at the top of her game when we catch up with her in A Year in the Life. It's disappointing that she and Doyle got divorced, but Paris is doing everything she ever set out to do and hasn't lost an ounce of her high-achieving spirit. This is a sharp foil to Rory's floundering, and is a reminder that though Rory often bested Paris when they were young, that dynamic wasn't permanent.

Paris' insults on Gilmore Girls are some of the funniest moments in the show, and the whip-smart character doesn't disappoint audiences in A Year in the Life. She's hilarious and great to spend time with in the revival, even if her anxiety at seeing Tristan again at Chilton was a little unbelievable, since Paris has come so far since high school. Paris as an adult is still intense, but she's a more compassionate and evolved person.

In her breakout role of Sookie in Gilmore Girls, Melissa McCarthy is as charming and hilarious as ever. It was a treat to see McCarthy make a cameo in A Year in the Life​​​​​​, and hear about the amazing work Sookie is doing as a chef in the series. Of course, we wish we got to spend more time with Sookie in the revival, but her appearance provided the nostalgic moment fans needed.

Though it seems like her career and family were in a good place in A Year in the Life, it's hard not to remember the difficulties Sookie faced in Gilmore Girls season 7. Jackson lying about his vasectomy and Sookie's accidental pregnancy is one of the worst parts of the final season. Though the couple works through it, this betrayal taints what was one of the best relationships on the show. The main series sees her pregnant and happy to send Rory off into the world, but we can't forget the trials of season 7.

Michel is one of Gilmore Girls' best scene stealers throughout the series, always providing a quip or sarcastic comment that makes it impossible not to appreciate his character. However, as a more supporting character, his personal life and development outside the Dragonfly Inn and his relationship with Lorelai aren't explored very deeply in the main show.

Fortunately, A Year in the Life not only confirmed that Michel was part of the LGBTQ+ community, but the series also gave him a husband who seemed to be the other half Michel was looking for. It's incredibly satisfying to see this happen for Michel, and it gives him a fitting ending for a character whose romantic life was always implied but never confirmed.

Jess has a few "endings" on Gilmore Girls, as the misunderstood, angry young man whom the Gilmores meet in season 2 changes a lot by the time he returns as an adult. Rory and Jess's romance in Gilmore Girls has been the subject of hot debate for years. When Jess was young, there's no question he didn't treat Rory well, even if he was a romantic bad boy viewers could idealize.

However, it's when Jess comes back in season 6 that viewers can appreciate how vital it was that he grew up and found his purpose. Moving to a new city and following his dreams of writing and working in publishing is the kind of growth that Jess fans were hoping for. However, he continues carrying a torch for Rory throughout season 6 and A Year in the Life, which is compelling for the plot, but it's a part of his character that keeps him stuck in the past.

Watching Luke grapple with his loss of Lorelai and the poor way he handled integrating April into his life in seasons 6 and 7 is a moment of character development for Stars Hollow's diner owner. However, he comes back around to their relationship and learns how to be the partner Lorelai needs, and vice versa.

In A Year in the Life, Luke couldn't be more committed to their life together and is able to weather Lorelai's struggle with finding her life's purpose better than he ever did in the past. He's serious and all in to their relationship and isn't afraid of making this known, telling her how he feels and how important she is in ways he failed to in the original series. For Luke's character, this is a big step, and his marriage to Lorelai is a beautiful full-circle moment for him.

One of the saddest parts of A Year in the Life is the passing of Richard, and this loss and its aftereffects are the primary character for Emily Gilmore. In the main series, the viewer witnesses Emily, the third Gilmore girl, grow as an individual and begin to define herself and her value outside of the traditional rules she was raised with and attempted to pass down to Lorelai and Rory.

Though Emily is far from perfect, even in the later seasons of Gilmore Girls, she becomes more understanding of her daughter and her choices and learns how to have a relationship with her through the repetition of her mistakes with Rory in season 6, when she drops out of Yale. Throughout A Year in the Life, Emily agrees to do therapy sessions with Lorelai, and while they don't always go well, she gains more respect for her daughter and is able to grieve Richard while finding new ways to enjoy her life without him.

After the season 7 finale, audiences could rest assured that Luke and Lorelai ended up the way they were supposed to, so when Lorelai returns for A Year in the Life, her arc had to be deeper than an extension of her will-they-won't-they dynamic with Luke. Of course, Lorelai was always much more than her romantic relationships, and this is clear in her ending. While it hits home when she and Luke finally, officially get married, it's her journey getting there that's the most compelling.

Lorelai achieves actualization and a sense of contentment in her ending, allowing her to fully commit to her life with Luke and let go of some of the anger she was still carrying toward her parents. Though Lorelai will likely continue indulging in some moments of regression in the future, Gilmore Girls gave one of its protagonists a fitting conclusion, allowing her to move forward and support Rory as she figures out her path.

In the fictional town of Star's Hollow, single mother Lorelai Gilmore raises her high-achieving teenage daughter Rory. Mother and daughter rely on each other throughout their own life changes, romantic entanglements, and friendships.

#3491. 'Marshals' Cast Reveals the 'Yellowstone' Characters They Want Back the Most

A visit to the 'Marshals' set shows just how much work goes into producing CBS' major procedural series.

When Yellowstone ended, it felt like the Dutton family story was essentially over, especially for someone like Kayce Dutton (Luke Grimes), who turned over a new leaf after selling his family's ranch back to the Broken Rock Tribe. He wrapped the series by finding peace with his wife, Monica (Kelsey Asbille), and son, Tate (Brecken Merrill) in East Camp. However, in Marshals, Kayce has been thrust back into the action. While Beth (Kelly Reilly) and Rip (Cole Hauser) have moved to Texas to build a new life, Kayce remains in Montana but now with a new role. As a U.S. marshal, Kayce has to face new threats, not only as a member of law enforcement, but also as a Dutton (with all of the baggage that comes with that name) and as a single father who has recently lost his wife.

Season 1 might have gotten off to a rocky start, especially due to the sharp format shift from Yellowstone's cable drama to Marshals' network TV procedural, but audiences still can't get enough of Taylor Sheridan's franchise. When Season 1 concluded with a cliffhanger ending, it felt inevitable that we would get more of Kayce's story. CBS renewed Marshals for 20 episodes for Season 2 (a step up from the 13-episode Season 1), giving the series more room to grow and develop its new cast of characters.

While Grimes and Merrill are reprising their roles, the show brings in some new faces with Logan Marshall Green as Pete "Cal" Calvin, the chief of the marshals team and Kayce's former U.S. Navy SEAL senior chief. There's also Belle Turek-Skinner (Arielle Kebbel), Andrea Cruz (Ash Santos), and Miles Kittel (Tatanka Means), who all work alongside Cal and Kayce week to week. From Broken Rock, both Gil Birmingham and Mo Brings Plenty return to play Thomas Rainwater and Mo, respectively. Despite its procedural format, Marshals still brings boatloads of action and thrills each week on CBS, and Collider had a chance to head to Park City, Utah, where the cast films the majority of the series to take a look at just what it takes to bring this Yellowstone spin-off to life.

Although both Yellowstone and Marshals technically take place in Montana, close to Bozeman, the majority of Marshals is filmed in Park City, Utah. At the Utah Film Studios, there are massive sets built in extreme detail. From the Marshals' headquarters office to Kayce's cabin to the Bullet 'n Barrel Saloon, each set is bursting at the seams with detail. There are news articles about Cal's past victories as a Navy SEAL on the walls, pictures of Monica and Tate in Kayce's cabin, and shotgun shell string lights decorating the rafters of the bar. The fireplace at the headquarters is made of real stone rather than foam, the beams of the bar and Kayce's cabin are made of real wood, and every inch of these sets is decorated and dressed with meticulous attention.

While the interiors are shot in a studio, the exteriors are shot around the area in Park City. One of the most significant locations seems to be Thousand Peaks Ranch, where Sheridan filmed his first few seasons of Yellowstone and Wind River. Locations like the historic Ontario Mine serve as the exterior to the marshals' headquarters, often filming on location when the team needs to head out of the office on a mission. On top of their typical filming locations, the production team also teased an upcoming train episode that is not only action-packed, but required that the production abide by federal regulations as they were filming on a real train.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

The costumes the characters wear are also looked at closely, with some of them carrying over from Yellowstone. Grimes still wears the same boots, jeans, belt, and hat as Kayce did in the original show. The hat, which comes from the Colorado shop Greeley Hat Works, is one of a kind. In a recent shoot that took Kayce to New York, the hat had to be handled with care during transportation, lest our cowboy U.S. marshal end up losing a key part of his look permanently. The costuming department sources the other cowboy hats from the local hat store in Park City called Warbonnet, while belt buckles specific to each character and their rodeo sports are made by retired Judge Leo Smith in Texas. If clothes need to be aged to look more worn in, the costuming department also has that down on lock, doing everything from spattering clothes with blood to tying a pair of boots to the back of a van so they can be banged up and aged to look weathered and worn.

Sitting down with the cast of Marshals — sans Marshall-Green, who just happened to be taking the day off — is a wild experience. Especially as the panel of stars takes seats at the Bullet 'n Barrell Saloon set, ready to dig into Season 2 of their CBS series. Alongside Grimes, Kebbel, Santos, Means, and Merrill is also Jefferson White, who is returning as Jimmy Hurdstrom from Yellowstone. For the large cast, the sophomore season is not only a boon but the increase of episodes is a sign of the network's faith in the show.

Santos, who immediately gets emotional, reveals that when she got the news about Season 2 from showrunner Spencer Hudnut, she sobbed in her car, calling the renewal a "tremendous win" and mentioning that the show helped her buy a house for herself. "I'll still cry about it today if I talk about it, because I just think it's amazing. It's wonderful," she says, her voice cracking a little. "The show changed my life overnight — financially, personally, and professionally. It's a huge gift, and it's not happening to everyone right now across our industry. There's a lot of actors who are unemployed, and a lot of crew members who are unemployed. So every day that I step on the set, I'm just grateful."

White, who is joining the show as a guest star, also notes that the higher episode count means more roles not only on the cast but in the crew. "It's a win for us personally, but it also makes me very proud and impressed with the work that these guys do to keep this show up and running, because there really is a trickle-down effect that affects everybody," White explains. "Because of this show, so many more people get their insurance, so many more people get their union hours." And despite a higher episode count meaning more work that might be ultimately more tiring, he calls the show "a win for the whole entertainment industry," saying, "I'm very proud to be a small part of it, and incredibly impressed by the Herculean effort that these guys do."

Of course, because Marshals exists in the same universe as Dutton Ranch, Santos is quick to mention Reilly as one of her ideal guest stars on the show, an idea that's not necessarily outside the realm of possibility considering both shows exist under the umbrella of Paramount. Less practical is Kebbel's desire to see Sam Elliott on their series. Elliott played Shea Brennan, a Pinkerton agent tasked with helping the Dutton family move west in 1883, and while there's no way his character could be in Marshals even if he had survived 1883, Kebbel still expresses wanting to see the iconic Western actor on the series.

Means mentions Tanaya Beatty who played Avery in Yellowstone, while Merrill gives a nod to Jen Landon's Teeter, and White wants to see Forrie J. Smith's Lloyd back to see how far Jimmy has come. For Grimes, the answer seems obvious and the one that has the largest potential of becoming a reality. "I'd like to see some flashbacks with Monica. She's the most important character to my character other than, you know, this one right here," he says, thumbing to Merrill seated next to him. "Obviously a lot happened that we didn't get to see, so I think those would be really hard scenes, because they wouldn't be the happiest, but I think it'd be great to just fill the audience in a little bit about how that all went out."

But although he is still mourning his wife, that doesn't mean that romance is completely out of the question, as Marshals is very clearly setting up a relationship between Kayce and Andrea. Grimes admits that he and Hudnut both knew that there would have to be a romantic interest for Kayce. But Grimes had a caveat. "I was like, it's gotta take a long time, because let's give Kayce and the audience some time to deal with Monica's passing, and let's really honor that and respect that," Grimes explains. While it seemed obvious to them that his love interest would ideally be someone on the marshals team, Grimes isn't interested in rushing into things. Comparing Kayce and Andrea to The Office's Jim and Pam, he calls the relationship a "real nice old-school slow play," jokingly adding, "Let's just really try and act like it's not going to happen for a while. That's been in the plans before there ever was a first script."

For Birmingham, who is returning to the role of Thomas Rainwater, the new series operates at a much faster pace. "You don't have the time allotment to really play the characters out as much because the format is different." But the show does offer a chance to explore the internal dynamics of the reservation more as Season 2 digs into the conflict between the people of Broken Rock and their opposition to Rainwater's leadership.

"I've had conversations with Spencer, talking about storylines in that regard, how closely do these follow the culture itself, relationships, and how the tribe behaves toward the chairman, and the responsibilities the chairman has," Birmingham explains. "I think that's the biggest lesson I've learned is how heavy that load is. He's responsible for the welfare — psychologically, spiritually, economically — and then you're getting monetary influxes that are necessary to sustain, but cross a moral ambiguity, and makes it tough."

It turns out that Kayce can't fully forget his past, after all.

The franchise has always been very conscious of the way it mingles the Duttons with the Native Americans of Broken Rock. Birmingham points out that when Sheridan was younger, he found clarity after sitting in a sweat lodge. "He was on a personal spiritual journey of his own. He was younger, and nothing really resonated for him until he did a sweat. And then the man who directed that sweat was saying, 'Well, if you are apprehensive about this, let me refer you over to the Lakota people, and he got introduced to some elders there," Birmingham explains.

"He lived over there for several years, and that's where some of his stories come out of. He's heard them, hundreds of them. Wind River spin out of that. So he has a real understanding of the culture." However, Birmingham notes that Marshals faces challenges because Sheridan is not as closely involved. "We're relied upon for collaborating, Mo [Brings Plenty], and I, Tatanka, with the native culture element. It's just a learning curve," he says, "because if you're not immersed in it, if you're not familiar with it, then you won't really know how to depict these characters or their relationships."

Marshals also offers the opportunity for someone like Mo Brings Plenty to expand on his character a bit more, and Birmingham refers to him as a cultural anchor for the series, saying, "I don't think Taylor was aware that Mo's an elder in the Lakota nation," and that Brings Plenty's experience as a cowboy Indian will bring aspects of the culture that aren't often portrayed in television. For Brings Plenty, the opportunity to expand his character also allows the show to explore more Native American storylines.

One personal story to Brings Plenty ties back to his recently deceased nephew, Cole Brings Plenty, who was reported missing in March 2024 and then found dead in a wooded area in Kansas a month later. For Brings Plenty, having a storyline on Marshals that reflects the frustration and struggle his family has had trying to figure out the truth of what happened to his nephew is pivotal. "It's a storyline that has impacted our family very much, and we're not the only family in this country that has experienced this situation," he explains, referencing the upcoming Episode 6 "Roughstock" that will focus in on Mo bringing in Kayce to help investigate his missing nephew.

"I can't wait for it to come out," Brings Plenty says. "I'm hopeful that it'll evolve into something that will spark an interest in this country, to get more people in society involved and care about what's occurring to American Indian peoples throughout this country." Although Brings Plenty acknowledges that it won't bring his nephew back, the impact of the story could make a difference for the other young people in America.

"If we don't start making noise about it or speaking to our senators or Congresspeople, then it's something that will continue: the lawlessness. Because the wheels of justice don't really turn for us as American Indian people, we have to get involved. It's something that's near and dear to my heart." For Brings Plenty, the opportunity to highlight his culture and show more than just the stereotypical depiction of Native Americans is something he can be grateful to CBS for. "I'm thankful because a lot of networks wouldn't take that chance. They wouldn't be supportive of that," he explains, pointing out that just seeing this representation at work means that "the good outlasts the bad."
