#3467. Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It?

Don’t be surprised if you emerge from Alex Thompson and Kelly O’Sullivan’s piercingly moving coming-of-age grief dramedy “Mouse” in a puddle of tears. Graceful in technique, compassionate in its writing, this movie, one of the year’s best, is a crying machine. But that’s not to say this story of a high school girl’s (Katherine Mallen Kupferer, astonishing) formative first encounter with major loss is any bit manipulative.

As heartbreak ripples through a small town, “Mouse” has the texture and deep feeling of Kenneth Lonergan’s post-9/11 New York City drama “Margaret,” starring Anna Paquin as a precocious teenager in freefall after witnessing a pedestrian’s brutal death. Unlike “Margaret,” “Mouse” didn’t take over half a decade to reach screens after production wrapped, but the road was still paved with rejection (baffling in retrospect) for Chicago directing duo Thompson and O’Sullivan. Related Stories From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race How John Malkovich Nailed the Role of His Career with ‘Wild Horse Nine’

With “Mouse,” the filmmakers found themselves at the Berlin Film Festival for the first time back in February — even as an American indie set in Arkansas about the challenges of coming of age feels like catnip for a festival like Sundance, where such topics are historically de rigueur. And Thompson and O’Sullivan had been to Sundance before, with their critically championed 2024 comedy-drama “Ghostlight,” about an emotionally ramshackle, rookie community theater production of “Romeo and Juliet.” While placement at the legacy indie festival, headed to Boulder in January, doesn’t always mean you’re grandfathered into the acceptance pipeline for your next movie, it was still a surprise to the directors (who are also life partners with two children) when Sundance turned down “Mouse” not once, but twice.

“To be totally fair, we submitted before we probably should have, with a long cut,” O’Sullivan told IndieWire over Zoom. “Apparently, it didn’t matter,” Thompson added.

“We submitted it again the next year, when it was tighter,” added O’Sullivan, though the filmmakers were dismissed again. “The feedback that we got — and again, this is a game of telephone, so we don’t know — is that it had real champions, but that it also had people who didn’t get it. Yes, it was crushing. It was confusing. More than anything, I was like, ‘Wait, but people did such great work on this movie. The work is incredible.’ And not ours even, but Sophie [Okonedo] and Katherine [Mallen Kupferer], and the crew, I was like, ‘I feel like they deserve a really big stage.’”

Luckily, the Berlin Film Festival stepped in to program “Mouse” in the Panorama section, marking Thompson and O’Sullivan’s first bow at a European fest, where it grabbed strong reviews. And, as the filmmakers point out, that festival turned out to be the proper home. (Berlin, after all, just had its strongest lineup in years, under artistic director Tricia Tuttle’s second festival.)

“It really was hard for a moment, and then we heard back from Berlin, and it kind of felt like a career opportunity that went way beyond Sundance,” Thompson said. “Tapping into the narrative outside of the American indie felt like something we’d always aspired to. And those are the films that I identify with the most, the sort of work that comes out of those great European festivals. The most jealous and childish I am is every year when the Venice reviews start coming out, and it’s like, ‘Ah, well, those all sound great.’ And Cannes and Berlin, and our favorite festivals, we have a relationship with Thessaloniki and American Film Festival in Wrocław, and to have that stage at Berlin, it’s like this sort of historic stage. It’s absolutely mind-blowing. I’ve never been in a theater that big with a movie.”

A Gotham nominee for Best Feature, “Mouse” is now quietly in theaters from Independent Film Company. (A sparsely attended Academy screening also took place in Los Angeles over the weekend.) Film chatterers may deem this a “small” movie in a year of “You Can See Everything” and “La Bola Negra,” it is huge in every way.

The film follows Minnie Dunn (Kupferer), who, just as she’s about to enter her senior year, is dealt a life-altering loss. It’s 2002, Michelle Branch is on the radio, and September 11 is not even a year out of view. Faced with a hole in her life in the shape of her lifelong best friend after a tragic accident, Minnie forms a tight bond with the girl’s British stay-at-home mother, Helen (Sophie Okonedo, luminescent here), mourning on her own. Meanwhile, Minnie’s classmates all but literally compete to see who can grieve the loudest in the form of a talent show. “Mouse” is about the centrifugal force of grief and how life goes on around you, but you’re still stuck in the same place.

Big on emotional generosity and ace turns from the filmmakers’ stable of theater-based Chicago actors — including Kupferer and her real-life mother Tara Mallen, who plays Minnie’s struggling, lower-middle-class mom onscreen — “Mouse” deserves as much attention as any of the year’s best films. The grand ambition of “Mouse” and its emotional dividends and wonderful performances suggest it could’ve cleaned up at Telluride or even Toronto, where, in the latter case, a number of indie films flopped, and even the most acclaimed are still searching for distribution.

“Rejected, rejected,” O’Sullivan laughed, later adding, “We understand how complicated programming a festival is, and we don’t feel entitled to be programmed anywhere. We’re grateful to every festival that’s given us a slot.”

She wrote the script for “Mouse” in 2019, around the time their debut feature as collaborators, “Saint Frances,” opened at SXSW. That microbudget indie, directed by Thompson and starring O’Sullivan as a drifting 34-year-old nanny in Chicago, won the Austin festival’s audience award and later earned a John Cassavetes Spirit Award nomination. “Mouse” was actually meant to be their next feature, with one financier, a cushier budget, and a slightly different cast — until the strikes changed their plans, leading to “Ghostlight” as their Sundance debut on a smaller scale.

Based on O’Sullivan’s own experience with loss as a teen, “Mouse” picked back up in fall 2024, shooting on location in her home state of Arkansas. “We were amazingly able to retain the vision” of “Mouse” from before the strikes, she said. “Nothing got cut for budget.”

Thompson, who produced the film, said, “Knowing the budget so intimately, I guess that’s my superpower on the producing side that most directors don’t have is I just get really intimate with the budget. And it seems really boring, but it’s kind of like a script where if you don’t have the means, if it’s not there in the budget, it’s not going to happen… A lot of directors I talked to have been like, ‘Oh, well, my producer said we couldn’t do a rain tower, or my producers said we couldn’t do this shot because we can’t afford it.’ And it’s like, well, you can pretty much afford anything. You just have to give somewhere else. We tend to make really ambitious one-liners like schedules. We had 30 days on this, but that ended up being a two-hour and 15-minute movie, and we cut 20 minutes.”

When asked about the “Mouse” budget, he said, “I think we can say. We’re already underdogs. We might as well say. It was $3 million.”

And it’s $3 million, well-budgeted and in true indie spirit — like a scene where Minnie and her friends watch “Titanic” in a parent’s basement during one of those classic sleepovers where private confidences spill out, insulated from the adult world upstairs and outside.

“We didn’t even try to get the rights to ‘Titanic,’ but we’re mixing at Skywalker,” Thompson said. “They have the entire effects library for ‘Titanic’ … so we rebuilt the dance scene in ‘Titanic’ and used public-domain Irish music, and then Kelly and [producer] Pierce Cravens do the voices of Leo and Kate off in a room being like, ‘I feel so young,’ or something, whatever that is. If you watch the movie, you think they’re watching ‘Titanic’ in the basement, but it’s a totally constructed thing because we’re like, ‘We can’t get the rights to this.'”

On top of “Mouse” already dwelling on a very specific point of loss from O’Sullivan’s own childhood, the filmmaker’s mother also died in Arkansas toward the end of production. That meant she was actively grieving while also leading a set, alongside her partner.

“It was so bizarre,” O’Sullivan said. “She died when we had a week and a half left to shoot… It was incredibly complicated. I just couldn’t believe the timing of it for so many different reasons. I mean, one of which is just that it took forever to make this movie, but the movie allowed me to be there literally when she died. I didn’t have to get on a plane. But then when I was back on set, I just kept hearing these lines that I had written, and they took on a whole new meaning… lines that I had sort of written in a very theoretical way all of a sudden were hitting me in a, ‘God, I can’t believe how true this was, and I didn’t even know.'”

The autobiography that drove “Mouse” extended behind the scenes in even more literal ways. Christen Pitts, the choreographer behind the movie’s climactic ballet elegy sequence set to a cover of Cyndi Lauper’s “Time After Time,” was O’Sullivan’s high school dance teacher. “It feels like so many different chapters of my life are just compressing into the same space, and it feels like a culmination of my entire adult life and teenage years and echoes of the past existing,” O’Sullivan said.

Thompson and O’Sullivan have maintained their filmmaking footprint in and around Chicago — even as “Mouse” brought them to Arkansas — and they don’t feel especially tempted to make the leap to Hollywood, though there have been offers.

“I just write from a place of experience most of the time, and I don’t know, I’ve seen so many movies set in L.A. and New York, and I actually don’t identify with those towns,” O’Sullivan said. “I feel like enough people are doing that, and I like writing from a place of specificity … I’ve spent maybe a year in both places cumulatively. It doesn’t feel like a character that I personally need to explore. But having said that, if I spent more time there, it felt like a story was necessarily set there. I’d be open to it. I just don’t feel compelled to.”

“We really want to have a body of work,” Thompson said. “The people I admire the most are Steven Soderbergh and Sidney Lumet, directors who have dozens of films by the time they stop, and Soderbergh has not stopped, obviously.” He doesn’t know that a move to Los Angeles is possible given their artistic goals. “We’ve gone out on meetings, we’ve done pitches, we’ve considered projects from studios, and the timeline always felt kind of like it just hasn’t really worked out. ‘Mouse’ was so close to being that thing, and then the writers’ strike, and the SAG strike, we lost a cast member, and it just all fell away. So we just thought, ‘What if we just do what we did on ‘Ghostlight,’ but on steroids? If I can raise half a million dollars, I wonder if we can raise three.”

With the filmmakers now set up at Gersh talent agency, he added, “If we want to make a movie every 15 months, we probably can’t do that in the studio system. But I think we both like the idea of playing in a bigger sandbox and taking the intimacy, taking all the things we’ve learned, and working in a bigger sandbox. I don’t think that’s unattractive, but it’s just, for the way we work, this has made the most sense so far.”

Next up, Thompson directed a high-concept body-swap comedy starring the “Ghostlight” father-daughter (and real-life father-daughter) team of “Mouse” star Katherine Mallen Kupferer with Keith Kupferer. Plus, they’ve co-directed “The Steel Harp,” starring Lois Smith and O’Sullivan in a return to acting. Both are expected in 2027.

“We shoot on the same lenses as ‘Saint Frances,’ same aspect ratio as ‘Mouse,’ in a world that winks at a bigger sandbox,” Thompson said of the body swap movie. “It’s a total gamble. I’ve got no idea if it’s going to work… It seems to be quite funny according to my three-year-old.”

“Mouse” is now playing in New York and Los Angeles, with a wider expansion to follow in November.

#3466. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: eight to 10 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

#3464. 2027 Will Give One Piece A New Lead Hero, And It's Not Luffy

For nearly three decades, Monkey D. Luffy has fronted One Piece, and its theatrical adventures have usually followed the Straw Hat captain or put his crew in a new crisis. That pattern is set to change in 2027. One Piece Film: God Valley explores a chapter of history that unfolded long before Luffy began his voyage.

The title points toward the infamous incident involving Gol D. Roger, Monkey D. Garp, and Rocks D. Xebec. Those three figures appeared in the official announcement teaser, signaling a different generation of heroes and threats. Luffy is not being replaced in the main series; this movie simply has a past-era story to tell.

Toei Animation announced One Piece Film: God Valley on August 23, 2026, during One Piece Day '26, confirming a Japanese theatrical release in summer 2027. The teaser offered no full synopsis, but its focus on Roger, Garp, and Rocks makes the historical setting unmistakable. This is not another adventure built around the Straw Hat crew.

The God Valley Incident took place 38 years before One Piece's present-day events. Luffy's voyage begins in a world shaped by its aftermath, not in the era when these legends were making history. A film set during that conflict naturally shifts attention to the people who fought there, rather than the pirate who inherited their legacy.

Roger is a compelling candidate to anchor the story. He was not yet the Pirate King remembered by the world, and his rivalry with Rocks preceded the final stretch of his journey to the One Piece. The teaser places him alongside Garp, suggesting the movie will explore the unlikely partnership that helped define the incident.

The island gives the story a darker foundation than a conventional treasure hunt. In the manga, God Valley was the site of a World Noble hunting competition, in which the island's people were treated as prey. The arrival of powerful pirates and Marines turned that atrocity into a battle whose truth the World Government later tried to erase.

Garp's role complicates the idea of a single central hero. A Marine, he joined forces with Roger, a pirate, during the crisis. The official version of events elevated Garp as the Hero of the Marines while concealing Roger's part in the battle. A film can dramatize the partnership behind a story the authorities deliberately distorted.

Rocks D. Xebec is not simply a name for Roger and Garp to defeat. He led the Rocks Pirates, a crew that included younger versions of future powerhouses such as Edward Newgate, Charlotte Linlin, and Kaido. The manga's extended flashback also gives Rocks personal history and motivations, making him central to the tragedy rather than a faceless villain.

God Valley appears set apart because its title points to a major event in Eiichiro Oda's manga, rather than another separate Straw Hat adventure. Earlier films have largely told original stories, while this project seems poised to bring a defining piece of the series' history to theaters. That could make its different lead perspective more than a casting change.

The timing adds to the film's importance and excitement. One Piece began serialization on July 22, 1997, so its 30th anniversary falls on July 22, 2027, the same year God Valley is scheduled to arrive. It will also be the franchise's first new theatrical feature since One Piece Film: Red opened in Japan in August 2022.

Weekly One Piece episodes are halting indefinitely, but the anime hiatus clears the runway for a major canon movie.

Toei has not revealed the director, screenplay, voice cast, exact Japanese premiere date, or international release plans. The studio has not formally identified one character as the protagonist, either. Roger may be the clearest candidate for the One Piece film's heroic point of view, but Garp and Rocks are essential to the story.

#3463. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3462. Our Plea to the New DC Studios Head: No More Shared Universe!

Four years ago, DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran relaunched the comics brand with grand ambitions to build a Marvel Cinematic Universe of their own with a crop of characters they believed to be superior to what Marvel and Disney had. They controlled Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Green Lantern, The Flash, and a whole bunch more they could mold as they saw fit, and they promised they would fix the flawed Marvel Studios system of greenlighting projects before a strong screenplay was in place. They announced a massive slate of 10 films and series right out of the gate and had other expectations that stars they cast today would appear in future DC films for the long haul. Above all, they were going to be careful with the brand. Related Stories DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn, Peter Safran Stepping Down as Co-CEOs, Marvel Vet Jeremy Latcham Named Chief Creative Officer James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next

“No one was minding the mint,” Gunn said back in January 2023 in a telling quote. “They were just giving away IP like they were party favors to any creators who smiled at them. What we are going to do is promise that everything from our first project going forward is going to be unified.”

The real world quickly caught up to Gunn and Safran. In a move beyond their control, ownership of DC Studios changed hands yet again from Warner Bros. Discovery to Skydance, and now just four years, three films, and a couple of TV shows into their tenure, they’re out. Taking the reins is Jeremy Latcham, not a household name the way Kevin Feige or some of his lieutenants have been, but an architect of the early stages of the MCU and a key, former executive at Marvel (he left for an independent label of his own in 2017). He has comic book chops, having produced “The Avengers,” the first MCU “Spider-Man,” and more.

Because the ball didn’t really get rolling at DC Studios in the short time Gunn and Safran were on board, and because Latcham still has a lingering slate that includes a second “Superman” movie that’s already in the can and a second “The Batman” movie in the works that isn’t even connected to the DCU anyway, as he begins to map out his own ambitions for the next era of DC movies and series, we have a simple plea: no more shared universes. Please. We beg you. Enough already.

Do not try and build the next MCU or even the next DC(E)U or whatever you want to call it. Just make some really good superhero movies with the characters and brands people love.

Books have been and will be written about the producing success story Kevin Feige managed with the MCU, and David Ellison, fanboy that he is, would surely love to have his own version of “The Avengers.” Who wouldn’t? We’ve seen other studios try and recreate the MCU formula with their own IP, like the Godzilla vs. Kong-iverse from WB and Legendary or the incredibly misguided plan for a Universal monster-verse that fizzled out with Tom Cruise’s “The Mummy.“

Truth be told, Marvel is trying to reconstruct its own formula ever since “Avengers: Endgame,” and it has been a mixed bag. Sure, there were a few billion-dollar hits in there like “Deadpool & Wolverine” and this year’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” and “Avengers: Doomsday” too figures to be huge, but other new characters and would-be franchises like “Eternals” or “Shang-Chi” have gone through fits and stops. Movies like a “Blade” reboot have never been able to get off the ground as Marvel tries to fit a square peg into a round hole. Marvel has been forced to recast and scramble its carefully laid plans amid the controversy around Jonathan Majors. And the sheer glut of TV shows over the last few years has created immense homework for people that has led the actual flagship movies to drop off precipitously at the box office.

Is that what DC Studios really wants? More of that drama and headache? It feels like we’re well beyond the era where audiences are willing to commit for every new episode of a yearslong cinematic saga. Surely whatever vision Gunn and Safran had was grand, especially if you’re a real fan of those characters and want to see them all come together as the Justice League yet again, but it doesn’t feel like today’s young audiences want to sign up for that.

Gunn and Safran actually immediately ran into this problem as they tried to bridge the gap between the old DCEU and the new DCU they were building. People knew “The Flash” and “Aquaman 2” weren’t going to be part of the future, even as Gunn and Safran paid lip service to the idea and played coy about having some of these actors reprising their roles in the new universe. (Remember when Henry Cavill thought for a minute he was playing Superman again?) The films underwhelmed at the box office as a result, and it created confusion among casual fans as the execs were forced to dance around the fanboys and the Snyder Army.

Audiences, though, have demonstrated that superhero movies still matter when they feature characters they care about. “Spider-Man” stayed away for about five years, and “Brand New Day” is now one of the highest-grossing movies of all time. We hadn’t had a proper, standalone “Superman” movie in years, and it proved to be a great launching pad for Gunn’s slate, earning $618.7 million worldwide. There’s still huge excitement for “The Batman: Part II” from Matt Reeves, and there’s never been any pretense that it’s connected to some more important lore or that Pattinson’s Bruce Wayne might show up in a theoretical “Wonder Woman” sequel a decade down the road. People just really like Batman.

So what do you do now if you’re Latcham and have to answer to Ellison and former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz? It would make sense to just demonstrate how you’re going to make the most of the IP that you have. Signaling to audiences (and shareholders) that your next Wonder Woman movie won’t come out until 2037 because you’re mapping out the shared universe for how to carefully introduce all these characters doesn’t sound like the best approach. Just hire smart writers, entrust visionary directors, and make some good movies. It worked with “The Batman.”

This, of course, does not mean don’t make your big “Justice League” team up movie or don’t build a new franchise out of “Teen Titans.” It just means that times and appetites have changed from the pre-Covid and even pre-streaming boom MCU era when “Guardians of the Galaxy” could be a hit (in part) because of how it teased the arrival of Thanos and the Infinity Stones. Audiences have become more discerning about what they define as an event film, and DC Studios can beat Marvel at its own game so long as DC stops trying to become Marvel.

#3461. Resident Evil director Zach Cregger explains why the iPhone is vital to his work

There have been a number of high-profile movies technically shot on iPhone, but in most cases they are using the same professional cinematography kit they would use with other cameras, including lenses costing tens of thousands of dollars.

Resident Evil director Zach Cregger uses his own iPhone in a rather different way, taking an approach that could be useful to amateur and professional filmmakers alike …

There’s an ongoing debate about how meaningful it is to claim that a high-profile movie, ad, or keynote video was shot on iPhone. Naysayers argue that the quality is all down to the professional lenses, lighting rigs, and editing employed, while those on the other side of the fence point out that everything was captured by the iPhone sensor.

Cregger mostly sidesteps all of that, describing his own use of an iPhone for shot planning, creating photo boards that accurately represent the image that will be captured by each of the Pro lenses he intends to use.

We grew up with video games informing our visual sense just as much as movies and television did, and I feel like I’m able to make a movie that involves the gameplay. [Here] I have a wide angle lens, our protagonist is in the center of the frame as he’s moving, we’re following locked right behind him when he looks right and we swing, right. His attention is dictating where the camera goes, and I think that the effect of that is is a much more immersive horror experience where you’re feeling informed.

I’m a hyper prepper. I’ve got the iPhone that is, like, always on me. I’ll go to the location with my cinematographer and I’ll use Cadrage, an app that approximates different lenses, and I will basically plan out the sequence. I will know exactly what shot is going to cut to what shot, and I will print out these images and everyone will know we’re using this lens for these shots. This is what’s going to be in the frame, and there’s no guesswork.

He does, however, add that an iPhone is all that you need to make a movie, even if his own budgets give him access to rather more expensive kit.

Anybody can make a movie with what’s in your pocket right now.

At the other end of the scale, I use my iPhone in a similar way to him when planning my own amateur videos. I take still photos to create a photo board so that I have a visual reference for each of my planned shots. The videos themselves may be shot on my Blackmagic rig, my iPhone, or some mix of the two.

You can watch Cregger talk through his process for Apple TV here.

Resident Evil director Zach Cregger counts iPhone among his go-to filmmaking tools.Go inside his unique approach to crafting immersive horror experiences, and watch his latest movie now on the Apple TV app. https://t.co/oOpQL0mJde pic.twitter.com/RHWwlPjFID

#3460. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3459. HomeView will support third-party AI chatbots, suggests code

Code discovered in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that HomeView is set to gain support for third-party AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude.

A leaker spotted the first clue to this a few days ago, and in an updated post says that this feature “is happening” …

Leaker pdfu said at the start of the month that ChatGPT, Claude and other AI apps “may” be coming to HomeView, after spotting an unused flag for ConversationalApps. They now say that the beta of iOS 26.3 confirms their suspicion.

It’s happening, folks: AI apps are coming to HomeView. PebblePlay, HomeView’s CarPlay bridge, gets the Conversational Apps category in iOS 27.3.

They also highlight other things discovered in the beta.

It’s happening, folks: AI apps are coming to HomeView.PebblePlay, HomeView’s CarPlay bridge, gets the Conversational Apps category in iOS 27.3.The update also adds bidirectional audio routing, session management, and interruption groundwork.Still not fully wired up. https://t.co/pzSv3cIsec

Apple uses these flags to determine which categories of third-party apps are allowed to run on the device, in the same way as it does with CarPlay.

The same leaker recently discovered evidence that HomeView will be able to serve as a HomeKit security camera.

#3458. Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’

“Hello, I’m Julie,” said a radiant Julianne Moore, holding out her hand as she popped out of the elevator at Middleburg, Virginia’s Salamander Resort. Her hair was red, her skin was white, her dress as yellow as gold. A few hours later after a rapturous Middleburg Film Festival reaction to “The Debut” (December 11), we talked in a hotel meeting room. The A24 crowdpleaser has been wowing audiences and critics since Telluride.

Jesse Eisenberg has done it again. His follow-up to “A Real Pain,” which won Kieran Culkin the Supporting Actor Oscar, could score Best Actress for Moore. The musical comedy has earned Moore raves on the festival circuit for her role as a sad suburban homemaker turned anxious aspiring actress in a New Jersey community theater. A sixth Oscar nomination is inevitable, and possibly a second Oscar win after “Still Alice” in 2015. It’s hard to believe she launched her career in 1988 as a regular on soap opera “As the World Turns.” Related Stories Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It? From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race

Moore is the current Best Actress frontrunner, even though she has won before. Sometimes nabbing an Oscar is a disadvantage in the Oscar race. But not if the performance is undeniable: Katharine Hepburn holds the record with four, while nipping at her heels are three-time winners Meryl Streep, Frances McDormand, Jack Nicholson, and Sean Penn.

Eisenberg wrote a rich character for Moore, knowing what the veteran actress could do with the childlike housewife Mona who, in order to learn how to act, must find herself. The director and actress had worked together on “When You Finish Saving the World” (2022). “[‘The Debut‘] is about this woman who has been chewed up but not spit out,” said Eisenberg, quoting Mona’s signature song. “It’s my point of view through somebody I consider a muse. I was writing something about myself as a seven-year-old in 1990, but I couldn’t picture anybody else except her doing it.”

It helped that Moore had told Eisenberg exactly what she was looking for. “I said I had just done ‘Dear Evan Hansen,’ and I loved singing, and I would love to have another opportunity,” she said. “I told him that I would love to do more comedy, and I didn’t want to play some suffering mom.”

Eisenberg put all of this in the screenplay, “but in the most surprising and inventive way,” she said. “He’s such a specific writer. He’s so incredibly empathetic. He has a compassionate worldview. He understands creativity. All of that stuff went into this wonderful and delightful story. It’s joyful and life-affirming too.”

Moore didn’t know she was playing a seven-year-old version of Eisenberg until he started telling that to the press. “Then he was like, ‘This is my experience of being a kid and going to community theater.’ But I could sense that there was a personal point of view in it. I very much felt with Mona that she was on a subjective journey, and that he was inside of that. With Mona, I always knew he was looking through her.”

“The Debut” is told from her point of view, as she tries to talk the overbearing local community theater director Jerry (Paul Giamatti) into hiring her, an untrained actress. He does it because he has no one else. But first, he must teach her how to act.

Mona dresses like a schoolgirl, with skirts, blouses, cardigan sweaters. “She’s so contained, and the way she learns is so literal,” said Moore, “the way a baby learns, like, you make a face at a baby, the baby makes a face back, but they don’t have intention behind it. But they’re learning things in an exterior way, and then they match it with feeling later on. So everything she’s doing is a childlike way of learning.”

Mona goes from an invisible nonentity in her own home to someone who demands attention. “She’s a kid who has found friends for the first time,” said Eisenberg. “She’s the girl who transferred to the right school at seven years old, and then the first rehearsal happens, and she is told she is terrible, and she has no idea why. And it’s the girl who transferred to the right school and gets an F on the very first test, and then the rest of the semester is panicking, and all she’s seeing is everybody else get A’s, and she still has the F, and she doesn’t know what to do. And then the teacher pulls her aside and says, ‘You either show up, or you are out on your ass.’ And something switches in her, and she makes the decision: ‘I am going to show up.’ And she begins to turn into a monster.”

The theater troupe embraces Mona as she unfolds like a flower. “We’ve been like those theater kids cracking corny jokes and finding community,” said Moore. “It’s all done with so much affection. Jesse looks at that world with not a hint of malice.”

Giamatti’s director relentlessly pushes the newbie through her paces until they have a powerful confrontation on the empty stage where he forces her to break down. Eisenberg reduced the actors’ anxiety by placing the eight-page showstopper in the middle of the shoot: not the beginning, and not the end. On the first day he went over to Moore’s apartment to talk about the movie. He said, “I really don’t want you to worry about that scene. I don’t want you to worry about memorizing that because I know that as an actor, I would I lose my mind. I would just be drilling it all the time, and I wouldn’t be able to concentrate. We’re going to have a teleprompter on that day. So don’t worry about it.”

So Moore worked on it normally, she said, “like I worked on everything else in the movie. So when we got to it, I knew it. I didn’t need a teleprompter. He knew instinctively as a director and an actor that what scares us sometimes is just a volume of language. He didn’t want to freeze me up. And having a partner like Paul who was so awake and aware and generous made it a pleasure. We were enjoying it when we did shoot it.”

Moore and Giamatti had never worked together before. She once introduced herself to him in a bookstore in Montauk. “He was very shy,” she said. “He is the greatest scene partner. I didn’t expect him to be so generous. He’s so funny, and he’s so dear. He’s present, incredibly modest, and as a partner, so available. Paul and I would work on it occasionally. When we were doing that scene, the rhythm was so important in it. You throw something, he hits it right back. It was our sense together of keeping it aloft, keeping it moving, keeping the river flowing. It felt electric with the two of us.”

The big blowout happens early in the story. “In a lot of movies, that kind of set piece would happen later,” said Moore. “Instead, it’s like a discovery place. It’s where she starts to begin to unlock herself emotionally, but she doesn’t learn from it. She comes in the next day, and starts to rehearse. And her belief is that acting is size, that it’s just huge, right? That’s when she starts yelling. She thinks it’s about being loud, which then allows her to go on the next journey with Jerry, where he says, ‘Let’s talk about feeling and reality and intention.’ So she’s slowly putting these pieces together. But that’s the first moment where she attaches something outside of herself to her own emotion.”

The whole shoot was fast, as Eisenberg didn’t have time to muck about and often shot just one take of a scene. “She and Paul Giamatti are so good on take one,” said Eisenberg. “It’s embarrassing. This is a small budget movie. The first two days of our schedule, we filmed in one day. The first two days, which were big ensemble musical numbers, we filmed in one day because we were prepared as a crew, but the actors were perfect on take one.”

Moore didn’t feel rushed. “It doesn’t feel, working with Jesse, like you’re moving too fast,” she said. “Working in independent film, you’re always moving quickly because you need to. You don’t have the time. You don’t have the money. So you want to move through things quickly. But I never felt rushed with him. I never I never felt like I was leaving something, that I didn’t get to complete something.”

The challenge for Moore, as it is for every actor shooting out of order, was making her character changes seamless. Eisenberg started with the theater scenes, then shot her family, and then jumped into Mona’s increasing weirdness. “The hardest thing always is making sure that you’ve pitched things correctly,” Moore said. “You want to make sure that you’ve managed to match it to another scene. So it was always hard to figure out. That’s our job.”

Eisenberg wanted Mona to move from looking quite childlike in the beginning, and swiftly move through her evolving transformations. Moore had fun with the costumes, figuring out the crazy wigs, makeup, and outfits in the second half. “Jesse had written that Mona electrocutes herself and destroys her hair, and that she was going to get her hair cut,” said Moore, “but he hadn’t written in a color change. We were messing around with it and trying to figure out what to do with hair and makeup and wardrobe and we had this idea that by having her dye her hair dark and chop it off, I wanted to homage the great ladies of musical theater, Liza Minnelli and Chita Rivera and Patti LuPone. It’s a wonderful Easter egg for that character.”

Making everything easier for Moore was actor-turned-director Eisenberg, who’d tell her when to ‘raise the stakes’ or ‘go hotter.’ “He’s maybe the most collaborative person I’ve ever worked with my entire life,” said Moore. “He listens to everyone. He asks people for opinions. He’ll ask people for notes, in a way that I would be like, ‘you don’t have to do that. This is your movie. It’s your creation.’ But he does collate opinion in a way. He’s fascinating in his generosity.”

Needless to say, singing her centerpiece song (“This City May Have Chewed Me Up (But It Hasn’t Spit Me Out”) was nervous-making, given that Moore was surrounded by Broadway super-belters like Tony winners Danny Burstein and Bonnie Tillman. “These people have the voices of angels,” said Moore. “When I did sing that song for the first time, and they’re all sitting there watching me, I think they did feel worried for me because they have so much ease. The song that she sings is so beautiful. In the singing of the song, she’s attaching her own emotional experience suddenly to the song. She understands the song in the moment she’s singing that. Somehow she wants more, and she knows that this is an avenue for her to find that. And so it’s a journey back to herself: finding that creativity and connection and community brings her to an essential sense of self.”

If degree of difficulty counts with Oscar voters, Moore may have that advantage.

#3457. This Eufy Robot Vacuum and Mop Is $400 Off Right Now

Robot vacuums have been around a while, but it can still be tough to find one that is also good at mopping. It's a smart design, and it's a great time to pick one up: Right now, the E25 is 40% off in an early Black Friday deal at Amazon, taking it down to $599.98 (originally $999.99).

Another perk is that the E25 is equipped with an anti-tangle brush and multiple side brushes that get into tight corners; this is a valuable feature at this price point, as is the 20,000 Pa suction power, which results in a deeper clean on both hard flooring and carpeting, features that are especially appealing for pet owners.

Users can map an area, set zones, schedule cleans, and define different features via the Eufy Clean app; the customizable options include cleaning intensity, suction power, water level, and deciding whether you want the E25 to make multiple passes in an area.  It uses LiDAR mapping and AI for obstacle detection and is highly automated, with a dock that empties the robot, washes and dries the roller mop, and refills its water supply. If you live in a home with pets and want a low-maintenance robot vacuum and mop that can handle routine floor cleaning with minimal intervention, the Eufy E25 can cut some serious time from your cleaning routine.

#3456. Nintendo Switch games running natively on Apple TV using Claude Code port

A Redditor has just released an open-source project allowing Switch and Switch 2 games to run natively on Apple TV.

So far, both Super Mario Odyssey and Animal Crossing: New Horizons are running, with work ongoing on The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom …

We’ve seen people using Claude Code to do some pretty wild things, like reverse engineering Adobe’s pro apps in order to create open-source versions of them. The latest example is a Redditor who’s created an open-source project called TVport to recompile Nintendo games from the Switch and Switch 2 to Apple TV.

Redditor FloatingFalafel shared the work on GitHub. They’ve so far ported three games to Apple TV, with one of them still a work in progress.

I have been working on a fork of nxnative that recompiles your OG Switch and Switch 2 dumps for AppleTV. Currently, this only works on a game-by-game basis. Most games run essentially the same on the switch, but some load textures into memory differently and need to be diagnosed and fixed before the game will run properly. My hope is to find outliers during this beta so more fixes can be added into the program, making it a seamless experience […]

Super Mario Odyssey – Runs at 60FPS, very slight stutters on occasion, and some audio issues around waterfalls specifically.

Animal Crossing: Horizon – Runs at 30FPS, zero issues so far on my plays.

Zelda: TOTK – Still being worked on, runs at 30FPS, gets thermal throttled. I have a work around for the thermal throttle. I have a render scale selection set at 75% and I am working on adding MetalFX upscaling.

They note you’ll need the 4th-gen Apple TV with its 8GB RAM in order to support some games, though these ones run on the 3rd-gen box.

Another Redditor is working on porting Nintendo 64 games to Apple TV using an app called Nativecade. How long any of these types of projects will survive is anyone’s guess.

#3455. Who Are The Clarks & Newmans In Black Doves? Crime Families Explained

WARNING: SPOILERS ahead for Black Doves season 1.

The Clarks and the Newmans are two feared and dangerous London-based crime family organizations in the Netflix espionage series Black Doves. Created by Joe Barton (The Lazarus Project, Giri/Haji), Black Doves has outstanding reviews, earning a 98% Rotten Tomatoes critic score after its December 5, 2024 release date. Knightley (Atonement, Pirates of the Caribbean) leads the cast of Black Doves along with Ben Whishaw's Sam Young, best known for playing Q in Daniel Craig's James Bond films. Black Doves features a stellar supporting cast, including Sarah Lancashire's Reed, Kathryn Hunter's Lenny, and Ella Lily Hyland's Williams.

Black Doves follows public figure Helen Webb, the loving and supportive wife of Andrew Buchan's Wallace Webb, a prominent British politician. Webb is also a secret agent working for the mysterious covert spy organization known as the Black Doves, which Mrs. Reed is the head of. Reed confronts Helen over an affair she was having with a civil servant named Jason (Andrew Koji), who was shockingly shot and killed in a park from long range. Suspecting that Helen could be in hot water with a powerful criminal conspiracy headed by the notorious Clark family, Reed enlists a trusted triggerman named Sam Young for assistance.

In Black Doves season 1, the Clarks and the Newmans are two separate organized crime families who operate out of London, England. The Newmans are the first of the two crime families to be introduced in the series through a flashback involving Sam several years before the main plot of the series takes place. As one of Sam's early assignments after Lenny ordered him to take out his father, Frank, for his first hit, Sam kills three of the four Newman brothers who were starting to make a name for themselves as drug dealers. The Newman brothers were a violent group of drug dealers with quite a gang at their disposal. Young Hector launched an attack on Sam with this gang to seek revenge for his brothers. He's played by Luther Ford.

The Clarks are a much bigger crime family conglomerate out of London. They have international outreach and have established connections in several countries, including the United States. Alex Clark was the head of the Clark family mob before Sam killed her at the end of Black Doves season 1. Her son, Trent Clark, was not a prominent figure in the organization apart from being Alex's son. He appears to be of little use to Alex in the series but is the main reason why several of the deaths take place, most significantly Ambassador Chen, who he accidentally killed, and Jason, who he hired another assassin named Elmore Fitch to murder.

Alex Clark, played by Tracey Ullman, is the London crime boss and the Clark matriarch in Black Doves. Her son, Trent, is meant to be her successor in the business. Helen confronts Alex in a showdown late in the season, and Alex claims she had no part to play in the death of Jason Davies.

Hector was the boy who Sam let live, which forced him to walk away from the assassin business and get out of London for seven years. When Sam returns to London, Lenny gets a hold of him and wants him to make good on the botched hit on Hector Newman, who had grown up and expanded his own profitable drug ring. Lenny still found Hector to be a nuisance in London even after all those years and forced Sam to make good on his promise. Newman had gotten more powerful and disruptive after Sam let him off the hook.

Sam didn't pull the trigger on Hector when he had the chance because he was just a kid and that would have violated his own moral code as a hitman. Apart from Hector, Black Doves season 1 doesn't introduce any other prominent Newmans, indicating that Hector may be the last man standing in his crime family. Hector's operation was weakened after the Clarks took out dozens of his men searching for Kai-Ming, Ambassador Chen's daughter. This is why Hector doesn't kill when he has the chance and why he shows up at Michale's apartment asking to join forces at the end of the season. Hector also thanks Sam for killing his bully brothers and offers him a job.

Trent Clark is the main reason why the entire plot unfolds in Black Doves and is why Ambassador Chen, Jason, Maggie, Phillip, Stephen Yarrick, and even Elmore Fitch, were all killed. Despite his pleas for innocence and his admission of guilt in the Black Doves season 1 finale, Trent had far too much blood on his hands. In the final moments of Black Doves season 1, Sam sensed that Helen was about to take revenge on Trent for killing Jason and taking more lives trying to cover it up. Sam takes out Trent, Alex, and their bodyguard so Helen doesn't bring danger to her family. In the Black Doves season 1 finale, Sam shoots Alex and then kills Trent before Helen has a chance to pull the trigger herself. He appears to be sparing her the burden of being a killer like him. A distraught Helen says Trent was hers to kill.

There's nothing really tragic about Trent's death since he is by far the most irredeemable character in the series. The same can be said for Alex Clar, who was completely unaware that Trent was trying to cover himself by ordering hits on everyone who knew about Ambassador Chen's death. While Alex and Trent are not featured much in Black Doves season 1, and won't be included in the eventual season 2, their deaths could spell trouble for Helen and Sam in future episodes.

If anything, the Clarks and the Newmans are rival crime families with very different levels of power and scale. The Clarks are internationally recognized, while the Newmans, or at least what's left of them with Hector, are a more local clan operating in the United Kingdom. Hector Newman may have additional connections throughout Europe since his primary trade appears to be selling and distributing drugs.

One of the biggest mysteries in Black Doves season 1 is how Hector Newman came to find Kai-Ming in the first place and why she was stuck in his warehouse. Since the Clarks were looking for Kai-Ming and shot up the Newmans' warehouse, it wouldn't make sense if the two crime families were operating on the same team. It's more than likely that the Newmans and the Clarks are rival gangs, although the Clarks are much more sophisticated than the Newmans in the first season. Since Alex Clark is dead, Hector Newman could try to gain power among the Clarks or enlist some of their henchmen and resources to expand his organization in Black Doves season 2.

After discovering her lover's murder, a spy masquerading as a politician's wife joins forces with an old assassin associate to uncover the truth and seek revenge.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Factually inaccurate: Alex Clark was not the head of the crime family, this is stated explicitly by her and about her.

KaiMing ended up with Hector Newman because she freaked out when she found out that her father's dead in her apartment. Then she ran to her drug dealer's place, which apparently turn out to be a warehouse/club owned by Hector.
