#3453. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display review: A lot more than touch

Apple unveiled the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display last week, and it brings some of the biggest changes to the Mac in years. There’s a tandem OLED screen, a significantly lighter design, and the long-awaited addition of touch. Oh, and the Apple logo glows again.

Here’s what it’s like actually using the new MacBook Pro.

In 2016, Apple unveiled an all-new MacBook Pro design that prioritized thinness and portability above almost everything else, kickstarting what proved to be a rocky period for Apple laptops. The thinner, lighter MacBook Pro was marred by the butterfly keyboard, poor thermals, and an overall focus on form over function.

In 2021, Apple righted the ship. It unveiled a completely redesigned MacBook Pro that reversed many of those controversial decisions, bringing back ports, replacing the Touch Bar with a physical function row, and dramatically improving performance with Apple Silicon.

There was a trade-off, though: the MacBook Pro got bigger and noticeably heavier. The smaller model grew from 13 inches and 3.1 pounds to 14 inches and 3.5 pounds, while the 16-inch model went from 4.3 pounds to 4.7 pounds.

At the time, we were all willing to make that compromise. Now, with the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, Apple is once again making its pro laptops lighter — but without sacrificing what made the 2021 redesign so great.

The 14-inch model has dropped from 3.5 pounds to just 3.0 pounds, while the 16-inch model has gone from 4.7 pounds to 4.0 pounds. In fact, both new MacBook Pro models weigh essentially the same as their 2016 counterparts, despite having larger displays, significantly more powerful hardware, and none of the compromises that defined that generation.

Both models are also slightly thinner than before, with the 14-inch model measuring 0.59 inches thick (down from 0.61 inches) and the 16-inch measuring 0.63 inches (down from 0.66 inches).

How did Apple pull this off? The biggest change is the switch from mini-LED to OLED. Because OLED doesn’t require a separate backlight, Apple could make the display assembly significantly thinner and lighter. The company is also using custom on-cell touch technology to integrate touch sensing into the display panel, instead of adding multiple separate layers.

But while the new display technology played a major role, the weight reduction also came from countless other smaller engineering optimizations throughout the machine.

You notice the lighter weight of the new MacBook Pro immediately when you pick it up. My review unit is the 16-inch MacBook Pro, and I’m genuinely surprised at how nice it feels. It’s not light, but it feels less like a tank.

I’ve always used the smaller of the two MacBook Pro models for portability, most recently a 14-inch M4 Pro. The weight of the new 16-inch MacBook Pro has me reconsidering that preference, though. It feels remarkably nice for a laptop with such a large display, and I’ve really enjoyed having the extra screen space without feeling like I’m sacrificing too much portability.

The new MacBook Pro also features slimmer bezels around the display. Apple has eliminated the thicker bottom bezel, and for the first time, all four corners of the display are rounded. It’s a relatively small change, but I think it gives the MacBook Pro a cleaner, more symmetrical look.

And finally: the glowing Apple logo is back. Unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.

The logo’s brightness is still tied to the display brightness, just like it was a decade ago. The higher your display brightness, the brighter the Apple logo on the back. It also factors in your environment’s ambient brightness.

When the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign. Open it up, and it glows. It’s unnecessary, but I’m so thrilled it’s back.

The display is what Apple is most proud of on this new MacBook Pro. After all, the full marketing name is apparently “MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.” It doesn’t exactly roll off the tongue, but I think it shows what Apple sees as the big differentiator compared to other MacBook Pro models it still sells.

And rightfully so. The PROLED XDR Display is stunning. It’s a major upgrade over the mini-LED display that Apple debuted in the MacBook Pro back in 2021 (which was no slouch, to be clear). The OLED panel’s color saturation, contrast, and deep blacks are miles better than any other laptop I’ve seen, including Windows PCs with high-end OLED displays.

The viewing angles are also noticeably better, with colors and brightness staying remarkably consistent even when you look at the display from the side.

One downside of the MacBook Pro with mini-LED is blooming. Because the mini-LED display used local dimming zones, there was a subtle halo around bright objects against dark backgrounds. With the OLED display on these new MacBook Pros, every pixel is independently illuminated, so that blooming effect is gone.

If you’re worried about burn-in, Apple says the new MacBook Pros have a revamped display engine that continuously monitors pixel usage, temperature, and other factors. It compensates individual pixels in real time to mitigate burn-in and maintain brightness. We’ll have to wait and see whether this holds true over time, but anecdotally I haven’t noticed any burn-in on my OLED iPad Pro after more than two years.

The improvements on the new MacBook Pro’s display go well beyond simply being OLED. Brightness is another area Apple emphasizes.

In direct sunlight by a window or on the patio, the display gets more than bright enough to remain easily readable. I rarely find myself needing to crank the brightness all the way up.

Those brightness improvements dovetail nicely with another area of emphasis on the new MacBook Pro: reflectivity. The new MacBook Pro’s glossy display has just 1% reflectance, which Apple says is due to two things. First, the OLED panel itself is designed to minimize reflections. It also has a custom antireflective coating that reduces reflections from the cover glass.

My review unit has a standard glossy display, and my previous MacBook Pro was a 14-inch model with nano-texture, so I’ve been paying especially close attention to the differences in reflectivity.

As I write this review, I’m sitting next to a large window that gets a lot of direct light. I’m very impressed with how well this glossy 16-inch MacBook Pro display handles reflections. It’s not, of course, as antireflective as my 14-inch MacBook Pro with nano-texture. But it’s much closer than I expected, and significantly better than my glossy MacBook Air.

I haven’t had a chance to try the nano-texture on the new MacBook Pro with PROLED, but Apple says the nano-texture is now “precisely etched into the cover glass,” so it should be even better than before.

All told, the PROLED XDR Display is impressive by every metric, both on paper and in the real world. Whether it’s the core improvements of an OLED panel, improved reflectivity, or higher brightness, you’ll notice the better display from the moment you turn the MacBook Pro on.

There’s something uncanny about using the new touchscreen MacBook Pro for the first time. This is still unmistakably macOS, with the same interface and software controls that we’ve known for years. Except now, you can reach out and touch the screen … and it actually responds.

Apple famously resisted adding touch to the Mac until now. Steve Jobs called the idea of a touchscreen Mac “ergonomically terrible” in 2010.

When Apple announced these touchscreen MacBooks, that clip of Jobs went viral. As usual, Jobs’ comments have more nuance than last week’s social media reaction suggests.

“Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical,” Jobs said at the time. “It gives great demo, but after a short period of time you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off.”

A lot has changed since those comments from Jobs, but I don’t think adding touch to the MacBook Pro proves him wrong. The ergonomics of using a touchscreen as the primary input method on a laptop-style device are, in fact, terrible. Your arm does get tired.

The good news, however, is that Apple is very intentionally not trying to make touch the primary interaction method on these new MacBook Pros. It’s clear from both using this touchscreen MacBook Pro and Apple’s own messaging that touch is intended to be a secondary input method. It’s there when you need it or want it, but you can also ignore it completely and never feel like you’re missing out.

So, with that out of the way: what’s it like using a touchscreen MacBook Pro?

Apple has made a variety of small tweaks throughout macOS to accommodate touch input. For example, when macOS detects touch input, items in contextual menus are spaced further apart.

When you long-press on something like an app icon in the Dock, it enlarges and shows you a more spaced-out list of contextual menu items. If you long-press an item in Finder, it lifts up under your finger, and you can drag it or drop it anywhere else.

The classic traffic light window controls also expand after you tap them. The first tap expands the controls without actually activating any of them. Then, tap a second time on the specific control you’re trying to activate. It’s a bit awkward having to tap the same spot twice in a row like that.

These tweaks are all about making macOS dynamically adapt to the fact that your finger is less precise than a pointer. Rather than redesigning macOS around touch, Apple has made the existing interface accommodate it when needed.

You also get all the typical touch gestures. You can pinch to zoom, swipe with four fingers to switch between Spaces or Mission Control, and swipe up to reveal the dock. You can pull to refresh in Safari, double-tap a window to fill the screen, and flick a window to the side to tile it.

Apple has also added automatic video stabilization that compensates for screen movement when you tap the display during a video call. This helps keep your camera feed steady, even when the screen itself wobbles slightly. It seems to work as advertised in my testing.

So far, I’ve found the touchscreen on MacBook Pro to be a “nice-to-have” addition, but not a reinvention of how I use the Mac. I catch myself idly reaching up to scroll a webpage instead of using the trackpad, tapping on the occasional Dock icon, and using pinch-to-zoom in the Photos app.

Touch input is also legitimately useful in places like iPhone Mirroring and the Xcode simulator. I can imagine people who regularly use rendering apps like Blender will find the touchscreen more useful than I do, since my primary job is manipulating text.

One reason I think touch might be less useful, or less important, on a Mac than on a Windows PC is that Apple’s trackpads are simply too good. There’s little reason for me to bother reaching up and using four fingers to swipe between Spaces when I can do it on the beautiful, big, glass trackpad. On a Windows PC with a crappy plastic trackpad? I bet multi-touch interaction is much more appealing on the touchscreen.

There have been a few instances where I just forget this MacBook Pro has a touchscreen until I reach up to flick a piece of lint or dog hair off the screen, and accidentally tap on something.

But I think that’s exactly how it should be. Using the touchscreen is a conscious choice, not a requirement. You can buy this computer and literally never touch the screen, or turn it off entirely via Accessibility in System Settings. For some Mac users, this is probably the most important thing. Apple hasn’t compromised the traditional macOS experience to accommodate touch.

The one thing that hasn’t changed with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is performance. Much like the standard MacBook Pro models unveiled earlier this year, the new PROLED models are available with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

Apple says that the new MacBook Pro has a redesigned thermal system optimized for the new design, while also maintaining the same performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max we’ve come to expect.

My review unit is the 16-inch M5 Pro configuration with an 18-core CPU, 20-core GPU, and 48GB of unified memory. In GeekBench testing, the new MacBook Pro performs virtually the same as the models introduced earlier this year.

In my day-to-day use, I haven’t noticed any differences in performance or thermal behavior compared to my previous MacBook Pro. Admittedly, my workflow of writing, researching, editing photos, and dozens of Safari tabs doesn’t come close to pushing the M5 Pro to its limits. But the new MacBook Pro handles all of that effortlessly, without noticeable heat or fan noise. In fact, I haven’t heard the fans kick in once.

That’s not a definitive test of Apple’s claims about sustained performance, but it’s reassuring that the thinner and lighter design hasn’t introduced any noticeable compromises in my everyday use or in benchmarks.

This makes for an interesting predicament for MacBook Pro shoppers. Rumors say that Apple believes the M7 generation will offer such a dramatic improvement in performance, particularly around AI, that it’s skipping the higher-end M6 chips altogether.

The first M7 chips are expected sometime next year, likely late in the year for the high-end MacBook Pro. This means that if you buy an M5-equipped MacBook Pro right now, you’re buying a computer with a chip that will effectively be two generations behind in less than a year.

The M5 Pro and M5 Max chips are plenty fast, and these MacBook Pros also come with OLED, touch, and other changes mentioned throughout this review. Still, there’s something a little strange about Apple pairing its biggest MacBook Pro redesign in five years with chips that debuted eight months ago, particularly with the next major leap in Apple silicon reportedly on the horizon.

The Dynamic Island comes to the Mac for the first time with the new MacBook Pro. It never made sense to me that Apple added the notch to the MacBook Pro with so little software accommodation. The Dynamic Island finally addresses that, bringing a familiar iPhone experience to the Mac.

Live Activities now show up in the Dynamic Island, along with Now Playing info from apps like Music and Podcasts. For example, clicking (or tapping) the Dynamic Island while Music is playing brings up the mini player for easy access to controls. From the mini player, you can click again to open the full Music app. Live Activities from your iPhone also show up in the Dynamic Island on MacBook Pro, rather than in your menu bar like on other Macs. Spotlight on Mac bounces out of the Dynamic Island.

I’ve very much enjoyed having the Dynamic Island on the Mac. It’s one of my favorite iPhone features, especially for Live Activities. The implementation on the Mac is a great continuation of that experience.

Apple says that the new MacBook Pro has a redesigned six-speaker system that delivers 50% deeper bass. The speakers do indeed sound fantastic. Apple also specifically calls out improved speaker tuning when using the MacBook Pro with its lid closed and connected to an external display. In my testing, the difference is noticeable. The speakers sound less muffled and significantly louder.

Apple says battery life is unchanged on the new MacBook Pro models compared to the non-OLED variants.

I haven’t done any scientific battery testing, but anecdotally, my 16-inch M5 Pro model seems on track to match Apple’s claim of up to 17 hours of wireless web browsing.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a fascinating product. It’s both a major evolution of the MacBook Pro and a better version of the same laptop we’ve come to love since its Apple Silicon reinvigoration in 2021.

The addition of touch is getting all the attention, but I think the lighter design is actually the more significant change in day-to-day use. I never expected a 16-inch MacBook Pro to have me reconsidering my longstanding preference for the 14-inch model.

Touch hasn’t fundamentally changed how I use the Mac, but it’s a welcome addition that feels overdue. People reasonably expect to touch their laptop screen and have it respond. Some people will undoubtedly find it more useful than I have, and Apple has done an excellent job integrating it into macOS without compromising the traditional experience.

With or without touch, the PROLED XDR display is a spectacular upgrade, with improvements in brightness, contrast, and reflectivity that you’ll notice every time you open the lid.

These new OLED MacBook Pro models command a $400 premium over the mini-LED M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro models Apple is still selling. Those machines are also heavier, lack touchscreens, and miss some of the bells and whistles of the pricier models. Presumably, these two product lines will eventually converge, but right now the MacBook Pro lineup is a little awkward. The 14-inch PROLED model starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399.

But that awkward positioning doesn’t take away from the product. This is still the same MacBook Pro we’ve come to love over the last five years. Apple has taken an already excellent laptop and made meaningful improvements to nearly every aspect of the experience. And it just so happens to have a touchscreen now, too.

#3452. King Ghidorah Is Ready for Its Close-Up: How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Cracked the Legendary Monster’s Next Evolution

“Godzilla Minus Zero” builds on the strong visual foundation — and/or the rubble of Tokyo’s Ginza district — that director Takashi Yamazaki pounded into his previous film, “Godzilla Minus One.” Like that first film, “Minus Zero” is in conversation with the big ideas and cultural/emotional resonances behind Toho’s giant monsters, and it’s attuned to the beloved visual details of the franchise, going all the way back to the original “Godzilla” and the Shōwa era.

But historically, for all kinds of budgetary and technological reasons, King Ghidorah is usually not ready for his close-up.

The amount of time that “Godzilla Minus Zero” spends with its three-headed mutant space dragon on the ground is a notable departure from how Ghidorah is most often depicted: in flight, or towering far above Godzilla. Even in closer shots in a CGI-rich film like “Godzilla: King of the Monsters,” when all three heads get ready to chomp up a puny human or 10, the emphasis is on Ghidorah’s scale. Three heads are more terrifying than one. Related Stories Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It? From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race

But “Godzilla Minus Zero” spends a lot of time with just one head, or focused on just one head, and its Ghidorah is as scary on the ground as it is in the air, and this is in part due to the particular design experience that director Yamazaki and his team brought to the world’s deadliest gold dragon. Yamazaki was tapped to design “Godzilla the Ride” at Seibuen Amusement Park (its full name is Godzilla the Ride: Giant Monsters Ultimate Battle) in 2021 and therefore had to figure out a version of Ghidorah that would work from the other side of a safety rail.

Yamazaki and animation studio Shirogumi worked on a monster concept that would feel, according to “Minus One” and “Minus Zero” producer Kazuaki Kishida, “as though the audience was under attack by Ghidorah itself. So it had to be very scary and very close-up,” Kishida told IndieWire. “[In the ride,] we see Ghidorah basically crawling on the ground with its neck, because it has a very long neck, and then really going after the audience. To bring King Ghidorah very close to humans and bring the eyeline closer was a huge core concept for this. So there was a lot of research that had gone into the ride that we were able to apply to ‘Godzilla Minus Zero.'”

The film uses Ghidorah’s eyeline to great effect. One of the most unnerving moments in its initial attack on Matsumoto City, as scientists Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka) and Akira Hagiwara (Ko Maehara) scramble to both document the new monster on the block and survive the utter destruction of whole city blocks, is a moment of getting really, uncomfortably close to Ghidorah’s eye.

That forced proximity to Ghidorah makes all the spectacular space-dragon stuff it can do even more effective, though these effects are also as grounded in the natural and the tangible as much as possible. For Ghidorah’s destructive beam, for instance, visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima did more research than even he thought he could do on how lightning visualizes itself.

“Everyone sort of recognized the string of light, that line of light. But if you look at lightning in slow motion, it leaves a line of something that lingers — this is apparently just water vaporizing instantly and turning into plasma,” Nojima told IndieWire. “I don’t fully know the science behind it, but there’s a visual effect that lightning leaves behind. So for Ghidorah’s destruction beam, I wanted to emphasize that element of it. I scatter particles around, kind of blur the imagery, and then let it linger longer than it normally would.”

Of course, whenever the destruction beam hits something, Nojima and the VFX team got to build the explosion. But it’s that visual sense of Ghidorah’s power lingering, and of getting too close to where Ghidorah can see you, that makes this version of the monster feel so dangerous.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now playing in theaters.

#3449. James Gunn’s DC Studios Exit Came at the Worst Time

The news that James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-heads of DC Studios was a major shock, whether you're a longtime comic book fan or someone who's been enjoying the current slate of DC-themed projects. It also felt out of nowhere: while DC Studios had a bit of a road bump due to Supergirl's less-than-stellar reception, it more than made up for it with two critically acclaimed projects in Lanterns and Clayface. This decision will loom over future DC projects, and it comes at the wrong time.

While Gunn has taken to social media to stress that stepping down as co-CEO was his decision, eyebrows are being raised at the man chosen to replace him and Safran. Skydance has tapped Jeremy Latcham as DC Studios' new president and chief creative officer, and Latcham isn't lacking in terms of box office credits; he produced some of Marvel Studios' biggest movies, including The Avengers and Guardians of the Galaxy (which Gunn directed) alongside the highly underrated Dungeons and Dragons: Honor Among Thieves. Latcham's Marvel work likely led to his top spot at DC Studios, but it also highlights a recurring trend in DC-based movies.

Jeremy Latcham's hiring is far from the first time that Warner Bros. has hired a creative best known for working at Marvel Studios. Back in 2017, Joss Whedon was hired to complete principal photography on Justice League after Zack Snyder departed the project following the loss of his daughter, Autumn. The result was a disaster; Snyder's more operatic filmmaking style clashed with Whedon's zippy, quippy approach to writing superheroes. Add in accusations of "gross misconduct" by star Ray Fisher, and Whedon's time on Justice League ended rather poorly. It also meant that DC's bid to reclaim some of the Marvel magic was dead in the water.

Though it's never been said out loud, some fans have speculated that a large part of the reason Gunn was chosen as DC Studios' CEO, beyond his work on The Suicide Squad and Peacemaker, is his previous work on the Guardians of the Galaxy trilogy. However, Gunn proved that he could make DC Studios its own thing by delivering character-driven stories, whether it's the blood-soaked chaos of Creature Commandos or the sci-fi spectacle of Superman. Latcham needs to keep that in mind, rather than chasing Marvel Studios' success.

James Gunn and Peter Safran's departures come as DC Studios prepares to release its biggest movie yet, Man of Tomorrow. Written and directed by Gunn, Man of Tomorrow will feature Clark Kent (David Corenswet) and Lex Luthor (Nicholas Hoult) joining forces to battle the malevolent artificial intelligence, Brainiac (Lars Eidinger). #3447. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

This odd-looking variation on a basic move is surprisingly effective

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Spare a thought for the push-up, that most humble of body-weight exercises, and almost certainly the best known. It is as simple as exercise gets — lie on the floor, support your weight with your arms, lower to the ground, push back up, and repeat — it can be done almost anywhere and it is hugely effective, building strength and definition in the arms, chest, and shoulders. It also works the core, if you’re doing it properly. And if you want to challenge yourself, just do a few more. It is, I would suggest, a perfect exercise. And why mess with perfection? On the other hand, why not?

Which brings me neatly to the Hindu push-up, a dynamic variation on the basic move. It’s not new, having been a core training move for Indian wrestlers since at least the 19th century. Ghulam Mohammad Baksh Butt, an undefeated giant of the sport (he was known, deservedly, as The Great Gama) purportedly did 3,000 Hindu push-ups every day as part of his savage training regimen.

The basic push-up is hard for beginners and even if you do them regularly, adding reps is tough, but the Hindu push-up is much harder, so I would not recommend this move for newcomers. However, if you’re up for it, it will improve your flexibility and work your back, glutes and legs in addition to the benefits listed above. If you do Pilates or yoga, you will probably find this a little more comfortable, in terms of form, at least.

I am inherently suspicious of any move that involves or is adjacent to yoga, as I am not nearly as flexible as I’d like to be, but I’ve been doing pushups for as long as I’ve been exercising (as with most people, I imagine, it was the first body-weight move I ever attempted — thanks, Dad).

For that reason, I approached this challenge with a mixture of confidence and trepidation, which is enormously confusing. I suspected I’d be undone by the inverted V and end cobra position, but I found I could do both reasonably well. What got me was the incredible strain it put on my arms, which was also what impressed me.

On day one, I struggled mightily with the movement from downward dog and was inclined to come up too early, which put a strain on my lower back. Bad idea. I restarted, going more slowly. This made for better form but an astonishing level of stress on my triceps as I swept down and then up into the cobra position, or as close as I could get to it.

Afterwards, I felt the effort in my arms, across my shoulders, and, to a lesser extent, in my lower back (in a good way). I managed two sets of 10, with some wobbling towards the end of each set. I strongly recommend you use a mat for this move, as your feet will slide back on a bare floor. When I finished, my triceps let me know someone had been working them in a way they did not recognize.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The following day, I still had the not displeasing ache in my triceps, which I do not feel after traditional push-ups (mind you, I could just add more reps). This time, I worked on controlling the downward and upward movement, rather than the weight-bearing part of the move. I kept my elbows close to my sides (do not let them flare out) and completed three sets of 10. Obviously, I had not become stronger after one day, so this considerable improvement was entirely down to better form.

For the rest of the week, I continued to pay close attention to my form. If you begin in the high inverted V position, your arms will not be too far forward when you sweep down, which will make things easier. Not easy. Easier. Very slightly easier. I began to enjoy the effort and the flowing motion when things were going well.

That said, I never went beyond three sets of 12 — this is a difficult, challenging move and I would only recommend it if you’re already very comfortable doing regular push-ups and have no lower back issues (you might want to check with a medical professional before you try the Hindu pushup). But if you do feel you are ready, then I can heartily recommend this exercise.

By the end of the week, I was feeling it across my chest, as well as in my upper arms and shoulders, and I was more than happy to be adding some flexibility work to a strength move. The ache in my muscles stayed with me for the week, which suggested the move continued to work my arms and chest in a way regular push-ups do not. I won’t be doing 3,000 of these every day, but that’s only because I have no desire to preface my name with The Great. I’ll settle for The Didn’t Fall On His Face…

#3442. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

iOS 27.3 is coming next month and is packed with new features, including some that make Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Apple One launched in 2019 with Individual, Family, and Premier plans. And in the seven years since, the service bundle has stayed remarkably consistent.

Every plan has always included Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, and iCloud+. And the high-end Premier option adds Apple News+ and Fitness+ alongside more iCloud storage.

Apple News+ has gotten a lot better over the years. Following the New York Times playbook, Apple has added daily puzzle games, food-focused content like recipes, and audio stories, all while continuing to improve the basic news experience.

Apple Fitness+ keeps improving too, but there’s an upgrade in iOS 27.3 that makes it far more compelling in my view: Gym Strength.

Built-in video demonstrations accompany your personalized plan, making strength training accessible even for newcomers. And you can track your progress in the app, with key Apple Watch integration too.

I’ve used Fitness+ plenty and enjoyed it, but a comprehensive strength plan like this was a big gap in the service previously. With iOS 27.3 though, Fitness+ takes a big leap forward and makes Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Also relevant: with the new HomeView product and other Apple Home accessories almost here, Apple One Premier’s support for Apple Intelligence video summaries and clips with HomeKit Secure Video becomes more valuable. All of this together amounts to a stronger-than-ever Premier plan.

Apple One starts at $21.95/month and includes services like Apple TV, Apple Music, iCloud+, and more.

#3440. FBI Investigating Suspected Homicide Aboard Cruise Ship in Texas

A Caribbean cruise has taken a deadly turn ... with the FBI investigating a suspected homicide aboard a massive cruise ship that was forced to return to port in Texas.

Federal authorities say they're investigating a possible murder aboard the MSC Seascape, which docked in Galveston Monday morning after departing Sunday for a weeklong Caribbean vacation.

The ship was only hours into its voyage when it turned around at around 12:20 AM Monday morning ... returning to port at the direction of authorities.

MSC Cruises confirmed the unexpected detour, saying in a statement ... "On reporting a guest incident aboard our ship, we were instructed by the authorities to return to the Port of Galveston."

The cruise line says it's cooperating fully with investigators and providing support to those affected ... while the FBI is working alongside the U.S. Coast Guard, port police and Customs and Border Protection.

Authorities have not identified the deceased person or revealed how the death occurred ... and no arrests have been publicly announced.

Despite the investigation, the ship has since left Galveston and resumed its planned itinerary.

#3439. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

#3434. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

#3433. tvOS 27.2 adds new Apple TV 4K setting that’s an instant favorite

tvOS 27.2 launched last week as the latest software update for Apple TV 4K, and it includes a new setting I’m a big fan of: Shuffle for screen savers.

Screen savers have been one of the best Apple TV features since tvOS first launched in 2015. Largely that’s due to the gorgeous aerials captured around the world (and even from space).

Aerials are still my favorite type of Apple TV screen saver, but tvOS has steadily added other categories worth checking out too.

Currently inside Settings ⇾ Screen Saver you’ll find four categories:

The second and third options tap into your Apple Photos library and introduce the joy of seeing your favorite memories pop up on the big screen. Snoopy screen savers feature the beloved Peanuts character in a variety of entertaining scenes.

All of these screen saver options are great. But until tvOS 27.2, you had to select just one category and that’s all you’d ever see.

Now with tvOS 27.2, Apple has introduced a ‘Shuffle’ option that randomly cycles through screen savers from across all four categories.

It’s a welcome new setting, long overdue but I’ve been enjoying it a lot. The ability to be surprised by more different screen savers may sound like a small thing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to the Apple TV 4K experience.

Have you tried the new Shuffle setting for screen savers in tvOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

#3431. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3430. Anthropic upgrades Claude with new Personal Finance feature

Having the right context is what makes AI tools useful. Anthropic just launched the ability to securely use personal finance data with Claude. The company emphasizes that the feature is read-only and can’t take financial actions.

“Getting answers about your money no longer means opening every banking app and doing the math yourself,” Anthropic says. “With Personal Finance in Claude, you can securely connect your bank and card accounts and ask in your own words. Access is read-only, and Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest your money.”

Similar to ChatGPT’s finances feature, Claude’s new capabilities essentially give you a way to use chat as a way to make sense of your finance data. It can also present data in dashboards, calendars, and more.

Given the importance of security, here’s what Anthropic has to say regarding the new finance feature and Claude:

Claude’s access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn’t designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank.

Your accounts are only connected once you sign in to your bank yourself through Plaid, a service that connects apps to banks. That’s where you agree to its terms and approve Claude’s read-only access, so Claude doesn’t ask for or see your bank password.

#3428. I spent 2 weeks playing the Acer Predator Atlas 8, and this big gaming handheld (almost) made me ditch my PC

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Acer Predator Atlas 8 is a big, bold and beautiful handheld that delivers the ultimate portable gaming experience with the might of its Intel Arc G3 Extreme backing it up. For its price, you're getting incredible power for a Windows handheld PC, and it helps that its bright, 8-inch 1200p display with a 120Hz refresh rate is a treat for the eyes. It's held back by some cheap-feeling parts, and it may be a tad too chunky for many to hold, but the Atlas 8 shows off exactly how incredible handheld gaming is right now.

Satisfying TMR sticks and Hall Effect triggers

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The next standard of handheld gaming continues with the Acer Predator Atlas 8, the striking 8-inch Windows handheld featuring the most powerful chips I've seen for handheld gaming on the go: the Intel Arc G3 Extreme. What really sets this big beauty apart from its rivals, though? It offers a lot for less than you'd think, and I'd be happy to ditch a gaming PC to play on this all day long.

Having seen the Predator Atlas 8's potential back at Computex 2026, I was delighted to see it had met my expectations and gone further, from playing Star Wars: Galactic Racer on the couch to delving deeper into Gears of War: E-Day while travelling with frame rates pushing to 90 frames per second (FPS) at medium to high settings — thanks to Intel's XeSS graphics upscaling and frame generation tech.

It's a marvel to play, only made better thanks to the sizeable 8-inch 1200p LCD display boasting a 120Hz variable refresh rate and the snappy TMR sticks and Hall Effect triggers. For $1,299 / £1,299? That's still pricey, sure, but not nearly as much as the equally powerful $1,799 MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. It's even the same price as the OLED-focused ROG Xbox Ally X20, but delivers even greater power.

All that said, Acer clearly has to make some sacrifices, and they're evident. That includes the cheap-feeling D-pad and adjustable triggers that sometimes don't register input. And don't expect the magic of Intel's XeSS tech to work on a majority of games (including Halo: Campaign Evolved specifically in the Xbox app, despite it being supported, for some odd reason).

In any case, the Acer Predator Atlas 8 is easily one of the best gaming handhelds you can buy right now. For a deeper dive on what to expect, read on.

8-inch FHD+ (1920 x 1200) LCD touchscreen | 120Hz VRR

8-inch FHD+ (1920 x 1200) LCD touchscreen | 120Hz VRR

1x microSD, 2x Thunderbolt 4, 1x 3.5mm audio jack

1x microSD, 2x Thunderbolt 4, 1x 3.5mm audio jack

The Acer Predator Atlas 8 couldn't have arrived in my hands at a better time. I had taken some time off to take care of a new addition to the family (a dog, if you must know), and that meant having plenty of time to build new routines and, of course, kick back. But that all had to be done away from my gaming PC, and my backlog has been piling up (it's been a phenomenal year of great games, and that's pre-GTA VI!).

Thankfully, the Atlas 8 arrived to clean up that backlog, and it's (mostly) been an absolute treat.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With a name like "Atlas," it's almost a given that this Windows gaming handheld had to be quite big in size. On paper, that should be counterproductive for a portable gaming handheld, but Acer fine-tuned the Predator Atlas 8 to make it a sizeable machine that's equally comfortable to hold, too.

At 11.7 x 5 x 2.2 inches and weighing 1.79 pounds, this is one of the biggest Windows handhelds ever, and that includes comparing it to the famously big Lenovo Legion Go 2 (11.64 x 5.38 x 1.66 inches, 2.09 pounds). At the very least, it isn't nearly as heavy.

But when it comes to the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 (11.8 x 4.8 x 2 inches, 1.67 pounds) or MSI Claw 8 EX AI Plus (11.6 x 5.1 x 1.9 inches, 1.7 pounds), it shows Acer couldn't quite trim as much fat off the Atlas 8's bulky design. Realistically, though, there isn't that much difference, and it's still an ergonomically pleasing handheld once put in hands.

From the contoured grip with anti-slip textures to the large layout that rest easy on your palm, the Predator Atlas 8 is great to hold while play all types of gaming genres, whether than be first-person precision in Halo or fast-paced racing in Forza Horizon 6 or Star Wars: Galactic Racer.

While I'd prefer to have an armrest to lay my elbows on while playing, as it is heavier than, say, a Nintendo Switch 2 (10.7 x 4.5 x 0.5 inches, 1.18 pounds), it's still comfy to use. Now, some may find this too bulky and heavy to handle for longer sessions, but setting up in a comfortable position on a couch can fix that issue.

Another major highlight is the 8-inch FHD+ (1920 x 1200) LCD touchscreen with 120Hz VRR. It's big enough to show off great detail and depth in the games I'd play, which is vital in titles like Star Wars: Galactic Racer and even Gears of War: E-Day, and bright enough so I could still see colorful visuals even in sunny environments. With its nicely color-coded face buttons and sticks with RGB-lit rings, it's a great-looking handheld to bring along.

I also really appreciate the satisfying-feeling TMR (Tunnel Magnetoresistance) joysticks and Hall Effect triggers, which make stick drift virtually nonexistent and make each touch feel precise. While the rear macro buttons don't quite feel as premium as the rest, I'm a fan of their placement, along with their customizability for what you need them to do.

A fantastic, great-feeling layout goes a long way in a gaming handheld, and the Atlas 8 nails the design. There's still a lot to be desired (more on that later), but I was always excited to pick this up to start gaming.

Ever since Intel revealed its gaming handheld-specific Intel Arc G3 Extreme, we've seen just how far this chipset has taken portable gaming. It's an incredible chip with plenty of raw power, brought to new heights with Intel XeSS upscaling and frame generation. The Acer Predator Atlas 8 takes that power and runs with it — and it made games I play look far more playable than I'd initially thought.

As in the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, the Intel Arc G3 Extreme is a wonder for portable power. That's both for graphics and processing power, mind you. AMD's Ryzen Z2 Extreme may have made huge strides to deliver great handheld performance in the ROG Xbox Ally X, but Intel's G3 Extreme takes performance up a notch by a considerable amount. And this shows in every 3DMark test I threw at it.

Acer Predator Atlas 8 (Intel Arc G3 Extreme)

Asus ROG Xbox Ally X (AMD Ryzen Z2 AI Extreme)

Interestingly, despite having the same chipset, the Predator Atlas 8 still fell short of the Claw 8 EX AI+. But that's due to the 24GB of DDR5X RAM my review unit came with compared to the 32GB of DDR5 RAM the Claw 8 EX AI+ boasts. As you can see, there's not a major difference, but do know you can grab a 32GB Atlas 8 model, and it's still less than MSI's handheld.

In any case, even if you wanted to hook up the Atlas 8 to one of the best monitors to get some work done in desktop mode, you can, thanks to the performance this chip offers. To put its Geekbench numbers into perspective, the Atlas 8 is well beyond something like the Dell XPS 13 (2026), and is actually nearly on par with a MacBook Air M4. Now that's impressive.

But this is made to play games, and it has plenty of power to do so. Even with its raw performance, the Atlas 8 offers great frame rates in games like Cyberpunk 2077 at 1080p with High settings and way more in classic titles, including Shadow of the Tomb Raider. Reminder: this is without Intel XeSS upscaling or frame gen.

Acer Predator Atlas 8 (Intel Arc G3 Extreme 35W)

Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 (AMD Ryzen Z2 AI Extreme 35W)

MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ (Intel Arc G3 Extreme 35W)

This outclasses what the ROG Xbox Ally X20 (and ROG Xbox Ally X, having the same chip) can offer, and surprisingly even beats the Claw 8 EX AI+ by a few frames. For the price, this is an amazing feat, and well worth the performance alone. That's especially true for older classics, too, as you can get over 80 FPS in the likes of Shadow of the Tomb Raider.

Of course, it wouldn't be enjoyable to play the latest titles at those measly frame rates. But even at Medium settings in Black Myth: Wukong, you can get a solid 47 FPS, and that's at 1200p resolution. With a bit of tinkering in the settings (like a resolution drop or some low settings), you can get this running at 60 FPS without frame gen needed.

Now, once I started bringing Intel XeSS upscaling into the fold, that's when you can really see the Atlas 8 work its magic. Think Cyberpunk 2077 at 1200p with frame rates reaching past 90 FPS, and that's with High settings and ray tracing turned on. Similarly, Star Wars: Galactic Racer at 1200p with Medium quality and Balanced resolution scaling was hitting over 70 FPS, which is needed for that type of fast-paced gameplay.

Even Gears of War: E-Day performed brilliantly, whether I wanted a solid 60 FPS with Quality upscaling or closer to 90 FPS and up for faster performance. As you can tell, there's a lot the Intel Arc G3 Extreme can handle, especially with XeSS tech to back it up (where it's supported). If you're after a gaming powerhouse for the road, the Acer Predator Atlas 8 is up to the challenge.

Despite the power the Predator Atlas 8 boasts, this Windows handheld has the battery life that can see you through gaming sessions that last hours — when you need it to.

Through the PredatorSense menu on the Atlas 8, Acer made it easy to switch between power wattage modes, including Quiet (25W), Balanced (30W) and Turbo (35W). But you can also manually change power from 10W all the way up to 40W (and up to 65W for short bursts of power, even though this isn't recommended by the system).

All of this to say you can have the Atlas 8 utilize a lot of power to push performance further, or have it sip on battery for less demanding games. The end result is long-lasting battery life, reaching nearly 4 hours in testing.

3DMark gaming battery life test result (hh:mm)

This isn't quite as long as the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, but it's nearly a full hour longer than what the ROG Xbox Ally X offers. It's nice to see handhelds now going past the 3-hour mark, as I could now get a proper gaming session in without needing to be tethered to a charger.

During real-world gameplay, I saw the Atlas 8 last 1 hour and 35 minutes while playing Gears of War: E-Day, and 1 hour and 41 minutes in Cyberpunk 2077, both at 35W. Switching to 25W while still getting good performance, Star Wars: Galactic Racer lasted 2 hours and 24 minutes. Not bad for those types of demanding titles! But when it comes to less-demanding games like Hades 2 or Marvel Cosmic Invasion, with only 10-15W, this only went down to 85% in an hour. That's a long time to game!

Usually, I'd imagine powerful performance results in incredibly short battery life. But more and more, we're seeing this isn't the case, and the Predator Atlas 8 is a fine example of this.

As much as I've enjoyed playing on the Acer Predator Atlas 8 any chance I got, it's still held back by a few sacrifices being made, which I imagine were done to keep the price down. That, and there are still some Windows 11 hiccups here and there (although, that's hardly surprising).

While the Acer Predator Atlas 8 feels comfy in the hand thanks to its ergonomic grips, anti-slip texture and satisfying heft, it's still quite a chunky piece of tech. Not everyone will appreciate holding nearly 1.8 pounds for hours on end, especially when its rivals are lighter.

This wasn't a major problem for me, especially when I had my elbows resting on the armrests of my office chair or the side of the couch. That said, the aches were starting to creep in while traveling. It's a big handheld to deliver a large 8-inch display and comfy grips, and I wouldn't expect otherwise from a device named "Atlas." Just know what you're signing up for. At the very least, you can drop to the Predator Atlas 7 for a smaller 7-inch design.

Bringing TMR joysticks for precise, good-feeling controls that are stick drift-resistant, along with Hall Effect analog triggers for pleasing responsiveness, is hugely welcome, but the D-pad seems to have been thrown in without much thought.

There's no tactile feel or satisfying actuation feedback for each direction here, just what feels like one big mushy button. For the majority of games, this isn't a huge deal, as you'll be using the analog sticks anyway. But for classic titles, fighting games, Metroidvanias and more, having a great D-pad makes a world of difference. I know this, as while playing Guile in Street Fighter 6, buttons just couldn't reliably register a charging-type "Sonic Boom." With how smooth the D-pad feels, I suppose it did make the input for Ryu's "Hadoken" somewhat easier, but never consistent.

It's also worth noting that the Predator Atlas 8 comes with adjustable trigger modes, which let you change the L2 and R2 triggers from full-travel analog press to shorter travel for faster inputs. This is a great addition, but I noticed that switching to a shorter trigger meant some actions didn't register (such as shooting a weapon). This could be a minor issue with my unit, but also something to keep aware of. Otherwise, switching back to full travel didn't make a huge difference anyway.

Microsoft's Xbox Mode has made a world of difference on Windows handhelds to deliver more of a console-like experience. But it still has some issues to iron out.

While I love bringing up the Xbox overlay to quickly switch gaming clients, check out my library of games, change settings and also see performance (that includes FPS), sometimes the overlay simply wouldn't come up unless I pressed the menu button a few times, or never at all until I switched apps. The same thing would happen when pressing the power button to put it to sleep — sometimes it powered down immediately, sometimes it didn't.

I also appreciate being able to switch to desktop mode to, essentially, use this like a proper PC. But again, nuisances like the keyboard not coming up when trying to find a game on Steam or the Xbox app being open but not showing up on screen make it all frustrating. Windows 11 on handhelds still isn't as clean to use as, say, SteamOS, but it's far from what it was.

Also, like the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, Intel's XeSS 3 support in games is still limited. While games like Star Wars: Galactic Racer, Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced and Forza Horizon 6 support this for Multi-Frame Generation (MFG), many of the biggest titles still don't. In fact, Halo: Campaign Evolved does support Intel XeSS 3, but it's "not available for Microsoft Store games," strangely. So, that means I would have to buy this on Steam to get access instead. That's annoying.

The Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip is still plenty powerful, and more games will be supported in the future, but there are some limits to know about.

The Acer Predator Atlas 8 has been hard for me to put down, and that should say plenty about how much I've enjoyed playing all the latest PC titles on this mighty machine. From the outstanding performance the Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip delivers in even demanding games to the big, bright 8-inch display to get stuck into, the Atlas 8 is a fantastic gaming handheld that I've been happy to use virtually anywhere instead of my gaming PC.

What sets it apart from its rivals? It's price-to-performance ratio. It's more affordable than the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ while delivering the same performance, and it's the same price as the ROG Xbox Ally X20 while being more powerful. But design-wise, Acer's handheld doesn't quite match all the premium trimmings of its competition.

In any case, that doesn't take away from the Acer Predator Atlas 8 being the best gaming handheld I've tested, so if you're looking for the ultimate gaming experience on the move, this will certainly fit the bill.
