#3422. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3418. Everything You Should Know About This Year's Black Friday Sales

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Best Buy, Target, Walmart, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers or refer to guides like our live blog that use price trackers for you, and don’t stress over finding the perfect timing. The “best” deal will always depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers that can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need and start tracking prices. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always do it for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

The WH-1000XM5 were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (originally $399.99).

The Bose SoundLink Plus hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers,” and it’s down to $179 (originally $269).

The all-in-one Eufy E25 robot vacuum and mop has a self-cleaning roller mop, and it is 40% off, reaching $599.98 (originally $999.99). The roller is rinsed with clean water as it mops, then cleaned at the dock, meaning you don't need to spend as much time cleaning it yourself.

Amazon is selling both right now at a $200 discount. That brings the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,099.99 (down from $1,299) and the 15-inch MacBook Air to $1,299 (originally $1,499), reaching their lowest prices since the June price hikes.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 only launched in September, and it’s already seeing an early Black Friday discount of $100 on Amazon, bringing it down to $699.99 (originally $799).

#3415. These Bose QuietComfort Headphones Are $160 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet, according to price trackers. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

Contrary to macOS 27.2, it looks like Apple had quite a bit in store for macOS 27.3 and its counterparts.

Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to create advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions, allowing the assistant to coordinate multistep actions across different apps.

Users who enjoyed the wallpaper introduced with the new touchscreen MacBook Pro will also find a new screensaver called Pro Lighteensaver, which features light moving along the metallic-looking lines that form the word “PRO.”

Earlier this week, Apple also confirmed that macOS 27.3 will introduce new checks for potentially harmful content shared through public iCloud links. Starting with the update, files and photos shared using the “Anyone with the link” option will be checked by Apple, which may remove flagged content or take action against accounts that violate its policies.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 1 is 26C5035r, which is the same as the developer build.

Celine Dion’s Paris residency has just finished its sold-out first run, and new data shows the legendary singer didn’t just bring the hits to the city — she brought big business, too.

According to Billboard, the first leg of the superstar singer’s residency, titled Celine Dion Paris, wrapped with more than $125 million in tickets sold across her 16 shows in September and October. But it wasn’t just ticket sales that saw a boon. Booking website Hotels.com says it saw a 49% increase in searches for accommodations in Paris corresponding to Dion’s tour dates, compared to the same time last year. Searches from Dion’s native Canada were up 20%, followed by searches from the U.S., which increased 15% over 2025.

Marriott, meantime, welcomed Dion fans to the city with a number of activations and special stays. While the hotel chain didn’t reveal exact numbers, they say they also saw a surge in interest for their Paris properties. “[Dion’s] residency, combined with our Marriott Bonvoy partnership, inspired many members to take an extra trip to Paris this year,” says Peggy Roe, Executive Vice President and Chief Customer Officer at Marriott International. “We had the pleasure of delighting our customers with access to their passions, and our hotels benefited, too.”

As the official hotel partner of Celine Dion Paris, Marriott Bonvoy allowed members to bid or redeem points for everything from concert tickets to Dion-themed hotel stays in the city. Marriott property Le Meridien Paris Arc de Triomphe, for example, offered a “Paris, I’m Ready” suite, inspired by Dion’s Eiffel Tower video announcing the show. The suite paid homage to the singer and the city, with Instagram-worthy photo walls, concert artwork, and even a microphone and speaker for a pre- or post-show karaoke session.

Part backstage dressing room and part Parisian sanctuary, Marriott says the room is “the ultimate pre-show retreat,” with guests able to “immerse themselves in a world of elegance, music and Parisian sophistication before stepping out into one of the city’s most exciting cultural moments.” It’s the ideal space for a girls night out (or fans night out) experience to top off your Celine-inspired stay.

You can book the “Paris, I’m Ready” suite at the Le Meridien Paris Arc de Triomphe online now with prices starting from €659. This is a limited-time activation tied to Dion’s string of shows, so we recommend booking ahead to ensure availability.

Marriott also offers rooms at two properties directly across from Plenitude Arena if you’re looking to book a place to stay when Dion returns next year. The singer has confirmed an additional 10 dates scheduled for 2027, beginning in May (find tickets here).

The Renaissance Paris La Defense is just steps from the arena, but the modern, industrial-style property offers a calming, spacious reprieve from the crowds and noise below. And if you do want to be closer to the action, the outdoor courtyard is filled with performers and buskers belting Dion songs on concert nights.

The citizenM Paris La Defense, meantime, offers a colorful and eclectic stay, whether you’re desiring work or play. Marriott’s citizenM brand is known for their art-filled spaces that encourage communal hangs and co-working. Modern touches abound like cozy nooks with plenty of outlets and lush indoor-outdoor spaces for drinks and networking. The citizenM Paris La Defense is just a few blocks away from Plenitude Arena, with metro and train lines to the city just minutes away.

Marriott had rolled out its popular 1-Point Drop moments for Dion’s first run of shows, allowing Bonvoy Members to bid on packages with just one point. Similar to say, a coveted sneaker release, the 1-Point Drop experiences were available on a first-come, first-served basis, to the first Bonvoy members to claim them after they were released online. Marriott has not yet revealed whether more 1-Point Drops will be available for Dion’s new string of concert dates.

For now, members can bid on “Marriott Bonvoy Moments” with their points for premium tickets to see the singer next year, along with stays at the hotel chain’s portfolio of properties across Paris. Current packages start at just 20,000 Bonvoy points as of this writing.

A sample package right now includes a pair of “Salon Premium” tickets to see Dion in May with hospitality access and reserved first-level seating, plus a one-night stay at Renaissance Paris Nobel Tour Eiffel Hotel, located in the city’s 16th Arrondissement near the Eiffel Tower. Similar to any auction, Bonvoy members can bid on the experiences using their points (rather than cash) and the highest bidder at the close of the auction wins the package.

Marriott Bonvoy is free to join, and the hotel loyalty program lets you earn points on Uber rides, Starbucks purchases and everyday dining, in addition to hotel stays.

As for the singer herself? Dion spent her time in Paris staying at the Le Royal Monceau – Raffles Paris in the city’s eighth arrondissement, drawing crowds of onlookers each night as she departed for her shows.

In addition to Dion, the tony hotel has welcomed A-listers from Michael Jackson to Madonna over the years. The Royal Monceau is beloved for being a peaceful sanctuary in the heart of the action without skimping on all the luxury amenities and touches you’d expect from a five-star stay. The hotel is also a hub for Paris’ art and fashion scene, with Philippe Starck-designed interiors and an in-house art gallery that’s become a destination for collectors and visitors alike.

Le Royal Monceau is set to celebrate its 100th anniversary in 2028. After closing for renovations in 2008, the property reopened under the Raffles brand in October 2010.

Dion, meantime, was recently spotted back in her adopted hometown of Las Vegas this month, attending one of Metallica’s shows at the Sphere.

“This beautiful adventure finishes tonight,” Dion said at her last performance in Paris for 2026. “But we’ll meet again next May. In the meantime, believe in yourselves and hold on to your dreams.”

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#3410. Nvidia: Securities Class Action Lawsuit Filed Amid CEO's Affair with Alleged Chinese Spy

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy has now resulted in a securities class action lawsuit against his company ... TMZ has learned.

According to court documents, obtained by TMZ, the tech company allegedly violated federal securities laws by making misleading and false statements in connection with the scandal.

The lawsuit calls into question several statements made by the company in response to multiple news articles about Jensen’s business relationship with Alice Huang -- the Megaspeed exec at the center of the affair story … who some claim is a Chinese spy.

The suit alleges that Jensen and Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo both made statements about the nature of the business relationship with Megaspeed that were misleading or false, claiming Jensen had been having an affair with Alice at the time.

According to the lawsuit, once news broke about the alleged affair, Nvidia stock plummeted, causing “significant losses and damages” to shareholders of the company.

The plaintiffs identified in the class action include anyone who purchased or acquired publicly traded shares of Nvidia between October 9, 2025, and November 8, 2026.

The class action is seeking monetary damages for losses sustained as a result of the allegedly false and misleading statements.

#3407. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

#3406. Judge Sets Steven Tyler Sex Assault Trial Date

The long-running lawsuit accusing Aerosmith frontman Steven Tyler of sexually abusing a minor in the 1970s is headed for a new May 3 trial before its fifth judge, who vowed Monday to see the case through to the end.

At a hearing in downtown Los Angeles, the new judge also said he was prepared to reconsider any rulings made by his predecessor, Judge Patricia Young, who stepped aside in September with just two weeks to go before a prior trial date in the case. Young voluntarily recused herself after disclosing that she had discussed the case with another judge who had previously been disqualified from the case.

On Monday, the new judge, Lawrence Riff, said he would toss out and reconsider any of Young’s rulings “from the beginning of her assignment” if either side requested it. Lawyers for the plaintiff, Julia Misley, said they would challenge a key ruling from earlier this year that gutted her case. The ruling, known as a summary adjudication, dismissed Misley’s claims involving alleged misconduct in Massachusetts, Oregon, and Washington, leaving only those involving California.

“Both parties here are entitled to have the peace of mind at the end of the case that everything was on the up and up and proper, and that there’s no lingering shadow of doubt of possible impropriety,” Riff said, explaining that he would review the earlier rulings based on arguments already submitted to the court, without allowing either side to file new ones.

Riff acknowledged that the additional hearings would increase legal costs for both sides, but he expected to keep the trial date in the first half of next year, regardless. “There will be more hearings, to say the least, but I don’t think it’s going to unduly prolong the pretrial proceedings,” he said.

In her lawsuit filed in December 2022 and first reported by Rolling Stone, Misley claimed that Tyler sexually abused her for years beginning in 1973, when she was a high school sophomore, and he was 25. Tyler denied the claims spanning three years and four states as he asked the court to dismiss the entire lawsuit. Tyler and his lawyers argued that he lived with Misley in Boston for most of their relationship, where the age of consent was 16. He argued that Massachusetts law governed them even when he traveled with Misley, formerly Julia Holcomb, in other states. After multiple hearings, Young rejected Misley’s claims of alleged misconduct in Massachusetts, Oregon, and Washington, saying they fell outside her authority or were filed too late. In asking Riff to reconsider those decisions, Misley’s lawyers are betting they can revive some of the dismissed claims without jeopardizing the rest of their case.

In Massachusetts, for example, Misley and her lawyers had argued that Tyler violated state law while living with Misley in Boston, despite the state’s age of consent being 16. They alleged he broke the law by giving her drugs before sex and by illegally inducing her into the sexual relationship while holding himself out as her legal guardian at the time. Misley said that reading Tyler’s memoir led her to a series of realizations about the trauma she had experienced, giving her grounds to sue despite the statute of limitations. Tyler countered that she had known about the alleged conduct all along and that the deadline to sue had therefore expired.

Before Riff’s ruling on Monday, Tyler’s lead lawyer, David Long-Daniels, argued that the court had no reason to revisit Young’s ruling tossing out the claims from the other three states. He said there was no evidence Young consulted the disqualified judge on that critical ruling. He said the record showed she only consulted the other judge more recently when she was weighing pre-trial rulings related to evidence that would be allowed at trial. “Summary adjudication is really a clear issue: California has no right to try what is happening in Massachusetts, or in Oregon, or in Washington,” Long-Daniels said. “I don’t think there’s any evidence that she had consulted [the disqualified judge] on that.”

But Misley’s lawyers disagreed, saying there was ambiguity in Young’s statements. They said the only way to clear up the issue would be “an extraordinary fact-finding issue.” Riff said court rules prohibited him from discussing the matter with Young unless both sides were present, and he did not want to pursue that option.

Riff set the new trial for May 3 and gave both sides until Nov. 20 to request review of any of Young’s orders. Any request to void one of her orders would be granted, he said, and he would then take it up himself. He expects to hold a new hearing in January on the key ruling that gutted Misley’s case, he said.

Misley’s lawsuit was filed in conjunction with the California Child Victims Act, a 2019 law that temporarily revived otherwise expired claims by giving survivors of childhood sexual abuse a three-year window to sue. The lawsuit said Misley first met Tyler in Portland, Oregon, in 1973, a month after her 16th birthday. She said he had sex with her that night, and that they had sex again in Seattle, at the next stop on his concert tour. The age of consent in Oregon and Washington at the time was 18.

Misley alleges she was groomed into a three-year relationship, during which Tyler also brought her to California for an awards show and dragged her naked onto an elevator so he could have sex with her in a pool, she claimed.

In his 2011 memoir, Does the Noise in My Head Bother You?, Tyler recalled the guardianship arrangement, noting their age difference. “I was so in love, I almost took a teen bride. I went and slept at her parents’ house for a couple of nights, and her parents fell in love with me, signed papers over for me to have custody, so I wouldn’t get arrested if I took her out of state,” he wrote.

Tyler recounted having sex with Misley on a red-eye flight from Los Angeles to Boston. He also described the incident that Misley says took place at the Beverly Hills hotel. In her series of recent pretrial rulings leading up to her recusal, Young said Misley could present evidence to the jury that Tyler “held himself out to be her guardian,” as well as testimony about how she viewed her circumstances at the time. But in a victory for Tyler, Young ruled that jurors could hear evidence Misley had “consented” to the relationship.

Young’s rulings about evidence allowed at trial will be stricken and reconsidered, Judge Riff said Monday.

If one more audio brand releases earbuds/headphones with "AI features", I'm going to scream.

And, as it turns out, so will 98% of Tom's Guide readers. Or, put bluntly, so will you. Of 200 responses, only five readers said they specifically look for AI features in the best earbuds and best headphones. Most readers voted sound quality as their most important feature: 135 people, specifically. ANC came second with twenty-seven votes. Yes, first place received five times as many votes as second place.

This got me thinking: Why? Why do audio brands keep pushing AI features down our throats when we so clearly don't want them? Do said brands worry they'll be "left behind" in the AI race? Do brands consider sound quality, ANC, and call quality last year's news? Or is it something else...? Let's dig in.

I ran a poll for three weeks here on Tom's Guide. I asked, and you all answered! Here are the exact results.

As you can see, sound quality is by far the most important feature for you. ANC came second with 13% of the vote, then call quality and other came joint third with 6% of the vote. Second-to-last we have battery life, 4% of the vote. And, trailing last, we have AI features — with just 2% of the vote.

I could've predicted that sound quality would win, but I was genuinely surprised when I saw AI features lost by that much. I thought it would get more like... maybe 10%. I thought some people really liked having AI in earbuds, but evidently not.

I loved the Anker Soundcore Space One Pro headphones. They were my biggest surprise of 2025 and I ended up recommending them to pretty much everyone. I even got my sister a pair for college! They're the perfect headphones for studying thanks to the incredible ANC, comfort, and foldability.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I feel like Anker put so much effort into AI features, it forgot what the Soundcore Space 2 Pro were: headphones. For music. And ANC. Not glorified chatbot earmuffs.

So when I reviewed the successor, Space 2 Pro, they left me with a sour taste in my mouth. This was especially sour because I wasn't expecting it. I was expecting another Space One Pro: slam-dunk, instant favorite. But it wasn't.

The reason? The AI features. I feel like Anker put so much effort into AI features, it forgot what the Soundcore Space 2 Pro were: headphones. For music. And ANC. Not glorified chatbot earmuffs.

Don't get me wrong, I still awarded the Space 2 Pro 3.5 stars — this means "very good." And the headphones are very good. Sound quality is great, call quality is great, and ANC is great. Triple whammy there... as long as you ignore the purported AI functionality in the Anker app.

Let me set the scene: the Soundcore Space 2 Pro are advertised as having the "world's first neural-net compute-in-memory AI audio chip". If you don't know what that means, you're not alone!

Amanda Caswell, AI Editor here at Tom's Guide, translated this into real terms. "AI-powered audio processing inside that's efficient enough to run continuously on a tiny, battery-powered device.

"So this could help with smarter noise cancellation, voice isolation, always-on listening (to detect words). But "neural-net" is the chip that runs artificial neural networks trained to recognize and process sounds, such as speech, background noise and potentially voice commands."

And there's a lovely chatbot in the Anker Soundcore app! However, Anker's marketing doesn't actually specify that the Space 2 Pro are compatible with the in-app chatbot. Might it be my fault that I assumed the app features would work?

If I connect headphones to my phone, download the companion app, open the companion app, see a big "AI chatbot!" tab that can supposedly adjust my EQ in real-time, I'd assume it works, right?

Take a look at this. These are real screenshots from the Anker app.

When I asked Anker's representative about this, I was told, "Currently, Anka on Space 2 Pro only supports activation via “Hey Anka” and basic voice interactions or chats.

Other features, including voice controls, audio playback and text-based interactions in the app, are still in development, not ready for release."

So why are the features present in the app? I've been in further contact with Anker, which has informed me it is looking into the issue — so that's a win!

But the most frustrating part is this: I don't actually care if headphones or earbuds have (useless to me) AI features or not. I won't mark down audio products for simply including things like Live Translation — if it works, it's actually a huge plus, like with the AirPods Max 2 or Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro.

When I reviewed the Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max, which can accurately transcribe calls and meetings directly to the app, I gave them four stars and our coveted Recommended badge.

So what was different with the Space 2 Pro, then? Same audio brand, same AI features, right?

The Liberty 5 Pro Max's AI features actually worked. If the AI features work, regardless of my personal dislike of AI, I mark it as a positive and go on about my day. I don't write a 2,000-word long-read about the state of AI in earbuds and headphones (...).

The Space 2 Pro sound amazing. They don't need any gimmicky AI features. If Anker had positioned them as straightforward, comfy, great-ANC wireless headphones, they'd have received a 4.5-star rating.

Now let's go to the opposite side of the earbud/headphone coin: the Cambridge Audio Melomania A100 SE.

The Melomania A100 SE came out in October 2026. I loved these earbuds enough to award them four stars and the sought-after "Tom's Guide recommended" badge. The sound quality is supreme, they're comfy, and they have excellent battery life. The only thing holding them back is the mediocre ANC, but if you're not part of that 13% of readers who prioritize ANC, this shouldn't be an issue.

And the best part — they're just $149. At that price point, there's not much competition. Naturally, there's the AirPods 5 at $129/$149 or the Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 at $149, but the Melomania A100 SE are (literally) music to my ears. Pardon the cliché, but I said what I said.

Michael Laws, a product manager from Cambridge Audio, doesn't seem to think the Melomania A100 SE need AI. "We haven’t put resource into implementing AI features, because so far we haven’t found it’s a requirement when listening to your favourite music on the go. That’s not to say we won’t explore further if there prove to be ways in which, for instance, AI can “help” with different listening profiles."

I completely agree. AI is not a requirement at all. There's a reason why wired audio gear is making a comeback. Consumers are literally rejecting AI being forced into every aspect of our lives. Just this year, Sony has relaunched its original Walkman headphones, and Bose is releasing wired earbuds.

I don't think it's a coincidence. I think people are voting with their wallets, and showing audio brands what they really want.

"One thing that always gets commented on is the sound; that’s our bread and butter," said Cambridge Audio's Laws.

For me, too, sound is my bread and butter. I would much rather have earbuds and headphones that make my music sound alive than a chatbot built into the app — that doesn't even work.

I'm not saying these AI features can't be useful. Live Translation would be useful if it worked, but it's too slow to benefit real-time conversations. On top of that. we've coexisted with machine learning since the '70s — autofocus is machine learning. DSPs in various audio products, from mics to earbuds, use machine learning.

But what is new is a generative AI chatbot in my headphones' companion app. And I'm so over it. If this trend continues, I'll switch to Bose's new Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds (whenever they come back in stock).

#3404. Report: Apple’s planned $7 billion bond sale attracts four times as much demand

Apple has filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC outlining plans to issue seven series of bonds. Here are the details.

Over the past week, several Big Tech companies have turned to the bond market to raise billions of dollars amid growing investments in AI infrastructure.

Meta, for instance, just raised $15 billion through a US bond offering, followed by another €9 billion (roughly $10 billion) in European bonds. Earlier this week, Alphabet raised €6 billion (approximately $6.7 billion), while Microsoft completed a $25 billion bond sale last week, its first since 2017.

Apple has also turned to bond sales in the past to raise billions of dollars.

Previous offerings include those in 2015, 2019, 2020, and 2021. Most recently, Apple raised $4.5 billion through a four-part bond offering in May 2025, which attracted approximately $10 billion in investor orders.

Earlier today, Apple filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC outlining plans to issue seven series of bonds maturing between 2028 and 2036.

However, while other Big Tech companies have been borrowing heavily amid growing AI infrastructure investments, Apple’s filing makes no specific mention of AI.

Instead, the company says it intends to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, potentially including stock buybacks, dividends, acquisitions, and debt repayment, as it has done in previous bond offerings.

And while the prospectus didn’t specify how much Apple intends to raise, Bloomberg reported soon after that the company is targeting approximately $7 billion, with investors already placing orders totaling around $31 billion.

According to Bloomberg, strong investor demand has also helped Apple secure more favorable borrowing terms, with investors willing to accept lower interest rates than those offered by Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle in their recent bond sales.

All of this is happening amid a massive tech sell-off, which saw the Nasdaq 100 plunge more than 6% at one point today, with Nvidia shares falling about 8% and the S&P 500 dropping nearly 4%.

Apple’s own stock is also taking a hit, trading down 1.49% at the time of publication, but it is faring better than those of its Big Tech peers, whose stocks have become more closely tied to the AI spending boom.

Be that as it may, Apple is expected to finalize the size and pricing of its bond offering soon, potentially as early as later today, after which the company will file the definitive terms with the SEC.

#3402. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

#3401. Colin Meloy on the Sixteen-Year Journey to ‘Wildwood’

Colin Meloy hadn’t even finished writing Wildwood before movie studios came calling. It was 2010, and HarperCollins had just acquired the Decemberists frontman’s first fantasy novel, which featured illustrations from his wife, the visual artist Carson Ellis. At that point, he’d only completed about a third of the draft. “We were already freaked out about the idea of it being a book,” Meloy says on a recent Zoom call from his home outside of Portland, Oregon. “The idea that it would then also be a movie was daunting, and we really wanted to pump the brakes on that.”

They relayed this concern to director Travis Knight, after the Pacific Northwest studio Laika (fresh off the success of the stop-motion classic Coraline) optioned Wildwood shortly after. “We just imagined that any movie would inevitably eclipse the book,” Meloy says. “So we were like, ‘Please, can it just be a book for a little bit, and then the movie comes out?’ And he was like, ‘Don’t worry about it. It’s going to take a very long time.’”

Knight was right: Wildwood took 16 years to complete. The film is a propulsive journey that stays extremely close to Meloy’s novel — even down to its 500-plus page length. With a 132-minute run time, it’s the longest stop-motion film ever made. “Travis did say it was going to be his masterpiece,” says Meloy, 52. “But I was like, ‘Oh yeah, I’m sure you tell that to everybody.’” He laughs. “It was cool to see him make good on that.”

Wildwood follows Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee), a sassy and strongwilled Portland teenager who is ordered by her parents to stay inside while she babysits her brother. Naturally she disobeys them, and has to go rescue him after he’s taken by a murder of crows. Joined by her schoolmate Curtis (Jacob Tremblay), they venture into the forbidden Impassable Forest, an enchanting yet dangerous world embroiled in a civil war. The film features a vengeful governess (Carey Mulligan), a Bandit King (Mahershala Ali), and an entire kingdom of talking animals (Tom Waits may or may not voice a coyote soldier). Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Wildwood has drawn comparisons to The Lord of the Rings, The Chronicles of Narnia, and other epics — which isn’t surprising, considering that’s the kind of reading that most interested Meloy while growing up in Helena, Montana. “I was a very bookish kid,” he says. “I just would just absorb books, particularly from fifth grade to eighth grade.” He cites Ray Bradbury, Lloyd Alexander, Ursula K. Le Guin, and Stephen King as his favorites. “Those books and those ideas informed Wildwood,” he says. “You want to write the book that you would’ve wanted to read as a kid.”

The idea for Wildwood was born more than 25 years ago, when Meloy and Ellis were living in a warehouse in Southeast Portland around 2000. The two had met at the University of Montana — Meloy was studying creative writing, while Ellis was in the art department — and bonded over their love of folklore. They were working service-industry jobs, and Meloy (who wouldn’t release his first album with the Decemberists for another couple of years) was playing open mics, and they got the idea to collaborate on a fantasy novel. “Honestly, it was a pastime, something to do [so] that we could hang out together,” he says. “I would write, and she would draw.”

The quirky spirit of Portland is felt all over Wildwood, particularly in the beginning of the film (pre-crow-kidnapping). We see the wonderfully weird city in its 2010s glory, featuring staples like Powell’s Books, Voodoo Doughnut, and specialty coffee shops, as well as a cameo from one of Fred Armisen’s Portlandia characters, Spyke the cyclist. “There was this rising tide happening in Portland at that time, and the Decemberists were certainly part of that,” Meloy says. “It’s interesting to come back 16 years later, where that tide has definitely ebbed. Recovering from Covid and stuff, it’s been having a hard time. So it’s cool to give the celebration of the city to the world.” Related Content The Dream of the Nineties Animation Boom Is Alive in ‘Wildwood’ See the Decemberists Showcase New Album Tracks for 'Saturday Sessions' The Decemberists Announce First Album in Six Years, Drop 19-Minute Song Social Distancing With Colin Meloy of the Decemberists: 'Astral Weeks,' Sourdough Starters and Dread

Meloy and Ellis get their own cameos, too: He’s seen busking on the street, while Ellis is shown selling her artwork. Meloy says Laika tried to keep it a secret, but he eventually put it together during one of several visits to the studio. “Every once in a while somebody would let it slip,” he says. “They would be like, ‘Hey, I animated you today!’ and I’d be like, ‘What are you talking about?’” Meloy says even Prue McKeel is named after a real 12-year-old. “We actually just did a friends and family screening of the film here in Portland, and there were a couple McKeels there,” Meloy says. “I’m like, ‘I’m so sorry! I just stole your name and gave it to the main character!’”

Meloy wrote several new songs for the film, and sings the triumphant end credit anthem “The Better Part of Bravery,” which he admits was a challenge. He wrote a first attempt in 2023, but Knight said it wasn’t quite right. “I’m not used to taking notes for songs,” Meloy jokes. “And also, there was a certain bit like, ‘I think I nailed the thesis of the story, having been the guy who wrote it.’ But Travis was very thoughtful and coddled my ego a little bit.”

Plus, Meloy adds, he hadn’t seen the film yet. Closer to deadline, he introduced his and Ellis’ 13-year-old son to the 1986 fantasy film Highlander, and he found himself reading about the soundtrack afterwards. “I was doing some Wikipedia-ing, as you do, and learned that Brian May from Queen only wrote the classic ‘Who Wants to Live Forever?’ after he’d seen the film,” he says. “This light bulb went off.” He watched an early cut of the film, and wrote “The Better Part of Bravery” within a few days. “I have Brian May to thank for that song,” he says.

Next spring will mark the 25th anniversary of the Decemberists’ debut, Castaways and Cutouts. And though they’ve performed the album in its entirety before, Meloy isn’t particularly interested in any kind of anniversary tour. “I feel like I’ve been resistant to that over the years just for my own sanity,” he says. “We still play a lot of those songs. Aside from the fact that you feel like, ‘Oh, now we’re just going out there and retreading old work,’ it’s more just me needing variety on tour that I would be resistant to that. But we’ve done it, and I could definitely see us doing it again.”

As far as new Decemberists music goes, though, a follow-up to 2024’s As It Ever Was, So It Will Be Again won’t be coming anytime soon. He has several new book projects on the way, including the novel Casadia and a pair of Arthurian books — Mordred Rex and Kestrel Magus — that make up the Heir to Magic duology. “I am squarely in book world,” he says. “It’s my happy place. I’m not really drawn to writing songs right now. I think I’m just following my natural path. It was super fun to write those songs for Wildwood, and if that sort of thing came up — writing songs for other people or other projects… But writing for myself and for the Decemberists right now, it’s just not where my heart is. So it’s sitting on the back burner for now.” Trending Stories Watch Ariana Grande, Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro Take Over ‘The Tonight Show’ Trump Finally Gets Around to Claiming the Midterms Were Rigged Fall Out Boy Announce Biggest Tour Yet — and New Single ‘Aces’ Oasis Won’t Be Attending Rock and Roll of Fame Induction Ceremony

There is, however, the possibility that Laika will adapt the other installments in the Wildwood trilogy: Under Wildwood (2012) and Wildwood Imperium (2014). “I would love it, [but] I have no idea if that will happen,” Meloy says. “If it was any other studio, maybe. But these movies are so labor-intensive, so long. I get it if they want to be like, ‘We did that.’ If they were banging out a movie a year kind of thing, it would probably be a totally different story.”

Either way, Meloy knows waiting 16 years for his characters to come to life on the big screen was definitely worth it. “One of the great things about making this movie happen at Laika is this tremendous pride, that I had some part in employing these legions of people with these very specific and super cool niche skillsets,” he says. “Making tiny clothes or machining armatures, and the patience to film two seconds over the course of a couple weeks… It’s been a real boon to the Portland creative community. I’m thrilled.”

#3399. Walmart Will Have Three Major Shopping Events This Holiday Season

If you're thinking of picking up any big-ticket items soon—whether for yourself or as a gift for someone on your list— I would advise you to wait until you see what retailers have in store for the holiday sales season, which will kick off in earnest in mid-November. Walmart is the first major retailer to announce its Black Friday and Cyber Monday plan for 2026, and they actually involve three major shopping events between now and the December holidays.

As it did in 2025, Walmart will hold three sales between Nov. 12 and Dec. 2, as outlined in a recent press release. The sales will be both online and in-store, and will target a mix of Walmart+ members and general shoppers.

The events will take place on three different dates:

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 1: Nov. 12–15

Available online and in stores starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access beginning online at 12:01 a.m. ET on November 12

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 2: Nov. 23–29

Online only: Nov. 23 starting at 12:01 a.m. ET

Online and in stores: Nov. 27 starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access online beginning Nov. 23 at 12:01 a.m. ET

Walmart's Cyber Monday Deals Event: Nov. 30-Dec. 2

Walmart says that you can expect discounts on electronics, toys, fashion, beauty, home goods, gifts, and everyday essentials. Although the company doesn't provide much in the way of specifics in its press release, last year's sales included discounts on TCL TVs, Dyson vacuums, Dreo appliances, and toys from LEGO.

Walmart already has plenty of good deals out early. You don't need to wait for the official sale to start to find some products going for their lowest prices ever. Here are some of the best ones I've found so far:

The holiday season will see major sales from the same list of retailers that compete for your dollars throughout the year—namely, Best Buy, Target, and Amazon. Each will have its own version of Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales. So far, only Walmart has revealed its plans.

In short, yes. Though they aren't quite as impactful as they once were, Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales offer discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Whether it's a major purchase you've been saving up for or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts, especially on items like appliances and electronics. Last year's sales included categories such as tech, home improvement, and fitness.

Black Friday used to be when major retailers offered their best deals on expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Now, however, the distinction is almost meaningless: Every major retailer offers sales on both days, which means the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers to monitor the deals, and refer to our Black Friday coverage, where we do all the searching, curating, and price tracking for you.

#3393. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

Nothing brightens a home quite like a vibrant bunch of hydrangeas. With their colorful blooms and distinctive cone-shaped clusters, it can be disappointing to watch them droop and lose their hue.

But what does it mean when those beautiful flowers start turning green?

I called on a gardening expert to reveal the reasons why your hydrangeas are fading to green — and top tips to help your blooms last longer throughout the season.

So if hydrangeas are known for their vibrant blooms, what's causing them to (surprisingly) turn green?

"As many hydrangea blooms mature, they naturally develop green tones,” states Paul Parker, plants and bulbs specialist at J. Parker’s. “This is part of the normal ageing process and often adds interest late in the season, particularly in autumn arrangements.

“Green tones are a natural stage in the life cycle of many hydrangea blooms, although the timing and extent of this colour change can vary depending on the variety and growing conditions.”

Harsh temperatures can often take their toll on your plants, and so you’ll need to safeguard hydrangeas against cold and frost ahead of time.

“To safeguard your hydrangeas from harsh weather, apply a layer of organic mulch around their base,” advises Parker.

“This will help retain moisture, provide some protection against cold temperatures, and suppress weeds. Organic mulches include composted bark, woodchip, straw, or leaves. These materials decompose over time, adding extra nutrients to the soil.”

Additionally, you’ll need to protect plants from heavy snowfall. “After a period of heavy snow, gently brush excess snow from branches using a broom to reduce the risk of damage caused by its weight, particularly during prolonged periods of bad winter weather."

Other top tips include removing damaged or diseased stems to keep your plants healthy all season. And it's recommended to leave faded flower heads intact through winter. This can help protect developing buds for spring, while adding seasonal texture in the garden.
